item.title: Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Albania's youth are protesting, not leaving the country anymore

November 26, 2026

Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.

In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.

For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.

It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.

'Flamingo revolution' has broad support

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.

Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

Alternating between Socialist and Democratic Party

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."

Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."

It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."

The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.

Protesters call out corruption, face high cost of living

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.…

Source: DW Top Stories | Published: 2026-11-26 20:44 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility

Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.

The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.

Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".

Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.

It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.

Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.

The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

Iranian-backed militias in the region have also carried out attacks on the US's Gulf allies.

On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.

Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.

Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.

Meanwhile, Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement: "An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working."

The two Italian nationals were working at an air defence detection station and performing maintenance work on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa, citing Italy's foreign ministry.

Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.

"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.

"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

Source: BBC World | Published: 2026-11-26 20:35 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39w9y5dx4k5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

item.title: Attack on Saudi’s Jazan refinery kills one person, disrupts operations
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Attack on Saudi’s Jazan refinery kills one person, disrupts operations

The attack killed a Nepali national, injured several people and sparked a fire, Saudi Energy Ministry says.

An aerial projectile has hit an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s city of Jazan, killing one worker and injuring several other people, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy.

Thursday’s attack on the facility on the kingdom’s Red Sea coast caused a fire and temporarily halted some operations, the ministry said.

The statement did not identify who carried out the strike, but earlier the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said that the Iranian-backed group had attacked the refinery. It came after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency had issued an alert about potential danger in Jazan province.

The strike was the Houthis‘ latest blow against key Saudi facilities, a day after the group claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom’s largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, amid escalating hostilities between the two sides.

The Saudi Ministry of Energy said the worker who died was Nepali, while the injured were of various nationalities.

The injured received medical care, while emergency personnel and specialised technical teams arrived at the site to assess the damage and verify the safety of the facilities following the attack, the ministry added.

The refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the Yemeni border, is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.

The Saudi-led coalition, which is backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its fight with the Houthis, condemned the strike and threatened a counterattack.

“Targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure would be met with a firm military ‌‌response,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki posted on X.

Later on Thursday, the coalition claimed its forces had destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launch platform in Yemen’s Hodeidah governorate used by the armed group to stage the attack on the Jazan refinery, according to al-Maliki. There was no immediate statement from the Houthis regarding the strike.

Fighting in Yemen

On the ground in Yemen, meanwhile, Saudi-backed government forces claimed they had carried out 767 strikes on Houthi positions on Thursday.

In a post on X, the forces’ spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the strikes had “neutralised” 117 Houthi fighters and destroyed 87 vehicles and combat assets.

Al-Nuzaili added that government forces continued to confront Houthi formations on the front lines in northern and western Marib governorate, as well as in the governorates of al-Jawf, Taiz, Lahj, Shabwah and Hajjah.

Earlier on Thursday, a series of air strikes targeted Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, according to media affiliated with the armed group, which is also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God.

Elsewhere, Houthi forces targeted Habib al-Sarm and al-Hujalla, as well as al-Aqroud in al-Masrakh district.

The Houthis, who control the most populous areas of Yemen, have launched missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings since the country’s civil war reignited in July, in a spillover from the US-Iran war.

The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco’s operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including football’s AFC Asian Cup and the flagship FII investment conference.

The fighting has also exacerbated dire humanitarian conditions for Yemeni civilians.

The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that as of Monday, 2,361 people had been killed and 10,982 injured since fighting in Yemen escalated in August. More than 360,000 people have also been forced to flee their homes in Yemen since the start of August, according to the UN.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-26 20:34 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Mexico seeks US talks about suspected SpaceX debris
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Mexico seeks US talks about suspected SpaceX debris

Mexico concerned as SpaceX ramps up rocket launches from Starbase near border in Texas.

The Mexican government is seeking talks with aviation authorities in the United States about falling rocket debris following SpaceX launches in Texas.

It is the latest sign of growing tensions between Mexico City and Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar company.

“What we are seeking, through the embassy, is a meeting between US and Mexican airspace authorities so that permission for the use of Mexican airspace can be established, how often it would be used, and, if necessary, the relocation of the launch site,” Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Thursday at a news conference in the capital.

“And then there’s the issue of the debris,” she added.

Earlier this month, Mexican authorities said they had to recover debris after a launch of a SpaceX Starship from its Starbase,Texas, facility near the Gulf of Mexico and nature reserves on both sides of the shared border.

Debris that officials said came from the launch washed ashore along Playa Bagdad in Matamoros in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas, according to PROFEPA, Mexico’s Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection.

It said it had collected material several days after part of the Starship was destroyed and fell into the sea. The debris was taken by the Mexican navy to be stored and PROFEPA said it would ask SpaceX to take possession of it.

SpaceX said it was working with Mexican authorities and disputed the claim that what was found was from its failed Starship launch.

“We continue to stay in contact with the Mexican government and are on standby to send support if authorities in Mexico tell us it is actually needed,” the company posted on X. “Partners on the ground relayed that they have found very little debris in their sweeps of the beach and the small amount they have found is not clearly from SpaceX operations.”

Musk’s SpaceX is seeking permission from the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to dramatically increase activity at the Starbase facility. Previously, the company was allowed 25 launches and 50 landings a year, but now it is seeking permission for 456 launches and 912 landings annually.

Earlier this week, the US Federal Communications Commission granted SpaceX permission to send up to one million satellites into space as part of Musk’s plans to develop data centres in orbit.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-26 20:31 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/mexico-seeks-us-talks-about-suspected-spacex-debris?traffic_source=rss

item.title: Gerard Depardieu to stand trial in France for rape and sexual assault
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Gerard Depardieu to stand trial in France for rape and sexual assault

The Paris Court of Appeal upheld the order for the 77-year-old French actor to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in 2018.

French actor Gerard Depardieu failed in his attempt to overturn an order for him to stand trial on rape charges.

On Thursday, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that Depardieu should face trial for the alleged rape and sexual assault that occurred on August 7, 2018. However, the court dismissed the allegations relating to a second incident that occurred six days later.

Depardieu still has the option of appealing to a higher court. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told the Associated Press that she disputes Thursday's ruling, though she did not specify whether she will challenge it in France's highest civil and criminal court.

This decision comes just two weeks after the 77-year-old Depardieu dropped his appeal against a sexual assault conviction in a separate case. He accepted an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issued a public apology.

What are the charges against Depardieu?

An actress, who was 22 years old at the time, accused Depardieu of raping and sexually assaulting her at his Paris apartment on August 7 and 13, 2018. Depardieu was 69 at the time of the alleged incident.

She reported the allegations to the police a few days later. Depardieu denies the allegations, claiming that the encounter was consensual.

Last year, a trial was ordered regarding the allegations. If the trial goes ahead, Depardieu could face up to 20 years in prison.

Carine Durrieu Diebolt, the victim's lawyer, said that the Thursday decision was a genuine relief and a victory for her client.

Accusations overshadow Depardieu's legacy

Depardieu was born in 1948 into a working-class family in Chateauroux, a city in central France. He overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors.

The film star was a dominant figure in French cinema for half a century, becoming a renowned cultural export. He earned an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."

Accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction, however, have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

The international media has also been paying attention to Depardieu's off-screen antics. One of the most notable instances was when he accepted a Russian passport from President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

Source: DW Top Stories | Published: 2026-11-26 20:41 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

President Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."

Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate. That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.

That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post, suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and even multiple governorships.

"I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.

However, the difference between the advance estimate and the figure in the second release is far from being an all-time record. It was the largest revision since the 1.2 percentage point revision seen in the second quarter of 2020.

On an absolute basis, the latest revision was tied for 16th among all revisions from the advance estimate to the second release since 1990. It also tied four other quarters with a similar 0.9 percentage point difference — and was approximately double the average revision of 0.43 percentage points for all 147 quarters.

The upward revision shows Trump's policies are "delivering results" that defy expectations, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC.

Nothing new

Revisions to U.S. economic numbers are not necessarily out of the ordinary. Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. Those data are later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.

GDP data is revised repeatedly over a five year period. By the time the final revision is done, the average absolute error from the second release to the final is 1.14 percentage points.

The advance estimate for Q3 U.S. GDP, which came just days before Election Day in early November, was still better than the figure economists had expected at the time. It also showed a significant step-up in growth from the second quarter.

Because that was a strong showing for the economy, some on Wall Street consider this week's revision to be a confirmation of the economy's recent growth trend.

Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors said immediately following the release that it "reinforces an increasingly familiar tension" that the economy is "performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."

"The economy isn't merely hanging in there. It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," the firm's chief investment officer said.

Traders are currently pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December meeting, per the CME FedWatch tool. They're also anticipating an additional hike in January.

— CNBC's Jeff Cox and Fred Imbert contributed reporting

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-26 20:25 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/26/trump-gdp-revision-investigation.html

item.title: Guinea-Bissau junta delays presidential vote for 2 years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Guinea-Bissau junta delays presidential vote for 2 years

November 26, 2026

The decision came exactly one year after the military took power on November 26, 2025. The junta said the conditions were insufficient to hold presidential elections for now.

The ruling junta in the West African nation of Guinea-Bissau announced Thursday that it is postponing elections by two years until November 26, 2028.

What do we know so far?

The decision came on the 1-year anniversary of the military takeover in Guinea-Bissau on November 26, 2025. The country is currently led by military general Horta Inta-a, who serves as transitional president.

Inta-a said in a statement that there was "an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the election.

"It is essential to guarantee effective conditions for preparing and holding elections in accordance with the principles of legality, democratic participation, equal opportunity, transparency and electoral integrity," he said.

The military coup in Guinea-Bissau came three days after a general election last year, with the military deposing incumbent President Umaro Sissoco Embalo. Both Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias da Costa claimed victory in the election, with the military arresting Embalo one day prior to the results being released.

What's the political and human rights situation in Guinea-Bissau?

West African bloc ECOWAS has urged Guinea-Bissau to transition back to civilian rule.

Guinea-Bissau is a small tropical Portuguese-speaking nation on the West African coast which has seen multiple coups in its history. The country faces a high level of corruption and is also a key point for cocaine trafficking to Europe.

According to Washington DC-based think tank Freedom House, Guinea-Bissau is only "partly free" due to military interference in elections.

Reporters without Borders ranksGuinea-Bissau 100 out of 180 countries on its press freedom index, saying the "sharp deterioration of security for media professionals, combined with political and economic pressure, has severely tested the practice of journalism in recent years."

item.title: JWST studies a tiny, metal-poor galaxy with just a fraction of the sun's oxygen abundance
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

November 26, 2026 report

JWST studies a tiny, metal-poor galaxy with just a fraction of the sun's oxygen abundance

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have studied one of the most metal-poor galaxies known. Seen as it was around 12.2 billion years ago, LAP2 is a tiny system with a stellar mass comparable to that of a massive star cluster. The research paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Nov. 3.

Poor in metals

Early galaxies have very little metal, and over time they build up metals. Observations show that a galaxy's metal content is linked to its mass in stars—a relationship known as the mass-metallicity relation.

JWST is now spotting a class of galaxies in the first billion years of the universe, called extremely metal-poor galaxies (EMPGs). These galaxies have only a few percent of the sun's metals or less, and they serve as natural laboratories to trace the earliest stages of star formation and galaxy evolution.

Astronomers have noticed that some of these early galaxies are more metal-poor than local relations predict. A few approach the regime of 'metal-free' systems made of pristine gas with only hydrogen and helium and no heavier elements. They offer conditions expected for Population III stars, the first stars to have formed in the universe from pristine gas. The gas lit up by such stars is predicted to show very weak oxygen lines and strong helium (He II) emission.

These galaxies are, however, very faint and Population III stars are short-lived, making them rare and hard to spot. Many of the best candidates are therefore seen through gravitational lensing. That's when the light from a distant object is magnified by a massive foreground object.

Oxygenless candidate

LAP2 was first identified in MUSE observations in 2021. It is a very faint galaxy, but is strongly magnified, roughly 50 times, by a foreground galaxy cluster called Abell 2744. This allows astronomers to examine its structure and chemical composition. When they first looked at it with the JWST, they detected no sign of oxygen at all. But that first look only covered a small part of the galaxy, so they were not so sure of the result.

In this new study, astronomers led by Matteo Messa of the INAF Astrophysics and Space Science Observatory of Bologna revisit LAP2 with JWST's NIRSpec integral field spectroscopy, which captures both lensed images in full.

The team found no oxygen signal in the new full-galaxy data. The method for turning line strength into an oxygen amount has never been used at such low levels, so the numbers are extrapolations and carry real uncertainty. Even then, LAP2 was found to have less than about 0.5% of the sun's oxygen. This placed it among the lowest ever measured but still above the expected levels for Population III star formation.

"The non-detection of [O iii]λ5007 in the integrated spectrum confirms LAP2 as an oxygen-deficient system…" as first suggested by the previous study, the team writes in the paper. The team says its light is consistent with a very metal-poor star, possibly mixed with some pristine gas.

Varying chemistry

The faint oxygen appeared only from the small, dense core, whereas the rest of the galaxy showed no signal. There may be two reasons for this. First, the harsh conditions of the dense core may simply make its oxygen glow brighter, even if the core has the same oxygen as the rest of the galaxy. Alternatively, the core probably made its own oxygen. This requires only 0.2 solar masses of oxygen produced by exploding stars.

By modeling the galaxy's colors and emission lines using the NIRCam imaging and spectrum, the team estimated the galaxy's stellar mass. It turned out to be around 80,000 solar masses, which is comparable to that of massive star clusters found in the local and distant universe.

"LAP2 is among the most metal-poor galaxies known to date and one of the few with a stellar mass comparable to that of individual star clusters," the team writes.

Colors combined with emission lines revealed the best-fit age of the stars to be around 7 million years. It also appeared to be undergoing a recent, dust-free burst of star formation.

Fairly empty region

A quick look at its surroundings showed that LAP2 sits in a fairly empty region with a few neighbors. LAP2 lies between two groups of galaxies. The team says that isolation like this protects gas from being polluted by nearby galaxies' winds. "This lets pockets of nearly pristine gas survive well after reionization, as predicted by models of late Pop III star formation," the team explains.

This isolation supports LAP2 as a site of pristine star formation at a redshift of 4, around 1.5 billion years after the Big Bang. The team notes that the galaxy catalog is uneven, so a proper measure of its isolation was not possible.

Although its chemistry varies across the galaxy, LAP2 is still extremely low in oxygen, which makes it one of the purest regions among such galaxies. The team says that with new diagnostics and spectroscopic follow-ups, the number of extremely metal-poor galaxy candidates is expected to grow, which would open an even wider window into early-universe star formation and galaxy evolution.

item.title: Inside the Hot Wheels Design Center
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Excerpted from HOT WHEELS: THE CREATIVE DRIVE: Imagination and Innovation at the Hot Wheels Design Center by Dan Bova and Freddie Holmes. HOT WHEELS™ and associated trademarks and trade dress are owned by Mattel. Reprinted by permission of Mattel Press.

Inside the Hot Wheels Design Center

“Those are some Hot Wheels!”

State-of-the-art car garage. Museum. Mad scientist’s lab. Stuntworks. The most incredible toy store on Earth—Mattel’s Handler Team Center, the company’s design hub tucked away on a nondescript stretch of road in El Segundo, California—is all these things and more.

From a giant mural, Mattel’s cofounders, Elliot and Ruth Handler, smile down on the building’s front lobby, where life-size Hot Wheels vehicles appear poised for action, and wall art displays iconic Mattel playsets and characters from the company’s inception through the present day. Down at the very far end of the lobby, the Epic Loop screams for attention. It is an eleven-foot-tall Hot Wheels duo racetrack with side-by-side loops. Visitors are encouraged to re-create a game played by millions of young Hot Wheels fans by climbing a flight of stairs and sending a die-cast car of their choice down the competing tracks in a race to launch their car into a bucket that marks the finish line.

There’s speed (the cars reach what would equate to 297 mph at full scale), experimentation (do you go with a weightier or sleeker car?), and crashes. Lots of crashes.

The message is clear: This place is a temple of wild design and outrageous fun.

Push deeper into the 200,000-square-foot building (which once housed an aerospace company), and you arrive at the beating heart of the world’s most famous brand on four wheels: the Hot Wheels Design Center.

Every inch of this place is filled with reminders of Hot Wheels’ storied past, as well as the schematics and prototypes that map out its high-tech future.

Oh, and there are toy cars. Everywhere. Toy cars on tables, toy cars in pristine display cases fit for the Louvre, smashed-up toy cars piled in cluttered cubicles. It’s every kid’s and every collector’s dream come true—as well as a dream come true for the people working inside these walls.

“We Start Wild”

The Hot Wheels die-cast design team sits together in a ring, their cubicles surrounding long tables that serve as a communal space for collaboration, display, tinkering, and sharing the occasional Friday morning donut.

Black light-blocking hoods arch over each cubicle, giving them the feeling of a custom car garage or the messiest kid’s bedroom ever. Within the cubicles, toy cars in every stage of design are piled up against keyboards, and the interior cube walls are plastered with pinned-up artwork, schematics, and toy racks.

Underneath one of these hoods sits Dwayne Vance, a longtime Hot Wheels designer who is now manager of product design and steers the visual direction of every graphic in die-cast for Hot Wheels. Vance has worked for other huge brands like DC Comics, EA Games, and Texaco, and his passion for art and automotive extends well beyond the walls of this place, from his creation and curation of art shows to his own book series, Masters of Chicken Scratch, devoted to futuristic and fantasy hot-rod artwork and designs.

An oversize rendering he created in the early 2000s of the Hot Wheels classic car Bone Shaker, with the word Attitude boldly emblazoned across the top, hangs over his work area. Unlike many of his fellow designers, Vance’s cubicle is neatly arranged and organized. “It helps me creatively to sit down in a nice clean space,” he says. Some of his favorite cars fill his shelves, as does his Matty Award.

Every designer has particular strengths, so when Hot Wheels decided it was time to breathe new life into the Custom Camaro, Vance was part of a small group of designers tasked with cooking up new concepts. “We wanted a licensed vehicle but with an extreme custom,” says Staff Product Designer Fraser Campbell. “Knowing Dwayne’s work, I knew he’d create something wild.”

As pens hit paper in a flurry of ideas, the designers soon faced a challenge not uncommon for Hot Wheels: the ticking clock. Campbell explains that when putting together a year’s lineup for initial concept review (ICR), where the cars get evaluated and refined to ensure a good overall mix before things move along to production, the designers need to fill in any perceived gaps—quickly.

“Several of us designers were going to be working on the Camaro, but the other guys got so busy that it was up to me to finish the project,” says Vance. “So, I was like, ‘Okay, cool!’ I got to spend maybe two weeks on the design—it wasn’t a lot. One thing we don’t have here is the luxury of time.”

But just like race car drivers behind the wheels of the cars they’re inspired by, Hot Wheels designers thrive under pressure.

Getting in Gear

Vance began where he always begins—sketching. “I usually just go straight to Photoshop. I have a monitor on my desk, and I actually sketch right on the monitor,” he explains. But the motor muse can strike at any time and any place, and in the case of this redesign, it hit Vance at thirty thousand feet.

“I was on a plane and pulled out my sketchbook and put down some initial ideas,” he says. He typically has a sketchbook within reach, but any piece of paper will do. “Sometimes I’ll draw a little piece of a car on a sticky note,” he says.

Whenever the muse speaks, he listens—and gives it a soundtrack with the help of a little music and his headphones. “I listen to a lot of deep house when I’m drawing in my cube,” he says. “It’s got good energy and is easy to draw to.”…

item.title: Wave-like displays in animal groups may have evolved to deceive predators
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Wave-like displays in animal groups may have evolved to deceive predators

Some of the most striking patterns in collective behavior emerge in the face of danger. When a predator approaches, some animal groups morph into a vision of pulsing waves. These patterns might be more than a side effect of group living; they could have evolved as a form of deception, argue Dr. Eduardo Sampaio and professor Iain Couzin of the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior (MPI-AB) and the University of Konstanz in a Perspectives piece published in Science.

For example, when a peregrine falcon attacks European starlings, dark bands sweep through the flock roughly every three-quarters of a second. In the sulfur-rich springs of Mexico, mollies in dense schools repeatedly dive and resurface, creating waves of motion that fend off predators. Giant honeybees shimmer their abdomens, propagating waves across the nest that drive away hornets.

"We propose that these collective displays exploit how predators see motion, confusing or misleading them," says Sampaio, who is a postdoctoral researcher at MPI-AB.

Nature abounds in collective animal motion, like flocking, schooling and swarming. Yet few studies have ever looked at these group patterns from the outside, through the eyes of a predator. The authors draw together disparate examples—starling murmurations, fish waves, honeybee shimmering—and present the common effect that those patterns can have on the eyes watching them.

In each case, the wave pattern travels faster than the animals producing it, repeats and often anticipates the strike of a predator. The trick is not limited to groups of prey: a hunting cuttlefish sends similar moving stripes down its own body, which may hide its approach from crabs.

"These systems might look different on the surface, but in each one we see the same decoupling of the collective pattern from the motion of the body, or bodies, that generate it," says Couzin, who is a director of collective behavior at MPI-AB and a professor at the University of Konstanz.

These collective waves may exploit the limits of how motion can be processed in the brain. By misleading biological vision, the pattern generators have better chances of survival. And this, the authors say, opens the door to natural selection. They outline how natural selection can act on individual-level rules, like how sensitive each animal is to its neighbors or its response threshold. These are heritable traits. How they vary can alter the effect on the predator, and therefore each individual's survival.

The next challenge is to test these ideas experimentally. Do these patterns simply happen to impair predators—in other words, are they just a lucky side effect—or did they evolve because they do? New experimental tools now make it possible to find out.

Computer models of animal vision, virtual reality and neural recordings allow researchers to test which features of the display actually affect predators. For example, the timing and coordination of collective responses can be adjusted while group size and density are kept constant. "Such experiments could reveal whether the timing of collective waves deters or deceives predators more effectively than fleeing alone does," says Sampaio.

Publication details

item.title: Runaway pulsar escapes the remnant of its own supernova
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

November 26, 2026 feature

Runaway pulsar escapes the remnant of its own supernova

A team of astronomers has spotted a rare example of a pulsar that has escaped the cloud of debris left by the supernova explosion in which it formed. Led by Rohit Dokara, formerly at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy, the team made the discovery by chance, adding to just a handful of similar known cases.

The team's discovery suggests that many similar observations could soon be made with new generations of radio telescopes: perhaps helping astronomers to solve unanswered questions surrounding the origins of fast-moving pulsars and the surprising sparsity of supernova remnants within the galaxy.

Their results have been accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics and are currently available on the arXiv preprint server.

Missing pulsars

A pulsar is a highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star that emits powerful beams of radiation from each of its poles. If one of these beams happens to point in Earth's direction, it will appear to astronomers as an intense electromagnetic flash pulsing with striking regularity, much like the beam from a lighthouse.

These strange bodies form when the cores of massive stars collapse in supernova explosions, which also blast out immense clouds of gas and dust called supernova remnants (SNRs). Each cloud forms a rapidly expanding shell, which thins out and dissipates into interstellar space within around 100,000 years.

Yet for reasons astronomers are still working to fully understand, the pulsar itself will often receive a powerful kick during the initial explosion, propelling it away from the center of the expanding cloud. As it plows through the surrounding gas, it can leave behind a comet-like tail.

In some rare cases, this kick is particularly extreme. "As far as I know, there are four cases where, after a core-collapse supernova explosion, a pulsar has formed moving faster than the diffuse ejecta that eventually becomes a shell," Dokara explains. "Such cases offer unique views of some of the fastest compact objects in our galaxy."

Alongside the mystery of these kicks, there are also unanswered questions surrounding the abundance of SNRs within the galaxy. Astronomers estimate that roughly 2,000 SNRs should exist in the Milky Way—but to date, only around 400 have ever been discovered.

Combined surveys

In their study, Dokara's team initially aimed to investigate this discrepancy using combined observations from several large-scale radio surveys, carried out by radio telescopes around the world over the past two decades and across a broad range of frequencies. These surveys capture radio waves created by electrons spiraling through magnetic fields within an SNR's expanding shell and can also reveal pulsars and their tails.

Combined with existing timing measurements of pulsars, this data allowed the astronomers to calculate three key factors for any pulsar–SNR pair. First, by measuring the rate at which the pulsar's spin is slowing down (as determined by precisely timing its pulses), they could roughly calculate its age. Second, by measuring the angular separation between the pulsar and the center of the shell in the radio images, they could work out how far apart the two appear on the sky.

Finally, they accounted for how lower-frequency radio waves are slowed down more by free electrons in their path—which are thinly spread through interstellar space. By measuring the delay in arrival time between radio waves with higher and lower frequencies, the team could estimate the pulsar's distance from Earth and, by extension, the SNR's.

From these three factors, Dokara's team could estimate both the pulsar's velocity and the SNR's size and evolutionary state—indicating where it lies along its transformation from the initial supernova to a fully dissipated cloud.

Chance discovery

While combing through the data, Dokara uncovered an association that had previously gone unnoticed. "By chance, I found a new supernova remnant shell and a known pulsar to be well outside this shell, but with its tail very clearly pointing to the center of the shell," he says. "We estimated its transverse velocity to be over 1,400 kilometers per second (870 miles per second), making it one of the largest values for Milky Way pulsars."

Since the new shell and the pulsar's tail were first spotted in images from MeerKAT—one of the latest generation of radio telescopes—the discovery holds promising implications for the observational abilities of newer facilities. With their improved sensitivity and resolution, the team now hopes that similar observations could appear regularly in future large-scale surveys.

"The science potential for each such survey is enormous, and this work is just one small example of combining data from such surveys using standard methods to discover and identify rare associations," Dokara adds.

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-26 18:50 UTC

item.title: Second court defeat for Trump's deep-sea mining ambitions
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Second court defeat for Trump's deep-sea mining ambitions

The Trump administration's plans to begin deep-sea mining in the Pacific have hit a second legal setback after a federal judge ruled plans to lease areas of sea-floor off the Northern Mariana Islands violated the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The court's decision follows a similar ruling over a proposed lease sale off American Samoa.

Opposition groups who lodged the Northern Mariana Islands lawsuit said they were concerned deep-sea mining could cause long-term damage to the ocean ecosystem.

The US government has said it wants to start deep-sea mining to enable access to critical minerals and to counter China's growing influence over crucial components needed for electronics.

The administration had planned to put up for sale leases for the Northern Mariana Islands on 16 December 2026.

It is not clear what will happen next as the administration chose not to recognise the first court ruling and went ahead with the sale of two leases covering 13 million hectares (more than 30 million acres) off American Samoa.

Opponents have vowed to challenge that sale.

Ruling on the Northern Mariana Islands case, District judge Jill Aiko Otake said the defendants, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), which provided the expert opinion behind the lease sales, and Howard Lutnick, who was named in his capacity as head of the department that oversees the agency, had failed to consider the potential effects that could follow once the leases were issued.

The ruling explained that while these leases would only authorise the leaseholder to conduct preliminary surveying activity, they might eventually allow the leaseholder to actually mine the ocean's floor.

The potential impact of that mining had not been addressed in the biodiversity assessment which was used to sign off the lease sales, the ruling said.

Using machines to mine for minerals in the deep ocean is highly controversial.

Some scientists have raised concerns that deep-sea mining could damage little-understood deep-ocean ecosystems, though industry supporters argue the environmental effects remain uncertain and require further study.

Deep-sea mining uses vacuum technology to suck up nodules from the muddy sediment., external However, this process also removes organisms that grow on them, including corals and sponges, many of which cannot grow anywhere else.

In one study of the impact of deep-sea mining, researchers found more than 4,000 animals, 90% of which were new species, living on the seafloor in a remote area of the Pacific Ocean.

Some critics of the industry fear that before we have the chance to explore the full nature of life in the undiscovered deep ocean, it could be endangered.

Norway was the first country in the world to approve commercial-scale deep-sea mining in 2024.

Over 2,000 of the world's scientists met in 2025 to review the data on ocean health and they recommended governments halt deep sea exploration while further research on the impacts was carried out.

More than 30 countries supported this position and called for a moratorium.

Shortly before that meeting, President Trump published executive orders to push ahead with mining and "unleash America's offshore critical minerals and resources".

He said "these resources are key to strengthening our economy, securing our energy future, and reducing dependence on foreign suppliers for critical minerals".

Part of the plan aims to "counter China's growing influence over seabed mineral resources".

Deep-sea mining targets polymetallic nodules, external â potato-sized rocks found over 4,000 metres below the ocean surface.

These contain minerals including nickel, cobalt, and manganese which are used in manufactruring electronics and batteries.

They are also important for renewable energy technologies to tackle climate change, including solar panels, wind turbines and electric vehicles.

The International Energy Agency predicts that demand for the minerals could at least double by 2040., external

U.S. Department of Commerceâs The National Marine Fisheries Service refused to comment.

Source: BBC Science & Environment | Published: 2026-11-26 18:22 UTC

item.title: In a fertility advance, engineered molecular glue stabilizes chromosomes in aging eggs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation, useful vocabulary

Around the world, people are increasingly choosing to have babies later in life for reasons both social and economic. As they get older though, they face a mounting biological challenge: genetic errors caused by chromosomes failing to separate correctly. This phenomenon, known as aneuploidy, is the leading cause of age-related infertility, failed in-vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles, and miscarriage, and it increases dramatically around the age of 40. Studies have shown that between 50% and 80% of embryos from women in their 40s carry chromosomal abnormalities.

One of the main drivers of aneuploidy is the loss of a protein complex called cohesin, which acts like a molecular glue holding chromosomes together. In a new study, researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, engineered a novel protein system capable of restoring normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs. The study, published Thursday in Science, raises the possibility of one day developing such a system into a treatment that could reduce aneuploidy in human eggs used for IVF.

“There is still work ahead, but their proof of concept was highly successful,” said Rajiv McCoy, a biologist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the work. McCoy’s lab is focused on pregnancy loss, the leading cause of which is aneuploidy. It is estimated that about half of all human conceptions are lost before birth, including the roughly 15% of known pregnancies that end in miscarriage. Technologies that could reduce the odds of miscarriage and expand women’s biological reproductive windows by addressing aneuploidy would have far-reaching consequences for the IVF industry and for society at large. “The stakes are very high,” McCoy said.

When a cell prepares to divide, its chromosomes replicate, forming two copies, or sister chromatids, that are all lined up and organized by a cellular winch system known as the spindle. Within the spindle, the sister chromatids are tethered to each other by cohesin — its ring-like structure traps DNA from both sisters inside it. In most cells, cohesin only has to do this work for a few hours before other enzymes cleave it apart, freeing the chromatids to separate into two new cells. But in oocytes, cohesin has to keep this bond going for decades.

That’s because female babies are born with all the oocytes they will ever have. And already at birth, those 1 to 2 million immature egg cells have begun to divide, and the cohesin’s job is only finished when fertilization occurs. That triggers the end of the division process called meiosis in which the egg cells eject half their genetic material so they can fuse with sperm to make an embryo.

Over all that time, the cohesin molecule doesn’t seem to be reloaded, said Melina Schuh, a director at the Max Planck Institute who led the new work.

For the last two decades, Schuh has been finding new ways of peering into egg cells to better understand how meiosis works and what happens when it goes awry. In 2015, her lab showed for the first time how the structures holding chromosomes together deteriorate in human eggs as they age. Not long after, Schuh began to wonder if they might be able to engineer a system of proteins that could step in and stabilize the chromosomes in older eggs. Over the last eight years, her team tested many different designs before settling on one that did everything they wanted it to.

Called TALhesins, the proteins are designed to attach to specific DNA regions near the centers of each chromosome, tethering them together. The research team also baked a deactivation switch into the TALhesin system —based on cohesin’s natural cleavage sites — so that it would automatically release the chromosomes only when fertilization occurs. In experiments with eggs from older mice, the team found that the TALhesin system reduced premature chromosome separation, increasing the proportion of eggs with properly connected chromatids from 47% to 74% — a level comparable to that found in young mice.

Schuh told STAT her lab has already taken the next step of adapting the TALhesin system to bind to chromosomes in human eggs. “We have initial signs that there is a positive effect on cohesion,” she said. “But what we have not done yet is to really test in human oocytes whether we can reduce errors by stabilizing the chromosomes.”

That’s a critical next step, said Eva Hoffman, a molecular geneticist at the University of Copenhagen, who was not involved in the work. After that, researchers would need to establish that this method for reducing aneuploidy doesn’t introduce other kinds of problems. “The clinical potential depends upon regulatory aspects including safety studies for embryonic development,” Hoffman said. Even with the long road ahead, she commended the German group for generating data that challenges the conventional view of aneuploidy as a condition impossible (or impractical) to intervene in. “Since cohesion is established during fetal life and has to be maintained for decades, its depletion over time was thought to be irreversible,” Hoffman said.

Efforts to address age-related ovarian infertility are long overdue. For older women struggling to get pregnant, currently the only solution that’s available to most patients is to try IVF over and over. (For women between 35 and 40, the odds of getting pregnant are about one in three IVF cycles; for women over 40 it drops to one in ten.) This is both expensive and inefficient, and online support groups are overflowing with heart-wrenching stories of women spending a fortune and years of their lives on failed fertility sagas.…

item.title: Novel platform reveals new metabolic targets for cancer treatment
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation, useful vocabulary

Novel platform reveals new metabolic targets for cancer treatment

Cancer cells are hungry beasts. To fuel growth and division, tumors rewire a cell's metabolism, diverting nutrients into the energy and raw materials they need to survive. But not all cancers have the same metabolic needs, and a new study reveals how different cancer-causing mutations can shape metabolism even within the same organ.

The findings, published in Science, identify distinct metabolic vulnerabilities in liver tumors that could open new avenues for treatment.

Uncovering these metabolic vulnerabilities requires a new approach to studying the inner workings of tumors. "Technology is what made this study possible," says Gökhan Ünlü of Kıvanç Birsoy's Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics at Rockefeller. "To get around a long-standing bottleneck in the field, we had to develop a platform that allows us to look directly inside cancer cell organelles in a living organism."

Early findings already suggest possible paths to more personalized medicine and strategies for improving existing therapeutics, such as immunotherapy.

Obstacles to studying cancer metabolism

Scientists have long known that cancer cells rewire their metabolism to survive and that these changes largely depend on where a cancer develops. Two tumors driven by the same genetic mutation, one in the lung and one in the pancreas, can have very different metabolic needs. But even within the same organ, different cancer-causing mutations can shape how tumors obtain and use energy. For instance, in the liver, several genetically distinct and particularly difficult-to-treat cancers can take hold.

One obstacle to better understanding such distinctions has been the difficulty of homing in on metabolism in tumors, which contain a mixture of cancerous and healthy cells. Additionally, conventional methods for isolating mitochondria, the cell's central metabolic hubs, can take hours, during which the molecules that researchers are trying to investigate may change or degrade. Moreover, Birsoy's group wanted to know not just what makes each tumor distinct, but which of those differences actually matter for the cancer cell's survival, a significantly more complex question.

"Most metabolic studies simply identify what goes up or down—they catalog biomarkers," Ünlü says. "Our goal was to develop a method to uncover truly actionable vulnerabilities."

New techniques

Birsoy, Ünlü and colleagues overcame these hurdles by adapting a previously established technique to rapidly isolate mitochondria specifically from cancer cells. They used this system to introduce cancer-causing genes into mouse liver cells alongside a molecular tag that attached to their mitochondria.

Because the tag was linked to the cancer genes, only the tumor cells produced tagged mitochondria, allowing researchers to separate them from healthy cells. And using magnetic beads that bind to the tag, the team could extract these mitochondria from tumor tissue in minutes, before their chemical contents could change or degrade.

With this new technique, the researchers then generated six genetically distinct types of liver tumors in mice and analyzed the proteins and metabolites within their mitochondria using mass spectrometry. Comparing these molecular profiles allowed them to pinpoint metabolic differences associated with specific cancer-causing mutations. They then tested whether these differences represented vulnerabilities that could be exploited to slow tumor growth.

The effort drew on collaborations across Rockefeller, particularly with the Proteomics Resource Center, and at other institutions across the United States and abroad. "Rockefeller has been an incredibly supportive, collaborative community," says Ünlü, who will start his own cancer biology lab at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center this December. "Kıvanç encouraged me from day one to try to turn a technical bottleneck into a powerful discovery platform."

New findings

The team found that tumors driven by the MYC gene depended heavily on oxidative phosphorylation, the process by which cells use oxygen to generate energy, and that blocking this pathway indeed slowed their growth. Tumors driven by the KRAS gene, on the other hand, relied on creatine metabolism and, as predicted, disrupting this pathway slowed tumor growth, while supplementing mice with creatine accelerated tumor growth and could shorten survival.

Most importantly, they also uncovered an unexpected link between metabolism and the immune system. In MYC-driven tumors that had also lost the tumor suppressor gene PTEN, cancer cells produced large amounts of a particular membrane lipid. This altered lipid buildup essentially acted as armor, reducing the availability of receptors that sense inflammatory death signals and shielding the cancer cells from being destroyed by immune cells. When the team blocked the production of this lipid armor, it restored the immune system's ability to attack the tumor.

Together, the findings point toward a more personalized approach to treating cancer, in which therapies target the particular metabolic vulnerabilities created by a tumor's genetic mutations. They also suggest that disrupting cancer metabolism could do more than slow tumor growth directly: It might make tumors more susceptible to existing treatments, including immunotherapy.

"There's real power in trying to make an existing therapy more effective, or hitting the tumor directly through its metabolic dependencies," says Ünlü. "In liver cancer, where patients have had few new options for decades, combining these approaches gives us a way forward."…

item.title: An engineered 'glue' for aged eggs could prevent premature chromosome separation
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation, useful vocabulary

An engineered 'glue' for aged eggs could prevent premature chromosome separation

As a woman ages, her eggs become more prone to errors. One reason for this is that the chromosomes fall apart into their two halves (the chromatids) too early while the eggs prepare for potential fertilization. Researchers led by Melina Schuh at the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen (Germany) have now developed a molecular "glue" that stabilizes the chromosomes in aged mouse eggs.

The system has already been adapted to human eggs: in initial experiments, it bound to the chromosomes and showed first signs of holding chromatids together. This is a first step towards developing a treatment that prevents premature separation of chromosomes even in aged eggs. The research is published in the journal Science.

Female fertility begins to decline significantly in the mid-30s. By then, the eggs formed before birth are also decades old. This makes them more prone to errors. In order for an egg to be fertilized and develop into new life, it must first halve its double set of chromosomes in a maturation division called meiosis, expelling one set from the cell.

Cohesin provides stability

The chromosomes' identical halves, the chromatids, are held together by a molecular "glue," the protein complex cohesin. It provides the necessary stability. However, as an egg ages, the cohesin detaches from the chromatids and is not replaced. This increases the likelihood that the chromatids will separate too early and fail to distribute correctly during meiosis.

After meiosis, the egg then contains either too many or too few chromosomes. This will lead to an embryo with an abnormal number of chromosomes after fertilization. In most cases, these embryos do not implant in the uterus or do not develop normally. As a result, fertility treatments involving assisted reproduction may be unsuccessful for women from their late 30s onward.

Until now, there has been no way to compensate for the loss of chromosome cohesion with age. "In our search for a solution, we asked ourselves, 'Can we replace cohesin?'" says Schuh, a biochemist and director at the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences. "We aimed to develop an artificial glue that could take over the role of cohesin and be applied to chromosomes."

Molecular glue to hold sister chromatids together

The TALhesin system, developed by Schuh and her team, offers hope for a replacement. It is based on a DNA-binding protein called a TAL effector. It can be programmed to target a region near the centromere, where natural cohesin helps hold the sister chromatids together. The researchers equipped two such proteins with coupling sites that form a firm chemical bond with each other. Together, these two proteins form the TALhesin system, which acts as an engineered molecular glue to hold sister chromatids together.

To determine if the new system takes over the role of cohesin, researchers first conducted experiments on young mouse eggs. When they removed the natural cohesin, the chromatids drifted apart within an hour. However, when the researchers added TALhesin, the chromatids remained together and only separated once the TALhesin was removed. Thus, the artificial glue was able to take over the binding function of cohesin.

It also held the chromatids together in aged mouse eggs. In aged mice, TALhesin raised the proportion of eggs without prematurely separated chromosomes from 46.7% to 74.1%. This was almost the same as the value for young animals, which was 74.7%.

Molecular 'scissors'

However, glues that hold things together reliably also have a potential downside: At a specific point during meiosis, the chromatids must separate from one another. To accomplish this, the TALhesin system, just like cohesin, must be deactivated at the right time. In the egg, a kind of molecular "scissors," the enzyme separase, cleaves cohesin at precisely defined sites at the exact right moment.

The researchers incorporated such a molecular cleavage site into TALhesin. In a subsequent experiment, they artificially activated TALhesin-treated eggs, which triggers the final division of meiosis just as fertilization would. Separase successfully cleaved TALhesin at the right time, and the chromatids separated normally.

Can these results be transferred to humans? To find out, the researchers adapted the TALhesin system to a target sequence on human chromosomes. In donated unfertilized eggs, it bound to the intended regions without visibly disrupting the first meiotic division. Chromosomes carrying a lot of TALhesin showed smaller distances between their chromatids than those carrying little, as would be expected if the system were holding them together.

The built-in cleavage site worked in human eggs too. Without it, the chromosomes carrying the most TALhesin stayed linked when they should have separated; with it, the chromatids separated normally. The Göttingen Fertility Center, the Bourn Hall Fertility Clinic in Cambridgeshire (UK) and the Fertility Center Berlin provided the unfertilized eggs for these experiments.

Future studies will investigate whether TALhesin can reduce chromosome errors in eggs donated by older women. "With TALhesin, we can replace lost chromatid cohesion for the first time," emphasizes Schuh. "Our long-term goal is to develop the system further so that it can be used safely in fertility treatment, although further research and safety testing will be needed before clinical use."

Publication details

Alexandre Webster et al., An engineered cohesion system reduces errors in aged mammalian eggs, Science (2026). DOI: 10.1126/science.aei5852. www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aei5852

Journal information: Science

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail, useful vocabulary

EPA testing for lead contamination after lead azide detonation in Iowa

The Army detonated the country's stockpile of lead azide. Now EPA teams are testing the soil, air and water for any lead contamination.

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:

Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in eastern Iowa for lead contamination. The Army detonated thousands of pounds of lead azide on Wednesday. That's the stuff bombs are made with. The Army said it was unstable and a controlled explosion would've been the only way to get rid of it.

Iowa Public Radio's Eliza Billingham is now with us. So, Eliza, let's start with the explosion itself and why the Army is calling it a success.

ELIZA BILLINGHAM, BYLINE: Of course. The detonation took place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, and the major concern around this detonation was how much lead would be released in the air when this lead azide exploded. The Army worked to mitigate the explosion. The barrels were already underground, and then those bunkers were covered with tarps, water, and particle-collecting foam. And the EPA has been running tests ever since the explosion, and so far, it has not found any lead in the air. Shortly after the detonation, Major General Eric Shirley said the results exceeded his expectations.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

ERIC SHIRLEY: Every indication is that all of the munitions that were employed absolutely reduced the lead azide threat.

MARTÍNEZ: All right. So tell us about the testing that's going on. How's it happening?

BILLINGHAM: The EPA says it has about 300 people sampling the air, ground and nearby surface water for lead contamination. Lead is dangerous because it's a neurotoxin. It's especially dangerous to children and people who are pregnant because of how it can inhibit childhood development. The EPA has set legal limits for how much lead can be on windowsills and floors of houses, for example, so it and the Army are watching for lead levels on surfaces near the detonation zone to see if they exceed those limits, but so far, the EPA says its measurements haven't shown any lead dust.

MARTÍNEZ: Now, what's been the reaction from residents? Because - I don't know - I'd be worried if I were there.

BILLINGHAM: Right. The reaction has been mixed. The Army told some residents who lived within 5 miles of the detonation that it might be best to evacuate. And some people in that radius did leave their houses, but not everyone. Alan Kleinkopf lives in a house right around the corner from the plant's headquarters. He and his wife did leave their house yesterday morning but came back around noon, and he saw his home didn't seem to have any damage, and Kleinkopf said that made him feel pretty good.

ALAN KLEINKOPF: I think the U.S. government has done the best that they could with their mitigating efforts that they put into place.

BILLINGHAM: But after this past week and a half of delays and mixed messaging about the detonation, other residents have lost trust in the Army, and they're hesitant to trust the EPA's initial readings. They want independent monitoring. And the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois are sampling around the region, so we should know in a few days if their measurements line up with the EPA's.

MARTÍNEZ: I wish them luck on that. Now, Iowa's governor, Kim Reynolds, she declared a disaster emergency for the three counties in southeastern Iowa. So what does a disaster emergency do for the people who actually live there?

BILLINGHAM: That opens up the path to FEMA funding, and FEMA says it's ready to assist anyone who thinks they need relief. The public library in Burlington, which is right next to Middletown, said it has service navigators every week who help people navigate state and federal aid, so those people will be a great resource for anyone looking for FEMA funding. And the Army claims office is also in touch with residents in case anyone wants to file personal injury or property damage claims with the Army.

MARTÍNEZ: All right. That's Eliza Billingham of Iowa Public Radio. Thanks a lot, Eliza.

BILLINGHAM: Happy Thanksgiving.

item.title: Oral nutrition supplement interventions show short-term benefits in patient outcomes at low cost for older adults
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation, useful vocabulary

Oral nutrition supplement interventions show short-term benefits in patient outcomes at low cost for older adults

A systematic review published in the journal Value in Health by Amarsinh Desai, Ph.D., Olivia M. Dong, Ph.D., and colleagues examines the health and economic effects of oral nutrition supplements in older adults, most with or at risk of malnutrition. The researchers found that oral nutrition supplement use, often as part of broader nutrition interventions, was generally associated with modest short-term improvements in health outcomes and was cost-effective or cost-saving, with economic benefits largely driven by reductions in health care resource utilization, such as fewer hospitalizations.

Older adults face an increased risk of malnutrition because of factors such as the accumulation of diseases and impairments over time, age-related physiological changes and social factors, like isolation, that can impact dietary intake. Oral nutrition supplements, including drinks, powders and other formats that provide specific nutrients, may be used under medical supervision when someone can eat by mouth but cannot meet nutritional needs through diet alone.

Earlier reviews of the economics of oral nutritional supplements included adults across a broad age range, focused on a narrow group of older adults or drew on only one cost-effectiveness study.

The new report brings together several types of economic evaluations across care settings to examine costs and health outcomes predominantly in older adults. By focusing on studies published from 2014 through 2024, the review reflects more recent approaches to diagnosing and managing malnutrition.

Seven studies reported per-patient cost savings ranging from $127 to $1,988 in 2024 U.S. dollars, primarily associated with reduced use of health care services. Five studies reported per-patient cost increases ranging from $356 to $672 in 2024 U.S. dollars, mainly associated with the costs of oral nutrition supplements and other intervention components, including nutrition-related services.

"Overall, studies reported favorable economic conclusions (cost-effective or cost-saving), which were largely driven by utilization-related cost offsets," wrote author Desai, Ph.D., of Nestlé Health Science in Bridgewater, New Jersey, U.S.

"Subgroup patterns suggest oral nutrition supplement interventions may offer the greatest economic value when targeted to higher-risk patients and implemented across care transitions, in which modest clinical improvements translate into reductions in hospital utilization," wrote author Dong, Ph.D., of RTI Health Solutions in Durham, North Carolina, U.S.

Nine studies reported favorable findings for their main health outcomes and measures of health care use, while three reported mixed results across several main outcomes. Outcomes examined across the studies varied and included hospital admissions, length of stay, nutritional status, clinical outcomes (such as pressure ulcer healing), life-years gained and quality of life. The reported health gains were generally modest and assessed over short periods.

The studies in the review covered the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Italy, France, Spain and Colombia, with 11 of the 12 conducted in high-income countries. Mean participant ages ranged from 63 to 88 years.

The authors cautioned that the long-term value of oral nutrition supplements and the intervention programs they were part of remains uncertain. Most studies assessed outcomes over six months or less. In eight studies, oral nutrition supplements were part of broader intervention programs that included other components, such as dietary counseling, making it difficult to isolate the effect of oral nutrition supplements. Differences in study design, settings and outcomes made it difficult to make comparisons across studies.

The authors also noted gaps in how some studies reported their methods and that most were industry-funded, which underscores the need for transparent reporting of data sources and uncertainty. Because the evidence comes largely from high-income countries, findings may not apply to other settings. Longer-term studies with more consistent reporting of key study methods could give health care decision-makers a clearer picture of the lasting value of oral nutrition supplements.

Overall, the findings support the targeted consideration of oral nutrition supplements as a potentially valuable strategy for improving outcomes in older adults at low or no net cost to health care systems, while highlighting the need for longer-term, methodologically robust studies that take a societal perspective, capturing costs such as caregiver time and out-of-pocket expenses, and that include a wider range of settings, such as low- and middle-income countries.

More information

Amarsinh Desai et al., Systematic Review of Health Economic Evaluations of Oral Nutritional Supplement Interventions in Older Adults: An ISPOR Special Interest Group Report, Value in Health (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jval.2026.06.023
