item.title: A protein that teaches cells to tolerate DNA damage points to a new vulnerability in cancer
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation, useful vocabulary

A protein that teaches cells to tolerate DNA damage points to a new vulnerability in cancer

Cancer begins in DNA, which is why everything about this well-known molecule is extensively studied at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO). For instance, what exactly happens when DNA is duplicated? Every time a cell divides into two daughter cells, its DNA is copied. Researchers at CNIO and Stanford University have now uncovered a new aspect of this complex process, which has been studied for decades but still holds many surprises.

The new findings, published in the journal Nature, could open up avenues for future cancer treatments.

The discovery concerns how cells deal with obstacles that arise during DNA replication. If a break or lesion occurs in the DNA being copied, does replication stop, or can it continue because the cell tolerates the damage? Chemotherapy and radiotherapy aim to eliminate cancer by inducing this kind of damage in tumor cells, which is why understanding its effects is so important. If cancer cells learn to tolerate DNA lesions and continue replicating, treatment will fail.

Blocking the protein that enables damaged DNA to be replicated

The research groups led by Juan Méndez at CNIO and Gheorghe Chistol at Stanford University School of Medicine (U.S.) are studying a protein called PRIMPOL, which enables DNA replication to proceed even when damage is present. In tumor cells, however, this is precisely what researchers want to prevent.

DNA damage in tumor cells may have been induced by the treatment itself, meaning that PRIMPOL could be helping cancer cells to continue replicating and survive. Researchers have been investigating for years how to prevent this by blocking PRIMPOL.

The CNIO and Stanford teams have now discovered that PRIMPOL relies on another protein, called CMG, to perform its function. Targeting CMG could offer a way to block PRIMPOL.

"Tumors are being identified, including some subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), that become resistant to treatment because of high PRIMPOL activity," explains Méndez, head of the DNA Replication Group at CNIO.

"In these cases, inhibiting its function could improve the effectiveness of treatments. In my laboratory, we have been trying to identify inhibitors for several years, and it has proved challenging. This discovery opens up the possibility of inhibiting PRIMPOL through its interaction with CMG."

Watching DNA replicate in real time

The team used advanced microscopy techniques to visualize DNA replication in real time. It is rather like spying on a process that takes place trillions of times a day in the human body: complex molecular machinery, just nanometers in size and made up of dozens of proteins, spends hours copying DNA inside the nucleus of our cells.

The researchers attached individual DNA molecules to a glass surface and added specific proteins that initiate replication and generate a fluorescent signal as the process unfolds. Using specialized microscopes, they can observe when DNA replication stops or resumes and measure the rate at which it occurs.

"In this study, we discovered how the PRIMPOL protein selects the sites where it needs to act and how it positions itself at the molecular level to perform its function correctly," explains Méndez.

"It does so through a physical interaction with another protein involved in DNA replication, the CMG helicase. This interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG not only determines where PRIMPOL needs to act, but also enables coordination with the DNA polymerases that can then resume replication quickly and efficiently."

His group at CNIO is already using artificial intelligence models to try to develop compounds that target CMG and PRIMPOL.

The study also involved Elena Blanco-Romero and Roberto Masdemont-Maestro from CNIO, and Jinho Park and Luke Lynch from Stanford University.

Publication details

Jinho Park et al., The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL, Nature (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11276-y

item.title: Experimental drug shows promise in overcoming treatment resistance in aggressive acute myeloid leukemia
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation, useful vocabulary

Experimental drug shows promise in overcoming treatment resistance in aggressive acute myeloid leukemia

Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center found that an experimental drug may help overcome one of the major challenges in treating an aggressive subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), known as FLT3-positive AML. In laboratory and animal studies, the drug, called PHI-101, was effective against leukemia cells carrying genetic mutations that cause resistance to existing FLT3-targeted therapies.

The findings, published Oct. 12 in Leukemia, suggest that PHI-101 could provide a new treatment option for patients whose leukemia stops responding to drugs designed to block FLT3, a protein that helps regulate the growth of blood cells.

Mutations in the FLT3 gene occur in approximately one-third of patients with AML and can cause leukemia cells to grow uncontrollably. Drugs called FLT3 inhibitors have significantly improved treatment options for patients with these mutations. However, some patients develop additional mutations that allow their cancer cells to evade the drugs, causing the leukemia to return or continue growing.

"FLT3 inhibitors have made an important difference in the treatment of AML, but resistance remains a significant limitation," says Marina Mitrou, M.D., a fellow in pediatric oncology and first author of the study. "What makes this drug particularly promising is its ability to target several mutations associated with resistance, including one that makes many existing FLT3 inhibitors ineffective."

The research focused particularly on a mutation called F691L, sometimes referred to as a "gatekeeper" mutation because it alters a critical region of the FLT3 protein where drugs bind. This change can prevent existing treatments from effectively blocking the protein's activity, allowing leukemia cells to continue growing. PHI-101 appears to overcome this obstacle by binding to the FLT3 protein in a way that is less affected by the genetic changes that interfere with other inhibitors.

To evaluate the drug, researchers tested PHI-101 in leukemia cell lines, samples from patients with AML and mouse models of the disease. They found that the drug effectively blocked FLT3 activity and inhibited the growth of leukemia cells carrying several mutations, including F691L and another resistance-associated mutation, D835.

In laboratory experiments, PHI-101 was more effective than two FDA-approved FLT3 inhibitors, gilteritinib and quizartinib, against leukemia cells carrying the F691L mutation. The drug caused leukemia cells with FLT3 mutations to die but had little effect on other cells.

The researchers observed promising results in mice as well. In one experiment involving mice transplanted with human AML cells carrying a FLT3 mutation, PHI-101 reduced leukemia in the bone marrow and extended median survival to 191 days, compared with 133 days for mice treated with gilteritinib and 108 days for untreated mice.

In a separate mouse model of leukemia carrying the treatment-resistant F691L mutation, PHI-101 extended median survival to 44.4 days, compared with 21.4 days for mice receiving gilteritinib and 19.4 days for untreated mice.

"One of the most encouraging findings was that PHI-101 remained effective against the F691L mutation, which is particularly difficult to treat," says Donald Small, M.D., Ph.D., the Kyle Haydock Professor of Oncology at the Kimmel Cancer Center and senior author. "These findings suggest we may be able to offer another treatment option for patients who develop resistance to existing FLT3 inhibitors."

The research builds upon decades of pioneering discoveries led by Small at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center that helped establish FLT3 as an important target for leukemia treatment.

In 1992, Small was the first scientist to clone the human FLT3 gene and subsequently demonstrated its important role in AML. His lab was also the first to discover a FLT3 inhibitor and to show its success in killing FLT3-mutant cell lines. They proceeded to screen thousands of compounds from a drug library and discovered very potent FLT3 inhibitors that eventually made their way into clinical trials.

Working with Small, Mark Levis, M.D., Ph.D., showed the preferential killing of FLT3-mutant leukemia cells from patients and, together with Doug Smith, M.D., helped design the first trials of FLT3 inhibitors for patients with FLT3-mutant AML. Levis and Small subsequently developed a test to determine whether FLT3 inhibitors were successfully blocking their intended target in patients. This research helped guide the development and clinical testing of more effective FLT3 inhibitors, establishing the foundation for treatments now used in patients with AML.

"Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center has a long history of research aimed at understanding FLT3 and developing drugs to target it," says Small. "We have made important advances, but we also know that leukemia can find ways around these treatments. Our goal is to continue developing better drugs that can overcome resistance and improve outcomes for patients."

PHI-101 is being evaluated in a phase 1 clinical trial in Korea and Australia involving patients with relapsed or refractory AML—leukemia that has returned after treatment or has not responded to treatment. Early clinical findings have shown encouraging activity, although additional studies are needed to further determine the drug's safety and effectiveness in patients.

Researchers are also interested in whether PHI-101 could be used earlier in treatment or combined with other drugs to improve responses and potentially prevent resistance from developing.…

Source: Medical Xpress | Published: 2026-11-26 16:40 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: A forgotten organ sheds new light on the origins of the ovary
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research, clear explanation, useful vocabulary

A forgotten organ sheds new light on the origins of the ovary

How do ovaries develop? Much remains unknown. By studying the "rete ovarii," a small anatomical structure that has long been overlooked, a team at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) has uncovered the dual origin of the cells that surround and protect oocytes. This discovery offers new insights into ovarian development and opens up new avenues for research into fertility and gynecological cancers.

The findings have been published in the scientific journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).

The ovaries play an essential role in reproduction and hormonal balance in women. Located on either side of the uterus, they contain a reserve of oocytes established before birth. This reserve gradually declines throughout life. At puberty, it comprises approximately 300,000 to 500,000 oocytes, contained within ovarian follicles. Each follicle consists of an oocyte surrounded by layers of cells called granulosa cells, which protect the oocyte and support its development. During each menstrual cycle, several follicles begin to develop, but usually only one reaches maturity and releases an oocyte during ovulation.

Yet ovarian development remains poorly understood. In particular, little is known about the origins of the different cell types that make up the ovaries or how they specialize during embryonic development. A team led by Serge Nef, a full professor in the Department of Genetic Medicine and Development at the UNIGE Faculty of Medicine, has discovered that granulosa cells have not one but two distinct origins.

Tracing the origins of follicular cells

"One previously known origin of these cells lies on the surface of the ovary," explains Chloé Mayère, a postdoctoral researcher and co-first author of the study. "By analyzing nearly 200,000 human and mouse cells, we showed that the cells lining this surface are not all alike. The surface is organized into several distinct regions, whose cells are already showing signs of specialization toward different functions. Some will give rise to granulosa cells, which surround the oocyte within the follicles, while others will form the stroma, the supporting tissue of the ovary."

The second source of granulosa cells—the study's key new finding—was identified by the UNIGE team through a fresh examination of the rete ovarii. This small structure, made up of a network of ducts, is located in an area crossed by blood vessels connecting the ovary to the surrounding tissues.

"The rete ovarii was first described in 1870, but gradually fell into obscurity as it was considered little more than a remnant of embryonic development," explains Cyril Djari, a senior researcher, co-first author and co-corresponding author of the study. "Its male counterpart, the rete testis, by contrast, has a well-established role in sperm transport."

Using state-of-the-art cell-tracing, microscopy and bioinformatics techniques, the UNIGE scientists discovered that the cells from which this structure develops also contribute to the formation of the ovary's follicular cells. The rete ovarii therefore appears to be closely involved in the development of certain ovarian follicles, rather than being merely an embryonic remnant.

The team also observed this early organization in humans, suggesting that the mechanisms underlying the diversity of ovarian cell types are conserved between mice and humans.

Beyond ovarian development

The discovery of this dual cellular origin provides new insights into ovarian development. It also opens up new avenues for research into fertility, ovarian developmental disorders and, potentially, certain gynecological cancers.

"We know, for example, that some ovarian cancer cells express a gene called PAX8, which is also expressed in cells of the rete ovarii—a structure that our findings are now bringing back into the spotlight," explains Nef.

"We now aim to investigate these observations further through a new project carried out in collaboration with professor Intidhar Labidi-Galy of HUG and UNIGE. The aim is to gain a better understanding of the characteristics of the rete ovarii in adult women and to explore its possible link with ovarian cancer."

Publication details

Cyril Djari et al., Spatiotemporally primed coelomic epithelium and supporting-like cells establish the dual origin of granulosa cells, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2026). DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2615939123

Journal information: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

item.title: sqlite3_rsync：无需本地完整副本的 SQLite 远程复制
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

对于磁盘空间紧张的小型服务器，备份 SQLite 数据库时经常会遇到一个问题：数据库本身还放得下，但第二份完整副本已经放不下了。

sqlite3_rsync 提供了另一种选择：通过 SSH 将数据库快照复制到另一台机器，不必先在本地生成完整副本。

为什么不必先生成本地副本很重要？

如果使用备份 API 或 VACUUM INTO 在本地创建数据库副本，就需要为这份副本预留足够的磁盘空间。当数据库已经占用磁盘容量的一半以上时，剩余空间可能不足以完成复制。

sqlite3_rsync 省去了先生成本地完整副本这一步，适合需要把数据库快照传到其他机器、但本地存储余量有限的场景。

对于写好标智库中关注数据库运维与工具选型的读者，这里值得区分的是两个问题：本地能否容纳完整副本，以及远程同步需要传输多少数据。sqlite3_rsync 分别从复制方式和差异比较机制上处理这两个问题。

已有远程副本时，按页比较差异

除了复制快照，sqlite3_rsync 还可以同步已有的数据库副本。它采用与常规 rsync 类似的差异比较思路，以数据库页为单位识别需要传输的内容：

- 副本端向发送端提交数据库页或页组的加密哈希值。

- 发送端比较哈希，返回存在差异的页内容。

- 如果某个页组的哈希不一致，发送端可以请求更细粒度的哈希，进一步定位差异。

因此，同步已有副本时，不必每次都重新传输整个数据库。

差异同步不代表传输量一定更小

比较差异本身也有开销。如果两端数据库最初差异很大，交换哈希产生的额外流量，可能使总传输量超过完整数据库的大小，不过超出幅度最多约为几个百分点。

换句话说，按页同步可以减少重复传输，但不能保证每次传输量都小于数据库体积。

工具沿革

sqlite3_rsync 于 2024 年 10 月随 SQLite 3.47.0 以实验性工具的形式加入，并在 2025 年 5 月的 SQLite 3.50.0 中得到增强。

它的两个关键特点可以概括为：

- 远程复制快照：无需先在本地创建完整副本，降低对本地剩余磁盘空间的要求。

- 同步已有副本：按数据库页比较差异，避免每次重复传输全部内容。

如果你的约束是“数据库还能运行，但磁盘已经容不下第二份完整副本”，这种复制方式值得纳入工具评估。

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-26 21:01 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Godot 4: Texture was downsized on import as its width exceeded the importable size limit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

What you see

When a texture finishes importing, the Editor logs Texture was downsized on import as its width (N pixels) exceeded the importable size limit (M pixels). The texture ends up smaller than the source file on disk, and when you use it in a sprite or atlas it looks softer or chunkier than the original art. The message names the source width, the limit that was hit, and the axis involved. A matching height variant exists when the source runs over the vertical ceiling instead, and the two warnings behave the same way.

Why it happens

The importer keeps every platform inside a maximum texture size. When the source image's width goes over that platform's importable limit, the importer does not fail the import. Instead it downsizes the texture proportionally to fit, and prints this warning so you know the on-disk source was larger than what actually entered the project. The limit comes from the project's platform texture size settings and the fallback size ceiling; the warning marks the branch where the fallback ceiling, rather than an explicit user setting, did the trimming. The proportional shrink keeps the aspect ratio, so nothing looks stretched, but every detail above the ceiling is lost in the imported copy.

The usual trigger is an oversized reference image left in the game assets: a full-resolution concept board, a 4k UI mockup, or a sprite sheet exported far wider than the sprites it contains. It also shows up after a platform switch, when a texture authored for a desktop size limit is moved to a mobile profile with a smaller ceiling. Because the downsize happens at import time, the editor preview may still look acceptable while the imported resource has already been rescaled, so the softness is easy to miss until the texture is used at runtime on a target device.

Confirm it

Select the texture in the Project window and open the Import tab. Read the source image dimensions shown for the file, then compare them against the platform size limit in Project Settings. The warning's width number should match the source width, and the limit number should match the ceiling the importer applied. Check whether the texture's imported preview is visibly smaller than the original file, and look at the other textures imported in the same batch for the same warning.

A healthy import keeps the source width at or under the limit and imports at native resolution. A downsized one reports a source width above the ceiling, and its imported texture dimensions reflect the proportional shrink rather than the source rectangle. Note which platform profile is active when you read the limit, because the same file can import at native size on one platform and be downsized on another. If the softness only shows on a build for a specific device, switch the editor to that platform profile before judging the numbers.

Fix it

Raise the limit where the project genuinely needs the larger texture, or shrink the source before it reaches the importer:

- In the importer or project platform settings, raise the corresponding texture size limit if the target hardware supports the larger texture.

- Otherwise pre-scale the source image to within the limit in your art tool, so the importer keeps it at native size instead of resizing it during import.

- Remove oversized reference boards and mockups from the export assets; reference art does not belong in the shipped sprite folders.

When you resize the source by hand, keep the dimensions sensible for the target and avoid stretching to an arbitrary number. If the atlas groups several sprites on one sheet, confirm the whole sheet, not just one sprite, fits under the ceiling, since the packer works from the combined sheet size. After the change, reimport the texture and read the imported dimensions back. The width must sit under the platform limit, the proportional downsize warning must be gone, and the sprite must show the detail you expect without the editor having rescaled it.

The exact engine message and source location for this import warning are documented in the error reference.

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-26 21:02 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Original link: https://dev.to/yirenlabs/godot-4-texture-was-downsized-on-import-as-its-width-exceeded-the-importable-size-limit-1j1k

item.title: The Immeasurable Value of Declarative Programming
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

1. Two Ways to Tell the Computer What You Want

There are two ways to build software.

The first is to tell the computer how to do something, step by step.

The second is to tell it what you want to hold true, and to write a common mechanism, which you build once, that applies what you told it.

The first is called imperative. The second is called declarative.

In imperative, you write the procedure yourself, every time.

In declarative, you describe the rule once, and the procedure is executed every time by the mechanism you wrote.

We all started with the first, the imperative way. It is the natural way. You write code that says: take this, put it there, check this, save the other.

And for small programs, it works wonderfully.

The problem begins when the program grows. When you go from 5 tables to 50. From 1 form to 200. From 1 developer to a team.

Then the "how" starts to repeat itself. The same thing, written again and again, in a thousand places, with small differences that nobody remembers why they exist.

That is where declarative shows its value. And its value is not small. It is immeasurable.

2. What Does Declarative Mean in Practice?

Declarative does not mean "without code". It means "code that describes".

Instead of writing:

Take the Product, take its price, put it in the Line, take its name, put it in the Line, take its VAT rate, put it in the Line...

You write:

The Order Line has a lookup to the Product. When a Product is selected, the fields Name, Price, VAT Rate are copied.

The first version is instructions. The second is a definition.

The definition is written once. And it is executed every time, by the framework, automatically, in the same way, without errors, without omissions.

That is the difference. It is not syntactic. It is architectural.

And there is something else, which is the key: a declarative definition is not just code that runs. It is knowledge that the system can use.

The copy mechanism uses it. The UI uses it. Validation uses it. Any code in your application can use it.

Nobody needs to discover inside the code what you meant. The system knows it. Because you told it once, clearly.

3. Example 1: Snapshot Fields

Let us take the most classic example from business applications: the Order.

We have a Customer, an Item, an Order and its Lines.

When the user creates an Order, they select a Customer and an Item. At that moment, we must keep a snapshot of the state as it was then.

Why? Because tomorrow the Customer may change their company name. They may change their billing address. They may change their shipping address. The Item may change its price. It may change its description. It may change its VAT rate.

The Order, however, must not change. The Order is a historical document. It must remember how the world was at the moment it was issued.

So in the Order table we must keep:

- The Customer's company name as it was

- The billing address as it was

- The shipping address as it was

- The phone, the email, the VAT number as they were

And in the OrderLine table we must keep:

- The Item's name as it was

- Its price as it was

- Its VAT rate as it was

- Its unit of measure as it was

These are the snapshot fields.

And for anyone who has built an ERP, CRM, accounting system, warehouse system, it is an obvious need that they exist and are kept up to date.

The question is: where is this defined?

In the Imperative Approach

It is defined nowhere. Or rather, it is defined everywhere.

It is defined in the Service that creates the Order. It is defined in the Service that processes it. It is defined in the API that accepts it. It is defined in the form that shows it. It is defined in the import that brings it in from elsewhere.

At every point, someone writes by hand:

Take the name from the Item, put it in the Line. Take the price from the Item, put it in the Line.

And if tomorrow we must also keep something else, for example the Item's barcode as it was then, we must find all these places and change them one by one.

And we will certainly forget one.

In the Declarative Approach

It is defined once, in the definition of the lookup.

The definition says, in plain language:

The field ProductId of the Line is a lookup to the Product table.

When it changes, the following fields are copied:

Product.Name -> OrderLine.ProductName

Product.Price -> OrderLine.Price

Product.VatRate -> OrderLine.VatRate

Product.Barcode -> OrderLine.Barcode

And in code, the same definition may look something like this. The example is indicative, it does not belong to a specific library:

{

"field": "ProductId",

"lookup": {

"source": "Product",

"key": "Id",

"copyOnSelection": {

"Name": "ProductName",

"UnitId": "UnitId",

"VatRate": "VatRate",

"Barcode": "Barcode"

}

}

}

That is all.

From then on, whoever creates an Order, from wherever they create it, from a form, from an API, from an import, from an automatic process, the snapshot will happen automatically, in the same way.

And if tomorrow we must add the barcode, we add it in one place: in the definition. Not in a thousand.

That is the difference between "we know it" and "we have defined it".

Copying fields is a mechanism. Which data we keep and when we change it is a business decision. A declarative definition lets us express our knowledge in a concentrated way.

4. Example 2: Adding a Field

Let us take the second example, which is perhaps even more revealing.

Suppose we have a system that works. It has 50 tables, 200 forms, 100 reports.

And the Customer comes and says: "I want to add the field 'Profession' to the Customer".

A simple request. One field.

What needs to happen in the imperative approach?

- Add a column to the database.

- Add a property to the entity / model.

- Add a field to the DTO.

- Add a mapping to the Mapper.

- Add a field to the entry form.

- Add a field to the search form.

- Add a field to the grid.

- Add a field to the filter.

- Add a field to validation.

- Add a field to the API.…

Source: Dev.to | Published: 2026-11-26 21:02 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://dev.to/tbebekis/the-immeasurable-value-of-declarative-programming-3ghd

item.title: 1Password says it was hacked but users' vaults are safe
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

1Password says it was hacked but users' vaults are safe

The attacker wasn't able to access people's vaults.

1Password has admitted that an attacker was able to infiltrate its system and steal some customer data, but it has assured users in its announcement that their vaults and logins are safe. On November 19, the company started investigating signs that an employee's corporate GitHub account had been compromised. The company found that the attacker used that account to access its source code and inject malicious code to its backend.

The attacker was then able to download customers' data, including people's names and email addresses, the dates their accounts were created and their last sign-in times. They were also able to steal users' public keys, but 1Password said it has no impact to their security. While the bad actor was also able to steal source code from the company itself, it doesn't contain customer data.

"Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected," 1Password wrote. The service doesn't have access to users' actual passwords, recovery keys and other credentials, as well as the secret keys that protect their vaults, so the attacker wasn't able to steal them. Since discovering the breach, 1Password has revoked the stolen token, disabled the affected GitHub account and added new detection tools for similar attacks.

While 1Password said that users' vaults remain safe, the company still advises being vigilant when it comes to phishing attempts. It warned that since users' emails were compromised in the breach, they could be used in attempts to grab people's passwords through fake account recovery and invitation emails.

Source: Engadget | Published: 2026-11-26 20:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.engadget.com/2329013/1password-hacked-but-users-vaults-are-safe/

item.title: Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week.

What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S. intelligence has reportedly tracked Alice Huang’s contact with an officer of China’s spy agency, but officials haven’t offered public evidence that she was commissioned to target Nvidia’s chief. In the past week, after President Trump successfully pushed to bring Jensen Huang back, the administration has played down the allegations it once circulated internally. Whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure is the big question.

Undisputed reporting shows the claim emerged from the White House itself. It first appeared in a highly classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump’s trip to China in May. The memo formed the partial basis for the New York Times’ initial reporting on the scandal, published Oct. 29 and its existence was first reported on Nov. 8.

The memo did not definitively say, according to the Wall Street Journal, that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. CNN, by contrast, has reported that the memo concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

What’s better established is that Alice Huang was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is Beijing’s civilian spy agency, responsible for both foreign intelligence and domestic counterintelligence. Last weekend, the Times, citing people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports, reported that Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from the spring of 2025 until this fall, a period that overlaps her relationship with Jensen Huang. (The Chinese government has called the spy claims a “smear,” and Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.)

Top Trump officials have nonetheless all but discredited the espionage claims, along with the suggestion that Nvidia fell prey to spying or foreign influence.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was Trump’s personal defense lawyer before taking over the Justice Department, told journalists on Tuesday: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.” On the same day, Trump said a pardon was an option for Jensen Huang but that he did not think one would be needed. Senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress that the government apparently has no actual evidence that the MSS directed Alice Huang to pursue an affair with Jensen Huang.

None of those statements necessarily exonerates Alice Huang as an intelligence agent. Instead, they support the alternate theory that the Chinese government didn’t tell her to begin the affair and that Jensen Huang broke no law by having it. Not being directed to have an affair isn’t the same as not being a spy, though.

From a certain angle, the circumstantial evidence surrounding Alice Huang looks quite suspicious. She was a top executive at a company investigated for illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband, Kang Wei, is said to have even closer ties to the MSS, with some sources saying he worked for the agency.

The timing of the government’s reversal is at the heart of the matter. Trump has said he lobbied the board “directly and indirectly” to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, so it wouldn’t be surprising if officials who serve at his pleasure were recasting the case in terms that satisfy his agenda. That wouldn’t necessarily make their assessments wrong. But unless new intelligence has actually resolved the question, and none has been publicly identified as yet, that backdrop is critical to keep in mind. CBS has also reported that Rubio, whose office oversaw the original memo, has privately voiced concerns about aspects of Jensen Huang’s return.

Doubts persist elsewhere, too. Earlier this month, CNN reported that the intelligence community was still working to understand Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing. After a briefing by top intelligence officials earlier this month, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said he was unsure whether she was a spy or a “useful idiot.” And this week, the Wall Street Journal pointed out that under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, top corporate executives routinely maintain ties to the country’s intelligence service without being formally deputized as assets.

The crush of conflicting claims, most from anonymous government sources, obviously leaves large questions unanswered as to what actually transpired. Some of those questions that naturally spring to mind:

- Alice Huang is said to have been under U.S. surveillance for over a year. If the government suspected her of espionage, why wasn’t Jensen Huang warned earlier (and privately, so as not to cause the stock-market-destabilizing maelstrom that followed the more recent disclosure)? One explanation that has been given is that alerting the Nvidia chief might have tipped off Huang that her cover had been blown.

- If Alice Huang was a spy, what information did she pass to the Chinese government, and what influence did she actually have?

- Most critically, how did the allegation reach the public at all?…

Source: TechCrunch | Published: 2026-11-26 20:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/26/is-alice-huang-a-spy-or-not/

item.title: Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

The bigger Netflix gets, the easier it is to miss stuff. This is true of all digital platforms, of course, but it’s especially true of Netflix of late, as the streaming service’s lineup now also includes a growing library of reality shows, live-programming, and even games. It makes it easy for some of the best shows to zoom right past you, unnoticed — which almost happened to me with Midnight Diner.

Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return

A new season of Midnight Diner: Tokyo Stories is streaming now, though it’s easy to miss.

If you haven’t seen it, Midnight Diner is probably the most comforting thing available on Netflix. The show follows the patrons of a cozy little restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which is only open during the unusual hours of midnight to 7:00AM. This, in turn, attracts a unique blend of customers, who help each other out under the watchful eye of the shop’s owner (Kaoru Kobayashi), known only as “master.” The show aired for three seasons on Japanese TV, before being picked up by Netflix for a handful more under the subtitle Tokyo Stories.

What’s especially notable about the show’s return is the huge gap: season 2 of the Netflix iteration streamed in 2019, and it took seven years for it to come back. The break was so long that season 3’s first episode, which premiered in October, is about the restaurant’s struggles during the pandemic. There are a bunch of cute scenes of the diner’s regulars sneaking outside to check if the restaurant is open yet, and wondering if it will ever be able to. If nothing else, the break was a chance for the reliable master to finally take a vacation.

But once Midnight Diner’s new season gets going, it’s right back to everything that made it beloved. Each episode uses a different dish as a way of exploring a particular story. An overworked manga artist imagines the life he missed out on over plates of spicy konjac, while a pair of old friends reconnect while munching on pork cutlet sandwiches. What’s remarkable about the show is the way it balances being a charming, comforting watch with exploring truly difficult and heartbreaking topics. It’s the combination of sweetness and sadness that makes it work so well. It’s as likely to make you laugh as it is to make you cry.

And unlike most Netflix series, the whole season isn’t streaming all at once. Instead, new episodes come out every Tuesday; so far six of a planned 10 episodes are available. It’s a welcome way to spend an evening, as the show’s slow pace and warm sense of humanity can feel like all-too rare traits in the current streaming landscape.

But the main reason I’m even writing about Midnight Diner’s return is that it has been so easy to miss. There’s been next to no promotion for it — all I could find was a trailer on Netflix’s Japanese YouTube channel — and I only happened upon it accidentally after the initial premiere while browsing aimlessly through Netflix’s new releases. This, despite being someone who has watched and rewatched the previous seasons multiple times. You’d think I’d get a notification or something. Netflix has always been full of hidden gems, but now that it’s busier than ever, those gems are all the more hidden.

Amazon workers around the world plan strikes and protests on Black Friday and Cyber Monday

Protests are planned in Los Angeles and Chicago, while a union called for strikes at 11 Amazon sites in Germany.

Amazon workers and their supporters are once again set to go on strike and hold protests in more than 20 countries across the Black Friday and Cyber Monday period. Trade union federation UNI Global said the workers are pushing Amazon to negotiate with unions and respect employees' right to organize.

Teamsters are planning protests on Cyber Monday (November 30) in Los Angeles and Chicago. "As part of a global day of action, Amazon workers are demanding fair wages, safer working conditions, union recognition and respect on the job," a local Teamsters union representing workers in Southern California said.

German trade union Verdi called strikes at 11 Amazon sites on Black Friday (November 27). It claimed the wages the company pays often aren't enough for workers to live on and that warehouse work puts a "considerable physical strain on employees." According to Deutsche Presse-Agentur, Verdi also said Amazon uses digital trackers to keep close tabs on around 40,000 employees. An Amazon spokesman denied Verdi's claims and said average starting pay was above the German minimum wage.

Amazon workers and their allies are also set to mobilize in Canada, Australia, India, Bangladesh, Poland, Luxembourg, Brazil, Colombia, Uruguay, Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, Thailand, Fiji, Singapore, South Africa and elsewhere. UNI Global said this is the seventh year of the Make Amazon Pay campaign, which it convenes alongside Progressive International. Engadget has contacted Amazon for comment.

Earlier this month, workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, became the first in North America to win a union contract with Amazon. The terms of the three-year pact were imposed through binding arbitration. Among other things, the contract ensures pay increases (up to $29 CAD per hour by the time it ends), an extra week of vacation for workers with 10 years of service and severance of up to 18 weeks.

British Columbia's labor relations board ordered arbitration in August despite Amazon's objections. After an arbitrator imposed the agreement, Amazon vice-president J. Ofori Agboka said the process was "improper [and] unfair" and that it "defies common sense," adding that the company would take the issue to court if need be.

In April, the NLRB ordered Amazon to recognize and bargain with a union at the JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island, New York. The company is contesting the order. JFK8 workers voted to unionize in 2022, becoming the first Amazon warehouse in the US to do so.

item.title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on tariffs with useful context

Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat

There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the USA is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively toâ¦ repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

- US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China

- Published5 hours ago

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto.

The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.

It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.

Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.

This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment.

Source: BBC Business | Published: 2026-11-26 19:55 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Detailed analysis of Poundland's collapse

When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered

- Published

Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.

The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.

1. When will Poundland shops close?

This is the question that is most difficult to answer.

Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.

Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.

Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.

But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.

A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.

2. Why is Poundland closing down?

That depends on who you ask.

When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for Â£1 it was struggling. It suffered a Â£68m loss that year.

Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.

Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.

The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.

Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.

However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.

A spokeswoman said while the management team had made Â£100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a Â£70m loss to "around break-even".

"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."

Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.

Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.

3. What will happen to staff?

Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable.

The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about Â£70m - have now been released by the administrators.

This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.

But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.

But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.

If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on.

4. Will shoppers still be able to buy from Poundland?

In the short term, yes.

From 26 November you will not get a refund for goods if you change your mind about the purchase. If the item is faulty you will still get a refund.

The immediate reason Poundland collapsed was that Gordon Brothers locked up funds for the day-to-day running of the business, including to pay suppliers.

This meant that stock was running low at Poundland.

But those funds have now been unlocked, meaning suppliers can be paid, and supply chains can be re-established, at least in the short term.

If an item is on the shelves, then shoppers can buy it.

5. How will Poundland's collapse change the High Street?

That depends on what happens next.

Administrators will have to get the best value for creditors, which could mean selling the business as it stands.

But if Poundland is broken up, administrators could sell the brand without the stores, or the brand along with some of the stores, or the stores without the Poundland brand, to other retailers.

As a result there could be fewer discount stores on the High Street, providing less incentive for other retailers to keep prices down.

"Poundland is a place they go on the High Street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told the BBC on Thursday.

Poundland's customers may well turn to rival budget retailers in the hunt for bargains.

Get in touch

Are you a Poundland employee? Tell us your story. Get in touch.

Source: BBC Business | Published: 2026-11-26 17:21 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: ‘An epic fail’: Crypto world blasts Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’ for turning SBF’s crimes into a love story
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth look at Netflix series and its portrayal of a controversial figure

A new Netflix series that tells the story of crypto crook Sam Bankman-Fried is winning decent reviews from TV critics and the public. People familiar with the crypto industry are taking to social media to blast the makers of “The Altruists” for distorting the nature of Bankman-Fried’s relationship with one-time girlfriend, Caroline Ellison, and for depicting the convicted felons as misguided idealists. The series, which dropped last week, is also taking fire for suggesting without evidence that Binance founder Changpeng Zhao is the real villain of the story—a depiction some claim is rooted in anti-Chinese racism.

The 8-part series, which lists Barack and Michelle Obama as executive producers, is based on real-world events that led to the 2022 collapse of Bankman-Fried’s crypto exchange, FTX. A subsequent FBI investigation resulted in Ellison pleading guilty and testifying against her former boyfriend, who is currently serving 25 years in federal prison for defrauding customers of billions of dollars.

Filmmakers regularly take liberties in order to increase dramatic impact. In the case of “The Altruists”, though, critics say the series engages in outright falsehoods by minimizing Bankman-Fried’s crimes, and depicting him as a victim who acted under duress from Binance’s Zhao. Don Wilson, the CEO of the crypto market-making firm DRW, posted a widely-shared clip from The Altruists showing Zhao and Bankman-Fried on X, describing it as “preposterous” and “an epic fail.”

This is an epic fail by Netflix. Recasting this as something @SBF_FTX and Caroline were forced to do in order to placate @cz_binance – instead of highlighting the effective altruist ethos that drove them to commit yet another crime is preposterous. https://t.co/bV6IsoG6mE

— Don Wilson (@drwconvexity) November 22, 2026

The clip itself shows Zhao’s character telling Ellison and Bankman-Fried that FTX is failing to grow fast enough to justify an early investment he made in the exchange, and declaring that he will financially destroy the exchange if the pair fail to collude with him in a criminal trading scheme.

While Zhao was indeed an early investor in FTX, the issue of coercion never came up at Bankman-Fried’s criminal trial, and there is no evidence the exchange depicted in the clip ever took place. Another crypto industry vet on X likewise objected to another scene for “making SBF and Caroline look like innocent victims who were bullied” by Zhao.

Netflix portrayed @cz_binance as a complete moron in its new FTX movie while making SBF and Caroline look like innocent victims who were bullied.

Who the hell wrote this script? pic.twitter.com/HjAwQ3N3W9

— Stacy Muur (@stacy_muur) November 20, 2026

Others objected to the heavy Cantonese accent affected by Zhao’s character, played by Terry Chen, complaining it promoted stereotypes. Zhao himself wrote on X, “hmm… I grew up in Canada, worked in the New York, Tokyo, many places. I almost never felt being targeted by racism. But something to think about…”. Veteran crypto journalist Laura Shin expressed a similar sentiment, stating “I’m just going to say it: Racism has to have played a role in how they portrayed [Zhao]. There’s no other explanation.”

Aside from the depictions of Zhao, other viewers complained that “The Altruists” wrongly portrayed Ellison as the mastermind behind a series of accounting frauds used to conceal holes in the balance sheet of FTX and of Bankman-Fried’s hedge fund, Alameda Research. This contradicts contemporary news accounts and evidence from the criminal trial, which unambiguously pointed to Bankman-Fried as the one responsible for a series of frauds.

Those weighing in to complain about the depictions included FTX’s former COO, Constance Wang, who wrote, “Maybe you’ll enjoy The Altruists as a romantic comedy. For those of us who watched it together, it felt like someone else’s story with our names attached.”

Meanwhile, some critics of “The Altruists” suggested that the numerous inaccuracies could be explained in part for political reasons. Lawyer Hailey Lennon pointed to the production’s ties to the Obamas and Bankman-Fried’s hefty donations to the Democratic party, writing “The framing of the movie as some love story and to make SBF look more innocent is even more calculated than I initially realized. Always follow the money.”

The Altruists was produced by Michelle and Barak Obama

SBF publicly donated $39.8 million to Democratic candidates and aligned outside groups during the 2021–2022 election cycle

The framing of the movie as some love story and to make SBF look more innocent is even more… pic.twitter.com/pzvWJP7tUH

— Hailey Lennon (@HaileyLennonBTC) October 9, 2026

Others on social media likewise pointed to the Obamas’ involvement, and Bankman-Fried’s donations to the Democratic party—including $5.2 million to former President Joe Biden’s campaign—as an explanation for the film’s depictions.

Bankman-Fried, who remains incarcerated in federal prison in California, has failed to express remorse for stealing over $8 billion from FTX customers and investors. He is currently slated to be released around 2047.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-26 17:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: Global stocks move upward despite shock warning from Panmure Liberum analyst who sold all equities in his personal portfolio
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of global stock market trends with expert opinion

With America offline for Thanksgiving, the rest of the world enjoyed a break from the market chaos caused by U.S. tariff policy, U.S. AI investment, and U.S. interest rate rises.

In Asia, stocks broadly rose. Europe was up strongly. And although New York was closed for the holiday, S&P 500 futures were up.

Nasdaq 100 futures were up 0.63%, and Nvidia was up 1.29% in after-market trading.

None of this should be happening!

There is nothing but bad news on the horizon, multiple Wall Street and London City analysts said in emails to Fortune.

The most dramatic warning came from Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement (who writes a well-regarded Substack on investing whose subtitle is “Thoughts on financial markets by a grumpy, middle-aged German. What more do you want?”)

He gave a video talk in which he announced he was selling all the equities—all of them!—in his personal investment portfolio because of the recent selloff in the S&P 500: “I think that we are heading towards a major bear market with more than 30% drawdown risk.” His official forecast for 2027 is that the S&P 500 will sink to 5,000—a level that right now seems unthinkable. His concern is that the index is currently trading below its 200-day moving average: “As Paul Tudor Jones the famous investor once said, nothing good happens below the 200-day moving average.”

“It doesn’t look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year”

Three factors are driving the gloom:

Firstly, inflation is still too high. The Fed’s preferred metric, the index for personal consumption expenditures, was up year-over-year to 3.8% in October, up from 3.7% the month before. “Undesirably strong,” as Lawrence Werther and Brendan Stuart of Daiwa Capital Markets said in a note. That will almost certainly push the Fed into raising interest rates in December in order to make money more scarce—a scenario that generally augurs poorly for stocks.

Many analysts pointed to a speech given Monday by John Williams, the President of the New York Fed. He all but telegraphed that the Fed was going to kick the rate up soon: “We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2 percent goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis. There is still work to do to get that done.” (There is a good analysis of the speech by economist Claudia Sahm here.)

Secondly, the U.S. economy is strong, so the Fed will feel it has the breathing space to dampen inflationary demand.

New jobless claims came in near their three-year low, and the long-term trend in jobless claims continues to point down, according to Thomas Simons and Blake Birkins of Jefferies.

“The big highlight … is GDP, which at 4.3% shows that the economy is booming, but unfortunately the inflation data is still too high and is unlikely to convince the Fed to remain on hold,” Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management, told Fortune via email.

“Between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn’t look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year,” he said.

Hold that thought!

Although U.S. stocks may be sliding, that’s mostly because the tech sector is a fiasco right now. Outside the tech sector (and the outperformance of European stocks vs U.S. stocks is a good example of this), things are going rather well. Before the turkey holiday, 372 stocks in the S&P 500 moved higher, and the equal-weight index was up 0.82% on the day, Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid noticed.

- S&P 500 futures were up 0.66% this morning. The U.S. markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday but had dropped 0.25% in the previous day’s trading.

- In Europe, the Stoxx 600 was up 2%, and the U.K.’s FTSE 100 rose 1.77%.

- Asia: South Korea’s KOSPI was up 0.29%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was up 0.86%. India’s Nifty 50 was up 0.25%. China’s CSI 300 was up 0.06%.

- Brent crude rose to $96 per barrel.

- Bitcoin was at $60,212.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-26 16:47 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Reddit’s stock has taken a battering this year, but its COO says it’s barely started banking ‘over a decade of karma’ from devoted users
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Discussion of Reddit's engagement and financial challenges

Reddit boasts engagement metrics that would be the envy of many other online platforms: Over 80% of its monetization comes from loyal, logged-in users, who spend eight times as much time on the site in their fifth year as they did in their first.

In its Q3 earnings call in October, Reddit’s CEO, Steve Huffman, said Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode were leading to a decline in search referrals to the site, the lifeblood of many social and media-adjacent businesses. The market did not like the implications, and the share price dropped from just shy of $130 apiece to a little under $91 overnight.

Chief Operating Officer Jen Wong told Fortune in an exclusive interview that some factors were lost in translation. The shifting relationship between Reddit and search engines “requires a different kind of partnership,” she said, rather than any separation. If anything, Wong believes Reddit is well-positioned to navigate the new era of online information gathering.

In their first year on Reddit, users tend to spend five minutes a day on the app or website. By their fifth year, that figure rises to 40 minutes, Wong tells Fortune. The number of “communities” (topic-focused discussion groups) that users are in jumps from 10 in the first year to more than 100 by their fifth.

“Reddit is really interesting because we have users who have over a decade of karma,” Wong said. “Reddit typically gets you as a young adult, and then you season over time in this incredible way. If you look at the chart, it’s very consistent.”

Wong sees users’ changing life stages reflected in the communities they join: “[They’ve] gone through life with Reddit. You started as a student, you got your first rental place, you got married, you had kids, and we see kind of your life’s journey.

“You just never age out of Reddit because all of those life stages are available to you on Reddit, and you’re always going through something that you have to traverse.”

Navigating different life stages appears to be a key differentiator of the Reddit platform. In 2024, an article published in “Higher Education Research and Development” found that one in three students use Reddit for study help, ahead of TikTok at 14.9% and Instagram at 12.7%. YouTube leads the pack, with more than 90% of the 1,000 students surveyed using it for educational purposes.

The site’s leadership wants to expand on that function. In early November, Reddit launched Reddit Reviews, organizing product feedback across multiple communities to provide overall ratings.

“Logged-in users season very, very well, which is another motivation for us to say we want more logged-in users, because we want the opportunity to teach you about all these other aspects of Reddit,” Wong adds, “Not just the information and retrieval part of Reddit, but the part of Reddit that is around the connection, the communities, and the conversation.”

The moderation question

Every media platform needs to maintain or grow its audience. But Reddit has a unique problem: It has more than 100,000 “communities,” according to various reports, all of which have volunteer moderators. These moderators are unpaid and are not Reddit employees, instead choosing to spend their free time building their communities and ensuring the content is fit for its purpose.

But with ever-evolving channels and new voices within them, demand for experienced moderators is high—in fact, Reddit even has a dedicated page where communities can recruit volunteer moderators.

In the recruitment group, individuals are either looking for or offering moderation skills for hours a day, on a daily basis. Posts include requests for moderators in specific time zones, often for about 3 hours a day.

But Wong says even if Reddit wanted to bring its moderators in-house and pay them, they probably wouldn’t take it. While moderators are interested in earning, she said, they didn’t want strings attached: “They really like their independence from us, to be able to say, ‘This is our community, we set the rules, and this is how we want to operate.’

“Our relationship with moderators, I think, has greatly improved. I’ve been with Reddit eight, almost nine years, and where at the beginning we were not investing as much as we could in creating moderator tools and making their lives better in terms of reducing some of the repetitive work, over the last few years we’ve done a much better job also applying AI to help them with a toolkit, so that they can spend the time on the things that they really care about.”

But overall, Wong is bullish on Reddit’s long-term position in the age of AI. “Reddit is basically the taste layer of the internet. No model and no recommendation system can be good, I think, without a dash of Reddit in it, because you just don’t have the freshness of information. That adds value in so many places.”

item.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Report on Norse Atlantic's financial troubles and potential collapse

Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse

The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.

The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.

The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.

Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.

Flight disruption

One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.

The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.

PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.

In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.

Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.

"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".

He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra Â£1,000.

Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.

"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.

"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."

Advice for passengers

Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.

Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."

Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.

Low-cost, long-haul

Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.

It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.

But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.

Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.

This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.

In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.

In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.

After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".

However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".

Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.

Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May. The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.

If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.

item.title: U.S. Judge rules FCC violated ABC's free speech rights to please Trump
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Legal perspective on FCC's actions and free speech

U.S. Judge rules FCC violated ABC's free speech rights to please Trump

U.S. judge rules FCC violated ABC’s free speech rights to please Trump

A federal judge has blocked President Trump and his administration from taking action to challenge the ABC television network's broadcast licenses, finding it to be an unconstitutional punishment for satire, commentary and news coverage that Trump doesn't like.

In her preliminary injunction filed Wednesday, U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan found that the federal agency's early reviews represented retaliation for speech the Trump administration resented.

Such perceived offenses included late-night host Jimmy Kimmel's jabs at the president, the critical remarks of hosts on the chat show The View, and the moderation of a presidential debate in September 2024.

ABC and its corporate parent, the Walt Disney Co., serve six of the 10 largest markets in the U.S., including New York, Los Angeles, and Houston. They contribute significantly to the network's bottom line.

"Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face -- loss of their broadcast licenses -- the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," Judge AliKhan wrote.

She rejected the Trump administration's motion to dismiss the lawsuit from ABC and Disney challenging the review of the local licenses. Usually the licenses last eight years and are up for review on a staggered basis. They are rarely taken away.

In her ruling, AliKhan relied heavily on public statements and social media postings in which Trump attacked ABC and Disney, as well as posts by Trump's pick as the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, Brendan Carr.

"What started in 2020 as questions about how ABC 'can keep getting a license' if it 'report[s] fake news,' ... has crescendoed into repeated calls for the Commission to strip ABC's broadcast licenses for their editorial decisions," she wrote. "The court counts eleven such calls made by President Trump over the past two years -- the most recent being in July 2026."

And the judge cited the administration's "tangible steps toward enforcing President Trump and Commissioner Carr's repeated threats to strip the Plaintiff Stations of their licenses."

"Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders," Judge AliKhan wrote.

Carr did not respond to NPR's request for comment Wednesday evening.

ABC hailed the ruling in a statement as "an important victory for the First Amendment."

Among the targets of ire from Trump and Carr was ABC's decision not to broadcast Trump's July 2026 Oval Office address on its television network. ABC's legal team said the network streamed it on its digital news service, but would not have done so absent the political pressure from the FCC.

It is one of several examples of newsroom decisions made under duress, the network's lawyers said in court. Kimmel's interview with then-Democratic U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico of Texas was uploaded to YouTube instead of being aired on ABC's late night television show. (Talarico won election to the U.S. Senate earlier this month.) And The View stopped hosting candidates for political office in 2026 in the months ahead of the fall elections.

Judge AliKhan rejected arguments from the FCC that the court could not take action because it has not yet rejected the license renewals. The very act of premature review for retaliatory reasons is unconstitutional and unlawful – and hard to reverse, she wrote.

"For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct," said Anna M. Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner on the FCC. "Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I've said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side."

This ruling comes six weeks after a parallel ruling in a case brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico against the Trump administration for restricting access. Officials barred journalists from the three news outlets from the White House after Trump lambasted them for "purposefully negative" news coverage.

In that case, U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly issued a preliminary injunction, writing, "It is not hard to conclude that President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him." That, he wrote, represents a form of unlawful retaliation. The administration is appealing. And despite the ruling, the White House continues to limit the three news outlets' access to the president.

Disney's shift in strategy

In December 2024, just a few weeks before Trump became president for the second time, Disney agreed to settle a lawsuit Trump had brought against ABC News by paying $16 million, including legal fees. Many outside legal experts believed Disney would have had the upper hand if it had stuck it out in court.

Now under new leadership, Disney has drawn the line at what it contends is a threat to its broadcast licenses — and profits — over its editorial independence.

"We're very principled on this," Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told CNBC in August, just days before the company filed its lawsuit. "We're going to stand up to what we believe is journalistic integrity, and we're not going to be told how to run that side of our business." D'Amaro became chief executive in March.

The FCC had already kicked off an investigation of Disney's diversity practices when it announced the review.

Carr, the agency's chief, has said it initiated the review of Disney's broadcast licenses over concerns that the company engaged in racial discrimination through its diversity, equity and inclusion actions.…
