item.title: Concrete Floods Walls and an Elevated East River Park Now Protect a Swath of Lower Manhattan
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant environmental project with technical detail and useful vocabulary.

The most critical parts of the East Side Coastal Resiliency Project’s flood protection system may be the ones New Yorkers will never see.

In the new John V. Lindsay East River Park in lower Manhattan, engineers have been working on an ambitious challenge: protecting the park and surrounding neighborhoods from coastal flooding.

Beneath a 2-foot-thick concrete wall designed to hold back coastal flooding, steel structures extend deep underground, anchoring the barrier and helping prevent water from finding a way underneath it.

Depending on the location, engineers supported the wall with steel sheets driven into the ground or large underground pipes. The latter were used in areas where existing utility lines prevented the installation of a continuous barrier, explained Eric Ilijevich, a director at the city’s Department of Design and Construction.

But keeping floodwater from flowing over the wall is only part of the challenge. Water can also seep through the soil beneath it. To prevent this, engineers installed underground barriers using a technique called jet grouting, which involves injecting cement-based material into the ground to seal gaps.

The greatest danger is not seepage during a single storm, but the cumulative damage caused by repeated flooding. Over time, water moving through the soil could erode the ground supporting the wall, potentially undermining the entire structure.

The system, nearing completion, is designed to protect against flooding up to 16.5 feet above sea level, but engineers built in an additional two feet of protection, bringing it to 18.5 feet in case the team “was wrong in their projection,” said Joseph G. Lione, associate commissioner for coastal resiliency at the Department of Design and Construction of New York City.

The East Side Coastal Resiliency Project, which extends from East 25th Street along the East River to Montgomery Street, between the Williamsburg and Manhattan Bridges, was developed in response to the devastation caused by Hurricane Sandy in 2012, when a storm surge flooded large parts of Lower Manhattan, including the neighborhoods surrounding East River Park. The disaster exposed the vulnerability of the city’s waterfront communities to coastal flooding, a threat expected to grow as sea level rises.

The $1.45 billion project aims to protect approximately 110,000 New Yorkers on Manhattan’s East Side from coastal flooding. It involves raising sections of East River Park by 8 to 10 feet and installing a system of floodwalls, berms and movable floodgates along the waterfront on either side of the elevated park.

Construction began in 2020 and is expected to be completed in 2027. Right now, only the northern section of the park is still under construction. “We’ve successfully completed over $1 billion” in construction, said Lione.

More than half of the park has now reopened to the public. Lione said the city was required to keep at least 41 percent of the park open throughout construction.

“They did a good job at keeping the park open,” said Wendy Brawer, a member of the Community Advisory Group and director of Green Map System, a sustainability nonprofit.

Raising the park has also improved accessibility by bringing it roughly to street level, as the city built bridges for better pedestrian access from the Lower East Side. “If the water rises, it will go on the steps; the park is now too high to be flooded,” said Lione.

The rebuilt park will also feature a continuous bike lane, “which the community really wants,” said Lione.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

The project also relies on an extensive flood-protection system, much of it hidden beneath the rebuilt park.

The East Side Coastal Resiliency Project first took shape twelve years ago, in 2014.

But in 2018, the city announced a major redesign that would require raising and rebuilding much of East River Park. The decision sparked fierce opposition from residents and environmental activists, who opposed the destruction of mature trees and the prolonged loss of access to one of the neighborhood’s few green spaces during construction. “It was difficult to start with activists a few years ago,” Lione remembers.

Despite protests and legal challenges, construction began near East 25th Street, at the northern end of the project, before reaching East River Park in December 2021. “Now, we have very little pushback,” said Lione. “People understood what it was for.”

But opposition to the project has not disappeared.

“We still exist,” said Pat Arnow, co-founder of the East River Park Action, one of the major community advocacy groups that has opposed the city’s redesign of the park since 2018.

Arnow is no longer calling for a different flood-protection plan, although she maintains that “they could have provided the same amount of flood protection without destroying the entire park.”

For East River Park Action, the main concern is now the lack of shade in the rebuilt park following the removal of mature trees. The newly planted trees are still small, offering little protection from the sun. A few umbrellas provide some shade, but large stretches of the park remain exposed, with concrete surfaces absorbing heat.

“Those little umbrellas don’t do too much,” Arnow said. Brawer estimates that it will take 40 years for the new trees to provide comparable benefits.

New York City plans to plant 2,000 trees, said Lione. So far, the construction team planted about 600.

Lione said many of the removed trees were in poor condition because of exposure to saltwater from the East River. This is something Arnow believes is not true: “We have proof that they were growing,” she said.…

item.title: Tequila’s hangover: How the drink’s success drove deforestation in Mexico
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains the environmental impact of a popular product with clear context and useful vocabulary.

- Between 2017 and 2022, increased tequila production in Mexico drove greater demand for its raw material, blue agave, but also caused social and environmental damages.

- The tequila regulatory body and state authorities have failed to halt the expansion of agave into forest areas.

- Jalisco lost around 23,368 hectares (about 57,740 acres) of forest annually between 2019 and 2021, a period that coincided with the expansion of blue agave fields.

- Between 2017 and 2025, the area planted with tequila agave nationwide increased by 218%, reaching 276,043 hectares (about 682,110 acres).

For decades, Manuel García Castro has grown corn, squash and beans to feed his family and livestock. In 2019, he followed in the footsteps of prosperous local farmers and dedicated a portion of his land in the highlands of Jalisco, western Mexico, to planting blue agave, used to make tequila.

A friend persuaded him to plant 15,000 shoots on 3 hectares (7.41 acres) of his land and in other areas where his cattle grazed. García Castro would provide the labor; his friend, the capital. “We have to give it a shot to see if there’s some way to make money from something else,” was their thinking, he told Mongabay. Back then, raising livestock didn’t bring in much money and expenses were high.

They invested 500,000 Mexican pesos (around $25,300) in plants, pesticides and fertilizers, not including payment for García Castro’s own labor and that of the farm worker who helped him. Four years later, in 2023, hopes of selling the blue agave began to fade. Sale prices per kilogram plunged by as much as 92% compared with those between 2017 and 2019. The business was no longer profitable in the short term. Manuel García and his partner abandoned the fields two years ago.

The tequila boom

Tequila has a protected designation of origin in the states of Guanajuato, Nayarit, Tamaulipas, Michoacán and Jalisco. The drink is considered a national brand and a symbol of Mexican identity.

Over the past decade, the tequila industry has boosted its exports and developed premium and niche brands.

Between 2016 and 2025, the Tequila Regulatory Council (CRT) recorded an increase in production from 273.3 million liters (72.2 million gallons) to 583.5 million l (154 million gal). Production peaked at 651.4 million liters in 2022.

In 2020, Mexico exported 286.7 million l (75.7 million gal) of tequila, and 418.9 million l (110.6 million gal) two years later.

Between 2017 and 2018, the sale price of blue agave remained between 26 and 30 pesos per kilogram (just under $2), peaking in 2021 at 32 pesos per kilogram, according to industry website agaves.pro.

Those economic conditions attracted new producers, including Manuel García, who replaced corn on his plots with blue agave.

Agave replacing forests

In 2019, when blue agave prices boomed, Maximiano Bautista Andalón, a geospatial specialist and academic at the Western Institute of Technology and Higher Education (Iteso) in Mexico, began using satellite imagery to document the expansion of agave farms in Jalisco.

That year, he counted roughly 100,000 hectares (about 247,100 acres) planted with agave only in Jalisco. Six years later, the area had reached 200,000 hectares (494,210 acres). The researcher found that this expansion affected natural ecosystems and created monocultures, as many farmers stopped growing food while others took over forest and rainforest areas.

“Agave is a complex issue, especially because of how it was distributed: in areas with pine forest, oak forest, or right next to mid or high-altitude areas where other crops used to grow,” Bautista Andalón said. “It is a highly industrial model in which almost no other little plant survived among the agave fields.”

In 2023, a report by the University of Guadalajara and a coalition of 43 states and provinces from 11 countries, including Mexico, highlighted the expansion of agave production for tequila and mezcal as one of the drivers of forest loss.

“The increase in demand and prices for these distilled beverages, especially tequila, has triggered a cyclical expansion of agave cultivation into these ecosystems,” the report warns. Between 2019 and 2021, a period coinciding with the tequila boom, Jalisco recorded its highest deforestation levels losing 23,368 hectares (about 57,740 acres) annually.

Neither the National Forestry Commission (Conafor) nor the Jalisco Department of Environment and Territorial Development responded to Mongabay’s interview requests for this article.

The agave landscape around the town of Tequila, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in western central Mexico, has spread indiscriminately across the state.

By analyzing satellite imagery, researcher Bautista Andalón found that some of the newest agave plantations were preceded by fires, land clearing or tree cutting, or were established near water sources important to local communities.

Southern Jalisco is also experiencing the impacts of agave expansion. University of Guadalajara researcher Oscar Raúl Mancilla is part of a scientific group that has studied land-use change in the region for 20 years and found that blue agave cultivation increased by 60% in the Autlán region, in southwestern Jalisco, between 2015 and 2026.

“Thousands of hectares have shifted from tropical dry forest, livestock farming or other types of crops to agave cultivation,” Mancilla told Mongabay.

Crossing the boundary

The area planted with tequila agave nationwide increased 218% between 2017 and 2025, according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development

In 2021, the Tequila Regulatory Council (CRT) and the Jalisco government implemented the Environmentally Responsible Agave (ARA) certification to guarantee deforestation-free brands that comply with international sustainability standards.…

item.title: Relearning how to live with wolves in Europe
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engages with a conservation issue in Europe with a nuanced perspective and useful vocabulary.

Across much of Europe, gray wolves were hunted to near extinction by the mid-20th century. In the past couple of decades, though, strict protections have helped the population rebound in some countries.

The return of the gray wolf (Canis lupus) has posed a conundrum. Conservation groups view it as a conservation success. However, wolves sometimes kill livestock, which brings them into conflict with some farmers. In response, the European Union recently weakened the wolf protections, making it easier to hunt the animals.

In a conversation with Mongabay’s Mike DiGirolamo, social scientist Emu-Felicitas Ostermann-Miyashita, from the Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology, argues the situation shouldn’t be seen as wolves versus livestock, but rather “livestock with wolves.”

“Looking back to the point when wolves were abundant in the landscape, it has always been livestock with wolves because people had no other choice,” Ostermann-Miyashita says in the Newscast episode. “And that’s why in the countries where there has been persistent wolf populations without them being exterminated … these protection measures are intact, like fencing or putting the sheep into enclosures during the evening to prevent livestock predation.”

By contrast, landscapes where wolves have been extinct for decades or centuries have become more populated with humans who have become habituated to living without wolves, Ostermann-Miyashita says. So the knowledge of how to protect livestock from large carnivores has also been lost, she adds.

Ostermann-Miyashita has studied the conflict between humans and wolves in Germany, where the canids were once exterminated and have since returned. In early 2025, she published suggestions for wolf-livestock coexistence.

One of these suggestions is for European countries to collaboratively assess their approaches to managing interactions with wolves. Ostermann-Miyashita says there are four broad ways to manage large carnivores across Europe: protect livestock using methods like fencing; provide compensation or financial measures for livestock losses; pay people for letting carnivores persist on their land; and lethal control.

Ostermann-Miyashita says it’s important that countries like Germany, which now have decades of experience with the return of wolves, share their experience with countries that are newer to wolf reintroduction, like the Netherlands or Belgium. This way, everybody doesn’t have “to go through the same process to adapt to the species,” Ostermann-Miyashita adds.

The effectiveness of each management method is highly context-dependent, Ostermann-Miyashita says, adding that more research is needed.

There are some studies to suggest that killing wolves, for example, may reduce damage temporarily by getting rid of a pack or an individual, but another wolf pack can fill its gap and the damage can restart, Ostermann-Miyashita says. “So at the moment, I would say there’s not enough evidence to say whether lethal control can be effective or not.”

item.title: International marine biodiversity conference emphasizes the unsung and the unknown
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Focuses on an international conference with implications for marine biodiversity, offering a broad view.

- More than 800 people gathered Nov. 17-20 in Bruges, Belgium, for the 7th World Conference on Marine Biodiversity.

- The conference covered a wide range of science and conservation topics, including the impacts of deep-sea mining; it featured a screening of a documentary that follows scientists on a deep-sea mission to an area in the Pacific Ocean targeted for deep-sea mining.

- The conference took place just after the midway point of the U.N. Ocean Decade, which runs 2021-2030, and the organizers called it a chance to take stock of progress.

BRUGES, Belgium — More than 800 people gathered for the 7th World Conference on Marine Biodiversity, held Nov. 17-20, in Bruges, Belgium.

The conference took on topics as varied as deep-sea mining impacts, ocean-related art, citizen science, methods for working with large datasets, environmental DNA and taxonomy. Yet it also raised broader questions about how people value the ocean and whether current approaches serve the health of marine ecosystems. David Obura, founder of Kenyan marine research nonprofit CORDIO East Africa, gave the opening keynote, calling for a shift in thinking about how people use the sea.

“If we just use the same values that have historically driven current markets to maximise further benefits from oceans … we just drive oceans farther into decline,” Obura told Mongabay in an email recapping his talk. “We’ve seen this already. Instead we need to apply values that prioritise balance and sustainability across multiple co-benefits, and deliver long term security and prosperity over short term gain.”

Many participants emphasized the need to catalog the world’s marine biodiversity and draw attention to overlooked species or those not yet described.

“We want to see how many species are there because we want to know what we need to conserve,” Bert Hoeksema, a guest researcher at Naturalis Biodiversity Center, a museum in the Netherlands, told Mongabay. Hoeksema has studied corals for more than four decades and recently published a paper identifying key countries involved in the marine aquarium trade. “There are so many species that are not known.”

The conference took place just after the midway point of the U.N. Ocean Decade, which runs 2021-2030. The initiative, decided by the U.N. General Assembly in 2017, aims to promote ocean science and use it to guide policy to support ocean health.

“It’s an excellent moment to take stock,” Leen Vandepitte, a conference organizer and project manager of the Flanders Marine Institute’s (VLIZ) data center, told Mongabay. “Where are we? Where do we still need to go?”

Worming out

The conference has its roots in the European marine research community. The first edition took place in Valencia, Spain, in 2008, near the end of a five-year EU-funded research project on marine biodiversity. The 2026 conference happened to follow a marine conservation conference held Nov. 13-16 in Edinburgh.

For the seventh edition, scientists, conservationists, policymakers and industry members gathered in Bruges, in Belgium’s Dutch-speaking Flanders region. They addressed issues such as plastic pollution in the ocean, how climate and fisheries impacts interact, and mangrove restoration in Latin America and the Caribbean.

VLIZ, the conference’s organizer, hosts the World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS), an inventory of the more than 250,000 marine species that are currently known to science. About 350 taxonomists help maintain WoRMS, adding some 2,000 newly described species each year, while estimates of the total number of marine species that exist range from 500,000 to 2 million, according to VLIZ.

Among the overlooked animals discussed at the conference were nematodes, small roundworms that live in the seafloor in astonishing numbers, which serve a key role as nutrient recyclers. Lara Macheriotou, a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University, spoke about how a deep-sea mining trial affected nematode diversity, drawing on samples collected before, during and after.

The Flanders-based company Global Sea Mineral Resources conducted the trial in 2021 in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone of the Pacific Ocean, a deep-sea abyssal plain located between Hawai‘i and Mexico. Ghent University, which is also in Flanders, is home to several researchers studying the potential impacts of deep-sea mining for polymetallic nodules, which are potato-sized lumps containing sought-after metals such as manganese. Many animals, like nematodes, live on them or in their crevices. Deep-sea mining hasn’t been done at a commercial scale.

Ann Vanreusel, an emeritus professor of marine biology at Ghent University who attended the conference, said the prospect of deep-sea mining was “concerning because you’re impacting a pristine untouched environment.” It also changed the nature of her work, which had been pure research aimed at building core knowledge of the sea and then became more oriented around mining-related questions.

“I could do 30 years of fundamental research with not any societal connection, and then all of a sudden you get deep-sea mining,” she told Mongabay.

Many sessions at the conference dealt with scientific methods such as environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis, which can detect the presence of species — many species, all at once — from traces of DNA they leave in the water. Such powerful molecular techniques can save scientists a lot of time and money. Yet several scientists stressed the continued importance of old-school taxonomic work that involves examining specimens to identify and describe them. Vanreusel said she was worried that this taxonomic expertise was being lost.

One session focused on the need for greater support and investment for taxonomic work in Africa.…

item.title: How Uttarakhand’s women farmers are reviving endangered Himalayan medicinal plants
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Describes a community-driven conservation effort with cultural and environmental significance.

- In Uttarakhand, India, high-altitude farmers are cultivating medicinal herbs that are in decline in the wild, helping these species revive.

- Women perform most of the labor in this enterprise, earning money to support their families and children’s education.

- Obstacles remain, however, as farmers often must obtain official certification requiring proof of land ownership — and only a small percentage of women own land in the region.

- “Because of this, we insist on issuing the certification in the female farmer’s name,” says Shivam Pandey of Udyogini, an NGO working toward women’s empowerment.

RAMNI, Uttarakhand, India — At state fairs across Uttarakhand, while most farmers set up stalls featuring local millet varieties, Guddi Devi and her fellow farmers showcase saplings of high-altitude medicinal plants.

“In the past, people used to bring kutki [Picrorhiza kurroa] and other herbs like sugandha bala [Valeriana jatamansi] from the bugyals [alpine meadows]. Since everyone was going there, digging and harvesting, everything was becoming extinct in the alpine meadows. It is a cumbersome task to even reach there, so you won’t easily find [these herbs] there anymore,” Guddi said.

Situated in the Indian Himalayan region, Uttarakhand’s medicinal plants, growing at 2,000 meters (6,500 feet) or more, are highly sought after. Traditionally, locals traveled up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) on foot to collect herbs like kutki — widely used to bring down fevers — when access to medical care was scarce. Globally, market demand for medicinal and aromatic plants (MAPs) has grown substantially, with $4.2 billion in exports in 2023, and due to unsustainable harvesting practices and overexploitation, many species are at risk.

With growing concern, scientists say controlled agricultural cultivation can be a sustainable method to meet the pharmaceutical demands for these plants.

“Uttarakhand has diverse agro-climatic conditions, therefore, mountain villages located at about 2500 to 3000 m altitude are suitable locations for domestication or for cultivation of high altitude medicinal and aromatic plants,” known as MAPs, Chandra P. Kuniyal, a scientist at the Herbal Research and Development Institute (HRDI), said in an email.

Since men of the hills often leave their homes for better financial opportunities, it is the women living in villages at high altitudes — where these MAPs thrive in the cold — who have become the cornerstone of medicinal herb conservation efforts.

“The feminization of hill agriculture is there because mostly the men migrate outside for their job,” said K.S. Kanwal, scientist at G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment.

Conservation through cultivation

“The goal is to conserve these species outside their natural habitats,” Kanwal said.

India is home to 8,000 medicinal plant species, of which 140 have been prioritized for national cultivation support. Uttarakhand has listed 38 such species. Because rising commercial demand threatens wild populations, both in situ (in-nature) and ex situ (off-site cultivation) strategies are being deployed.

In situ conservation focuses on preserving species within their natural environment by restricting harvesting or creating protected areas, providing protection to the species as well as the critical habitat. Kuniyal notes that in remote mountain terrains, limited enforcement personnel and strong illicit trade networks make in situ protection insufficient on its own.

This gave way to ex situ conservation strategies, particularly the cultivation of MAPS. Scientists assess species based on market demand and threat levels defined by the IUCN and the Indian Red Data Book.

“After prioritizing target species at state and regional levels, comprehensive conservation plans are drawn up, raising plants in institute nurseries and establishing new propagation sites directly in farmers’ fields,” Kanwal said.

It is mostly women who are engaged in agriculture in the mountains. “Not only do they know how to cultivate but they are micro-observers too. If there is something, an issue, any disease, another thing, they immediately inform us,” Kanwal said.

While women are key agricultural workers here, men help in transporting the material to nearby collection or purchasing destinations and also marketing the herbs.

Ecosystem conservation

Once species are selected by government scientific bodies like HRDI and the GB Pant Institute, saplings are distributed to high-altitude farmers either directly or through partner NGOs like Udyogini, which works with thousands of farmers across six regions in Uttarakhand. The central goal of Udyogini is women’s empowerment. For women in extreme remote villages, agriculture is a source of autonomy.

“Udyogini provides us with 2,000 free saplings for a 1-naali plot,” 200 square meters or 2,160 square feet, Guddi explained. “We receive plants based on our land size, and the plots are officially registered. With experience, we now know exactly how many plants a field can accommodate and how to plant them properly.”

Because these herbs need cooler conditions, cultivation cannot take place in lower village plots. The women farmers hike half a kilometer (0.3 miles) uphill to tend fields that were previously wastelands. Beyond farm plots, project interventions have also reintroduced rare and threatened species back into six degraded high-altitude pasture lands called bugyals.

The project also addresses another major agricultural challenge: human-wildlife conflict. Traditional crops are frequently destroyed by wild boars and monkeys, but wild animals often leave medicinal herbs untouched, offering farmers a viable way to utilize abandoned land. (In a recent study, for example, it was shown that some MAPs, containing antifeedants or chemicals that are unpalatable to pests, were less attractive to elephants than rice crops.)…

item.title: US gains foothold in race for Africa’s critical minerals in Kenya’s Mrima Hill project
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Reports on a mining project with implications for Africa's critical minerals, though less detailed.

Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for Mining and Blue Economy has announced that the mining ministry has issued a “notice of intention” to award the tender for the development of the Mrima Hill mining project to U.S.-based mining consortium Frontier Minerals. Mrima Hill is thought to be rich in critical minerals sought after by electronics, aerospace and energy industries,

“The choice of an American consortium reflects a commitment from the Kenyan government to develop their mining sector in a transparent manner that will bring market-leading innovation to Kenya, ensure local value addition, and create jobs and economic benefits [for the U.S. and Kenya],” said the U.S. State Department in a statement.

The U.S.’s interest in Kenya’s critical minerals is part of Washington’s effort to diversify supply chains and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the critical minerals market.

According to Kenya’s Ministry of Mining, Mrima Hill holds at least 5.8 million tons of material that may contain niobium pentoxide, which is used to make niobium, a critical element used in electronics, the aerospace industry and energy storage. Two-thirds of the world’s niobium reserves are currently held by Brazil; the remaining third are mostly held by China. The region is also potentially home to millions of metric tons of rare earth elements (REEs), which are key components in the manufacture of batteries, magnets, mobile phones and cars.

While in its statement, the U.S. State Department emphasized transparency in the mining sector, Kenyan civil society organizations raised concerns that the process has not fully included local communities. According to Kenya’s Ministry of Mining, a company must first obtain the consent of local communities before it can secure a mining license. However, in June 2026, the Centre for Litigation Trust (CLT) filed a petition with the High Court in Kwale County, southern Kenya, where the mining concession is located, alleging the agreement process in Mrima Hill “has been shrouded in secrecy and undertaken without public participation.”

CLT is seeking to suspend the agreement until local communities are fully involved in the negotiations.

Environmental impacts are another concern. Mrima Hill is located about 65 kilometers (40 miles) south of Mombasa, Kenya’s second-largest city and a major tourist destination on the Indian Ocean coast. Mrima Hill is also part of the Eastern African coastal forests ecoregion. It’s home to numerous bird species, including near-threatened Fischer’s turaco (Tauraco fischeri) and the vulnerable spotted ground thrush (Geokichla guttata).

According to the Kenya-based environmental organization Nature Kenya: “Exploration activities have already disturbed the habitat through excavation pits, vegetation clearance, and increased human activity in sensitive forest areas. Large-scale mining would accelerate forest degradation, habitat fragmentation, soil erosion, and water pollution, while also threatening the sacred Kaya sites of the local Digo community.”

Banner image: Niobium crystal bar, Niobium is used as an alloying agent in steels and in high-tech applications, such as electric car batteries. Image by Dnn87 via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0).

item.title: US bill to speed up clean energy projects could also fast-track fossil fuels
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Examines a complex policy issue with potential environmental implications, but less focused on concrete detail.

On Nov. 19, the U.S. Senate passed a bill that aims to speed up permitting for energy infrastructure projects.

The 62-33 vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) included support from pro-environment Democratic senators like Sheldon Whitehouse from Rhode Island.

The legislation would ease development for renewable energy and transmission lines, but environmental organizations warn it will also fast-track fossil fuels by undermining environmental regulations.

“A technology-neutral fast track in the hands of an administration openly hostile to clean energy is not a bargain. It is a one-way ratchet for fossil fuels,” Brad Campbell, CEO of the Conservation Law Foundation, said in a statement.

Currently, new U.S. infrastructure projects must comply with bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). If BAAJA becomes law, those environmental hurdles will become easier to clear.

Fewer projects would require NEPA review, the time frame for environmental assessments would be shorter, and the window to sue over approved projects would shrink. Consultation on potential impacts to endangered species would also be shortened.

Proponents of the bill say those changes would ease renewable energy development and lower U.S. carbon emissions.

“BAAJA is a big step forward in our fight against climate change,” Whitehouse, who co-sponsored the bill, wrote on social media. “The bill lowers emissions by 1.5 gigatons through 2040.”

However, the weakened environmental review would also apply to fossil fuel projects and data centers. In an open letter, more than 120 scientists urged the House of Representatives to reject the bill.

On land, BAAJA could lower barriers for oil, gas and mining projects on public and tribal lands. Several Native American organizations have condemned the bill.

At sea, BAAJA would “roll back ocean and wildlife protections, opening the door to more offshore oil and gas drilling, more pollution, and greater threats to marine life,” U.S.-based NGO Oceana said in a statement.

Section 1401 of the bill, also known as the “project certainty” provision, would bar agencies from making changes to permits once they’ve been granted.

“Once issued, these approvals would be nearly impossible to revisit in the future, even if they were expedited, legally flawed, or if new science uncovers serious harm,” Oceana said in a statement.

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, an environmental NGO based in American Samoa, told Mongabay by email that she welcomes economic development but not at the cost of jeopardizing American Samoa’s existing ocean-based economy. The U.S’s first-ever offshore critical mineral lease sale took place off America Samoa on Nov. 19, the same day BAAJA cleared the Senate.

“If progress requires weakening environmental protections, diminishing Indigenous voices, and asking communities with limited political power to shoulder disproportionate risks, then perhaps we need to reconsider our definition of progress,” she said.

The House of Representatives is expected to vote on the legislation next week.

item.title: Striped Malted Pound Cake
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: High-quality recipe with detailed explanation and useful vocabulary

My earliest dessert obsession was the malted milkshake, which I indulged in every time I had enough babysitting money. My oldest, best friend, Toi, was equally obsessed with Whoppers, and we both wondered why malted sweets were so good. Turns out, the secret is in the combination of malted barley, wheat flour, and evaporated whole milk that gets toasted to caramelize the sugars contained in it.

This cake is my latest malted creation. Layering the malted vanilla and chocolate batters so they create a striped pattern isn’t just an aesthetic choice. Doing so really does keep the flavors distinct. Starting off in a cold oven allows the cake to bake evenly without overbrowning and results in a smooth, fine, melt-in your-mouth crumb. For extra malted flavor, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with malted vanilla syrup in several additions, letting the syrup sink in after each addition.

I originally made this syrup to give my milkshakes that nostalgic, malt-shop flavor. But honey, it’s no one-hit wonder. It is a beautiful sweetener and is terrific when brushed on top of still-warm Striped Malted Pound Cake.

I also drizzle it over roasted fruit and mix it into buttercreams, glazes, and frostings. For breakfast, I stir it into coffee or lattes, smoothies, yogurt, and oatmeal. And it’s got savoy game, too. Try it on a dinner plate, spooned over roasted sweet potatoes or carrots alongside roasted chops or chicken.

Recipe information

- Total Time 2 hours 30 minutes

- Yield Makes one 9x5" loaf, 12 to 16 servings

Ingredients

Malted Pound Cake

1¾

¼

½

½

16

1¼

¼

3

4

1½

1½

3

½

Malted Vanilla Syrup

⅓

½

2

1

Need to make a substitution?

Preparation

- Malted Pound Cake Step 1 Grease a 9x5" loaf pan with softened butter or cooking spray. Dust the pan with all-purpose flour, shaking out any excess. Step 2 In a medium bowl, whisk together 1¾ cups / 220g all-purpose flour, 1⁄4 cup / 34g cornstarch, 1⁄2 tsp. fine sea salt, and 1⁄2 tsp. baking powder. Step 3 In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle, combine 16 Tbsp. / 2 sticks / 226g unsalted butter, at room temperature, 1¼ cups / 273g granulated sugar, and 1⁄4 cup / 37g malted milk powder. Beat, starting on low speed and increasing to medium-high speed until lightened in color and fluffy, 5–7 minutes, scraping down the sides of the bowl once or twice. Step 4 On medium-low speed, add 3 large eggs, at room temperature, one at a time, scraping down the sides of the bowl after each one is incorporated. Step 5 Add one-third of the flour mixture and beat on the lowest speed until just combined. Add 2 Tbsp. heavy cream and beat on low speed until just combined. Add another one-third of the flour mixture, beating until combined, and another 2 Tbsp. heavy cream to combine. Add the remaining one-third of the flour mixture and beat until the batter is smooth, scraping down the sides of the bowl as necessary. Mix in 1½ tsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract and 1½ tsp. whiskey or bourbon (if using). Step 6 Transfer 1½ cups of the batter to a medium bowl. Sift in 3 Tbsp. unsweetened cacao powder or cocoa powder and add the remaining 1⁄4 cup heavy cream, stirring to form a smooth chocolate batter. Step 7 To create the striped layers, drop 1 cup of the vanilla cake batter into the center of the loaf pan and then drop ½ cup of the chocolate batter on top of the vanilla batter. The alternating layers do not have to totally cover each other and let the layers spread naturally. Continue to drop those same-size portions of batter directly on top of each other, alternating the vanilla and chocolate, until all the batter is used. The batter should have spread to the corners, but if not, gently rap the pan on the counter to help it even out. Smooth the top with a small offset spatula. Step 8 Place the cake in a cold oven and set the temperature to 300°F. Bake until the loaf is golden, its top is slightly cracked, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes. Step 9 Let the cake cool in the pan on a wire rack for 10 minutes, then run a knife around the edges to release it. Invert the cake onto a wire rack, reinvert, and cover the warm cake loosely in plastic wrap until completely cooled. If desired, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with ½ cup Malted Vanilla Syrup several times, letting the syrup sink in after each addition. The cake will keep, wrapped in plastic at room temperature, for up to 5 days.

- Malted Vanilla Syrup Step 10 In a small saucepan, combine ⅓ cup / 73g granulated sugar, ½ cup / 120g water, 2 Tbsp. malted milk powder, and pinch of fine sea salt. Cook over medium heat until bubbling, whisking until the sugar and malt powder dissolve and the mixture becomes glossy, slightly thickened, and evenly beige, 2–3 minutes. Step 11 Remove from heat and whisk in 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract. Let cool slightly before using. This will keep in a covered jar or airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

item.title: Citrus Madeleines
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Cultural context and detailed recipe with useful vocabulary

Marcel Proust and madeleines are so intrinsically linked that in France, a madeleine de Proust has become a common expression used to describe a smell, sound, or taste that brings back old memories. Madeleines are small sponge cakes baked in molds shaped like seashells with the signature bump, la bosse, proudly protruding from the top. Freezing the pan and placing it on a hot sheet pan will make the bump pop even more!

As much as I love a plain madeleine, I adore a citrus-scented one. My first madeleine, my Proustian moment, was not at a lovely Parisian pâtisserie. No, my family and I were visiting some of my mother’s friends in Paris and not knowing what they were, I grabbed a bag of lemon madeleines in a local supermarket, simply because I thought the seashell-shaped cakes were the prettiest thing I had ever seen. I could have inhaled them all in an afternoon if I had been allowed.

Seasonal citrus zests—lemons, of course, yuzus, blood oranges, mandarins, or a medley of several—find their way into my madeleines, but the tart-sweet, fruity, floral flavor of Cara Cara oranges is my favorite. Dusting the still-warm madeleines with floral and citrusy coriander-scented powdered sugar just before serving sends them over the top.

Recipe information

- Total Time 40 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling)

- Yield Makes 12

Ingredients

Madeleines

½

1

½

¼

½

1

2

Coriander Sugar

¼

¾

Need to make a substitution?

Preparation

- Madeleines Step 1 Put ½ cup / 115 g unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat and melt, stirring and scraping the bottom with a rubber spatula, until the foaming subsides and the butter smells like toasted hazelnuts and the milk solids are golden brown, 5–7 minutes. Scrape the melted butter and milk solids into a small heatproof bowl and refrigerate until the butter is solid and creamy. Step 2 Sift together 1 cup / 125 g all-purpose flour, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ¼ tsp. salt in a small bowl and set aside. Step 3 Add ½ cup / 100 g light brown sugar to a small bowl and rub the sugar with zest of 1 Cara Cara orange. Combine the sugar, 1 Tbsp. honey, and 2 eggs in the bowl of a stand mixer, fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk for 2 minutes on medium-low speed, then increase the speed to medium-high and whisk for another 5–6 minutes, until very pale and airy. Step 4 Add the cooled butter to the egg mixture while whisking on low speed, then fold in the flour mixture until just combined. Step 5 Transfer the batter to an airtight container and refrigerate for at least 6 hours but preferably overnight. Step 6 Grease a madeleine pan with unsalted butter, then dust with all-purpose flour and knock out any excess. Place the pan in the freezer for at least an hour. Step 7 Use a 1-Tbsp. measure or transfer the cold batter to a piping bag and fill the center of each cup with 20 g of batter (three-quarters full, or a little more than 1 Tbsp.). Refrigerate the madeleine pan for 1 hour. Step 8 Place a sheet pan in the oven and preheat the oven to 350°F / 180°C. Step 9 Place the madeleine pan directly on the hot sheet pan and bake for 10–13 minutes, until the madeleines are golden brown and their signature bump springs back when pressed lightly. Step 10 Tap the tray to release the cakes and immediately turn out onto a wire rack to cool, turning them bump-side up.

- Coriander Sugar Step 11 Whisk together ¼ cup / 30 g powdered sugar and ¾ tsp. ground coriander in a small bowl and dust over the warm madeleines.

Best microwaves for everyday home cooking, tested and reviewed

Whether you're making curry in a hurry or mash in a flash, invest in a quality microwave. Discover which microwaves are best by reading our expert reviews

The microwave is one of the unsung heroes of the kitchen. From reheating leftovers and defrosting ingredients to cooking entire meals from scratch in little time, the microwave is a seriously versatile piece of kit. Not only do they save both time and effort, cooking in a microwave can also save energy, and therefore cost, when compared to using the oven.

And the benefits don’t stop there. When it comes to reheating food, using a microwave saves on washing up, as meals can be reheated in their serving dish, rather than decanted into saucepans or oven dishes.

While the most basic microwave models on the market are designed to simply heat or defrost foods, many of today’s models go far beyond these capabilities, offering multiple settings for different cooking needs, like grilling, steaming and baking. Some are also equipped with innovative settings to make life easier in the kitchen, whether it’s a ‘keep warm’ button, or a deodorising function to eliminate lingering odours.

With microwaves that came with a grill function, we then grilled the chicken breasts too, looking for a tender, juicy finish. If the microwave had a steam function, we made gooey toffee puddings.

- Ease of use: microwaves are used mainly by those who want to make life simpler. We looked for pared-down functionality, simple design and easy-to-follow instruction booklets.

- Defrosting: an essential function for most, we looked for effective thawing, with presets a bonus.

- Moisture retention: we checked the food didn't dry out before it had finished cooking.

- Additional features: small extra features like a child lock or kitchen timer were appreciated, plus we looked at how well more prominent features such as grills and convection ovens performed.

- Size: we assessed the size of the microwave and the space it took up in the kitchen. The models we tested need to be installed a specified height above the floor, with plenty of room all around for ventilation.

- Sustainability: we looked at everything from the recyclability of the packaging, spare parts information, the warranty of the microwave, the wattage and more.

- Cleaning: the ease of cleaning both inside and out and finger marks, especially on stainless steel.

item.title: White chocolate cake
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Recipe with some detail, but lacks cultural context and engagement

White chocolate cake

If you're celebrating a special occasion, this layer cake makes a great centrepiece. It's topped with silky white chocolate ganache and fresh raspberries

- 300g buttersoftened, plus extra for the tins

- 300g caster sugar

- 5 large eggsbeaten

- 1 tsp vanilla bean paste

- 1 tsp baking powder

- 300g self-raising flour

- 100g white chocolatefinely chopped

- 350g fresh raspberrieshalved

For the ganache

- 450g white chocolatefinely chopped

- 200ml double cream

- 1 tbsp vanilla paste

- kcal501

- fat31g

- saturates19g

- carbs48g

- sugars35g

- fibre1g

- protein7g

- salt0.67g

Method

- step 1 Heat the oven to 180C/160C fan/gas 4. Butter three 18cm sandwich cake tins and line with baking parchment. Beat together the butter, sugar, eggs, vanilla, baking powder and flour using a stand mixer or electric hand whisk until you have a fluffy mixture, about 5 mins. Fold in the white chocolate until it’s well distributed throughout.

- step 2 Divide the mixture evenly between the tins and level out using a palette knife or the back of a spoon until smooth. Bake for 25-30 mins until a skewer inserted into the middle comes out clean. Remove from the oven and leave the sponges to cool in the tins for 10 mins, then remove from the tins and transfer to a cooling rack, top side down, and leave to cool completely. If the sponges are not level use a serrated knife to cut away the peaks.

- step 3 While the sponges are cooling, make the ganache. Put the white chocolate in a large bowl. Pour the cream into a saucepan over a medium heat and bring to a simmer. Immediately pour the cream over the chocolate and leave to stand for 4-5 mins until the chocolate has melted. Mix together to form a smooth ganache, ensuring all the chocolate has fully melted, then mix in the vanilla. Chill in the fridge for 30 mins, stirring occasionally so it doesn't completely harden, until spreadable and thick enough to coat the cake.

- step 4 Once the sponges are cool and the ganache has set to a spreadable consistency, you can construct the cake. Place one sponge on a serving plate, spread over a thin layer of the chocolate ganache, then fill the middle with a third of the raspberries. Place another sponge on top and repeat with a layer of ganache and another third of raspberries. Put the final sponge on top and gently coat the whole cake with a thin layer of ganache. Leave in the fridge to set for at least 20 mins. To finish, spread over any remaining ganache and top with the remaining raspberries. Will keep chilled for up to three days in an airtight container.

item.title: Rare Marie Antoinette ‘Breast Bowl’ Hammers for $2.47 M. in Paris, Surpassing Top Estimate
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: rich in historical context and cultural significance, with a focus on a unique artifact

One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million) at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).

Legend has it that this series of 18th-century porcelain bowls, made by the Royal Sèvres manufacturers, was modeled after the ill-fated French queen’s real breasts. While no documented proof of such a legend exists, the so-called “jatte-téton” or “nipple bowls,” painted in fleshy light pink with an areola and nipple at the tip, do have a surrealistic, convincingly realistic quality, despite a too-perfectly circular shape.

Made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek mastos, or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC. It is one of four highly prized jatte-tétons delivered that year and in 1788, destined for the royal “pleasure dairy” in Rambouillet, near Versailles, that King Louis XVI gifted to Marie Antoinette. There, per the fashion of the time, nobility would gather to socialize and taste an assortment of fine milk, cream, and cheese delicacies prepared for them.

The rare breast bowl comes from the collection of French dealer Claude Meyer, who passed away in November 2025. His children happened upon it while going through boxes of storage, and learned that their late father, whose Paris gallery closed in the 1990s, had never offered it for sale. It is unclear how Meyer acquired the piece, which is known to have once belonged to the French Marquise de Chanaleilles.

Three of the four breast bowls made in 1787 and 1788 for the queen’s royal dairy dishes are housed in public collections today, including two at the Musée de Sèvres and one at the Museo Duca di Martina in Naples. The bowl that sold tonight is the last of that specific series. They are “the most celebrated and the most extravagant shape of the porcelain service,” by the royal Sèvres manufactory for the queen’s dairy, notes the auction house in its description.

With the bowl comes an intricately carved tripod stand decorated with goat heads in relief, as seen above. Indeed, the breast bowls require a pedestal to hold them upside down, as it were, so as to contain the milk and cream they were meant to serve.

Speaking to Le Journal des Arts about the bowl, auctioneer Alexandre de La Forest Divonne observed: “It has become something of a symbol of the queen; it is truly a totem.”

Source: ARTnews | Published: 2026-11-26 18:28 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Lisa Marei Schmidt Appointed Director of Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee
item.description:

Why it is here: high-level appointment with a focus on the director's background and the institutions involved

Lisa Marei Schmidt, the director of the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, is leaving her post to take over as director of the Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern, Switzerland, starting August 1, 2027. She will also chair the management board of both institutions and be responsible for their artistic direction. The Renzo Piano-designed Zentrum Paul Klee holds the world’s largest collection of works by Klee, while the Kunstmuseum Bern is Switzerland’s oldest fine art museum.

Schmidt has been at the Brücke-Museum since 2017 and has orchestrated many exhibitions, including Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019), Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22), and Confiscated and Forgotten: The Female Artists Targeted by the Nazi ‘Degenerate Art’ Campaign, which opens April 30 to July 25, 2027. The Berlin museum is currently exhibiting Swedish Modernism until February 28, 2027, with a focus on the artist groups De unga (The Young Ones), De åtta (The Eight) and the Gothenburg Colorists. “To me, museums are places where art and people meet. They provide space for encounters, new perspectives and dialogue across society,” said Schmidt, in a statement on Thursday. “I very much look forward to getting to know the two remarkable institutions, the teams and the people in the City and Canton of Bern. Together, I hope to build on the Kunstmuseum Bern’s and Zentrum Paul Klee’s distinctive qualities and shape their future development.”

Schmidt was chosen out of 97 candidates who applied for the position. Jonathan Gimmel, president of the umbrella foundation of Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee, said in a statement that Schmidt brings “remarkable professional expertise, international experience and a deep understanding of people” as she shapes the next “development phase of our museums.”

Before joining Brücke-Museum, Schmidt was a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and a curator at the Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. She studied art history and modern German literature in Marburg, Amsterdam, and Berlin before graduating from the Royal College of Art.

item.title: At the Broad, Six Decades of Art Question the Myth of Progress
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: examines the myth of progress through art, offering a nuanced perspective on social issues

Two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities. For years, she’d witnessed the chasm widen between women carrying $3,500 handbags and those wearing trash bags; from her “nice neighborhood where the helicopters don’t come,” she did little to address the disparity. Still, the unrest that followed the acquittal of four LAPD officers charged with beating Rodney King seemed to have broken through the collective apathy. Angelenos, she wrote, were suddenly talking about “things that matter”: race, guilt, poverty, urban policy, to name a few. Despite history offering little reason for optimism, Scott confessed to a sense of hope: “I’m nurturing my first illusion.”

More than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay. The headlines “Seeing Ourselves” and “Has the Myth Been Shattered?” registered the same discrepancy she sensed between what she remembered as a child growing up in East LA and how the press perpetuated myths about the city’s seeming collectivity. Rosales was 11 years old in 1992, and she has a distinct memory of her mother rushing the family home from school as smoke stained the usually sun-drenched California sky. As an adult, Rosales has amassed an archive of clippings, photographs, and other ephemera of Chicanx youth culture—much of it crowdsourced through social media—that serves as both a bulwark against that dissonance and a counter to historical erasure and amnesia. “I’m not looking for answers,” she told ARTnews. “But for some kind of physical proof that things really happened, that they’re not just in our memories.”

Rosales’s 2024 sculpture Has the myth been shattered encases that infamous yellowed newspaper in a nearly six-foot-tall aluminum frame fitted with a two-way mirror, illuminated by colorful LED lights. Though it resembles a doorway, the work offers no passage; instead, viewers face their own reflections superimposed over the 1992 text, along with photographs of palm trees and police. The temporal distance between then and now collapses onto a single plane, leaving Scott’s question perpetually suspended in the present.

The work also lends its title to a just-opened exhibition at the Broad in downtown LA. Organized by assistant curator Jen Vanegas Rocha, the presentation brings together works by more than a dozen artists spanning six decades. Recent acquisitions by Rosales and Hank Willis Thomas appear alongside art by Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, Glenn Ligon, and Robert Longo, among others. Across prints, paintings, drawings, sculpture, and tapestry, artists appropriate text and images from various forms of public record, drawing attention to the ways media shapes perception of major sociopolitical events. Seen together, the works undermine the assumption that exposing injustice inevitably leads to redress. “There are echoes of the present in the past,” Willis Thomas said. “So is the past present or is the present past?”

The Broad’s founding director, Joanne Heyler, sees that unease as central to the exhibition’s timeliness. “The notion of a linear progression of change unfolding in a dependable, escalating way,” she said, is “becoming harder and harder to believe in.”

Consider the oldest work in the show, Andy Warhol’s Race Riot (1963), in which police dogs attack Black civil-rights demonstrators in Birmingham, Alabama. In 2026, the decades-old image calls to mind the police response to the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd, as well as the more recent pro-Palestine and anti-ICE demonstrations nationwide, in which protestors were often battered and tear-gassed. Warhol lifted the photograph directly from a visual essay by Charles Moore in Life magazine, translating the confrontation into a monochromatic silkscreen. Adopting the incendiary rhetoric of contemporary news coverage, he labeled the peaceful demonstrators “rioters.” Race Riot reflects the artist’s own reckoning with the contradictions at the heart of American life: His obsession with celebrities and mass consumption give way to the sensationalized images of death and violence that belie it, like the mangled cars and electric chairs that also feature in his “Death and Disaster” series. Viewers are left to consider whether the relentless circulation of violence sharpens public outrage or gradually dulls our empathy.

For Willis Thomas, Warhol’s Birmingham silkscreen paintings function as “postcards to the future.” By transforming them from documentation to works of art, Warhol has made a case for their continued relevance. Nearby, Willis Thomas’s photo-based Black Survival Guide, or How to Live Through a Police Riot (2018) revisits the same era to recover another history largely omitted from public memory. While researching the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, he discovered a typewritten pamphlet offering practical advice to Black residents of Wilmington, Delaware, during the nine-month National Guard occupation in 1968. Onto retroreflective vinyl, Willis Thomas printed excerpts from the pamphlet—advice on how to staunch bleeding or communicate during a power outage, for example—atop archival News Journal photographs of confrontations between armed soldiers and the city’s Black communities. Installed in a darkened gallery, the black-and-white images are invisible until a flash of light illuminates them. Rather than merely encountering the past, the audience actively aids in its recovery. “In some ways the observers become the researchers,” he said.…

item.description:

Why it is here: features a celebrity's art collection, which may not be as relevant to the reader's interests

Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, which runs from December 4 to 6, NBA star Kevin Love reflects on his journey into art collecting, which has made him the proud owner of works by Antony Gormley, Rashid Johnson, Ed Ruscha and George Condo.

In an interview with Art Basel’s Miami Beach Magazine, the five-time NBA All-Star and 2016 NBA champion and his wife, Kate Bock, opened their Miami home to reporters, displaying an impressive art collection of paintings and sculptures. He reveals that he has Ed Ruscha’s The End (2021) hanging over his bed, a painting to which he feels a personal connection. “I hate to be one of those people who watches a lot of TV in bed, but we do, and The End has a connection to Ruscha and to film. It’s also very literal: It’s the end of the day, you’re in bed,” Love said. “And it’s a reminder: I’m thinking about the end of a career. Whether it’s in two months or two years, it’s there; and with that, new beginnings as well. I’ve always loved his work. He’s a great man, he’s empathetic and supportive. My wedding gift to my wife, Kate, was a Ruscha.” Love is also the owner of three other Ruscha artworks: Woman on Fire (2024), He Enjoys the Co. of Women (2025) and The Girl Always Did Have Good Taste (2021).

Even though Love can’t pinpoint when his enthusiasm for art collecting started, he said that around the 2012 Olympics he learned his peers, including Carmelo Anthony and LeBron James, were interested in art. “That made the whole world feel a little less intimidating. I asked a lot of questions. ‘Where do you start?’ ‘What should I be looking at?’” Love said, noting that art adviser Jane Suitor has always encouraged him to stay “curious.”

In the magazine photo shoot, four works by Johnson are displayed: Untitled Anxious Red (2020), Run (2018), Falling Man (2015), and another painting from the Anxious Drawing series. Other pieces in his home range from Antony Gormley’s sculpture SMALL LOOK V (2015), a George Condo line drawing Untitled (2017), Richard Prince’s Untitled (Palomino) (1982–86), Hank Willis Thomas’ O! thus be it ever (2021), and John Baldessari’s Aerial View/People (1988).

Over the years, Love has built a friendship with artists Jonas Wood and Rashid Johnson. “Jonas Wood is a crazy, avid basketball fan, and my second favorite sport is tennis, so personal stories are initially where the connection resides,” said the basketball player. “I’m very lucky to have Rashid Johnson in my life. I first connected [with the work] for emotional reasons without knowing much about him. I’m seven minutes down the road from his studio in the Hamptons.”

In the interview, Love recalls buying his wife a neon Tracey Emin heart with the words “An Insane Desire for You” written inside. He later followed up by buying her a 10-foot Dan Flavin in all his favorite colors, which they haven’t installed yet. “Turns out my wife doesn’t like neon,” Love said.

At Art Basel Miami Beach, Love will be joining the likes of Brooklyn Nets and New York Liberty co-owner Clara Wu Tsai, soccer player Crystal Dunn, and NFL chief marketing officer Tim Ellis in the fair’s Art & Sport day, a series of panel talks between the art and sports worlds. Love and Keith Rivers, a former professional football player, will be in conversation with each other on December 3 to discuss “when athletes become collectors.”

Why it is here: announces the curator of an upcoming biennale, with a brief overview of the curator's background

Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale, the world’s biggest recurring art exhibition running from April 8 to November 26, 2028. Al Qasimi is also president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, a member of the United Arab Emirates’s Sharjawi royal family and president of the Sharjah Museums Authority.

The board of La Biennale di Venezia said it met on November 20 to pick Al Qasimi on the recommendation of president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco. Al Qasimi will be tasked with curating the 62nd edition of the exhibition and will take on the title of director of the visual arts department.

“La Biennale di Venezia is a place where the world converges with art through its diverse visions. Throughout her career, Hoor Al Qasimi has succeeded in creating a caravanserai of geographies and the Universal, giving voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected,” said Buttafuoco in a statement on Thursday. “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people. I also recognize in her a quality of balance and composure, namely the vibrant presence of mīzān (inner harmony), which finds its strength in relationships.”

The taking of an art biennale is nothing new to Al Qasimi. In 2024, she was appointed by the Biennale of Sydney as the artistic director of the exhibition’s 25th edition, which ran from March 7 to June 8, 2026. However, the Venice Biennale is of a larger scale on an international stage. “The international art exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia has been an important platform for many of us around the world. I first visited the 50th edition in 2003 having recently stepped into my curatorial role at Sharjah Biennial,” said Al Qasimi in a statement on Monday. “For me, La Biennale continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators. I am honored to have been invited to curate this exhibition and grateful to president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, and the board for their confidence and trust.”

Why it is here: comprehensive coverage of a significant industry event

Royal Society for Arts appoints five Royal Designers for Industry

The UK’s Royal Society for Arts has announced five Royal Designers for Industry, who include Durrell Bishop and Bridget Baines, as well as naming an Honorary Royal Designer as it celebrates its 90th anniversary.

The awards, which were established in 1936, recognise outstanding talent across landscape architecture, technology, illustration, fashion and theatre. They are given by Royal Society for Arts (RSA) and can only be held by 200 designers at any one time.

This year’s winners are product and interaction designer Bishop, multidisciplinary designer Harris Elliott, illustrator Laura Carlin, costume designer Tahra Zafar and landscape architect Bridget Baines.

Baines co-founded international practice Gross Max, and her fellow Gross Max founder Eelco Hooftman (pictured in main image with Baines) was given the Honorary Royal Designer award this year.

The winners were chosen for their “joyful” designs,

“Ninety years on, the Royal Designers are still looking forward,” Keeper of the Faculty of Royal Designers for Industry Johanna Gibbons said. “This year’s appointments show how far design now reaches, from public landscapes and picture books to exhibitions, the stage and the objects we use every day.”

“Their work is joyful, and it is serious about making life better,” she continued. “That is what unites Royal Designers across the decades: a living entanglement of disciplines that, with the RSA Fellowship, is a profound force for good.”

Last year’s winners included designer Yinka Ilori and journalist Mona Chalabi, and the award has also been given to designers including Es Devlin, Vivienne Westwood, James Dyson and Zandra Rhodes.

According to the RSA, the winners represent the “sheer breadth of design today”.

“Great design changes how we experience the world, often in ways we barely notice,” RSA programme manager Catherine Joyce.

“For 90 years, Royal Designers have shown what extraordinary creativity can achieve, and how it can make life better for everyone,” she continued.

“These six appointments are a wonderful reminder of the sheer breadth of design today.”

Dezeen also recently celebrated the best designers of this year as part of our Dezeen Awards, including Ilori, Yasmine Ghoniem and Keiji Ashizawa.

Photography by Daniel Reiser

item.title: "Europe's largest museum development" opens in 1930s Citroën garage in Brussels
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique transformation of a historical building into a museum

“Europe’s largest museum development” opens in 1930s Citroën garage in Brussels

Brussels‘ former Citroën Garage has been transformed into Kanal, a 40,000-square-metre museum for modern art and architecture with an exhibition programme developed with the Parisian art institution Centre Pompidou.

The transformation was designed by Atelier Kanal, a consortium made up of architecture studio EM2N, NoAarchitecten and Sergison Bates Architects, with a team of construction workers, who restored the 1930s industrial building and added three new volumes within its structure.

Claiming to be “Europe’s largest museum development”, Kanal – sometimes referred to as Kanal-Centre Pompidou – hopes to provide space for people to gather to enjoy visual art, performance, dance, music, film and architecture.

Opening to the public on 28 November, the canal-side building was originally built in 1934 as a garage and showroom for the car company Citroën.

Atelier Kanal aimed to keep the industrial character of the building by implementing a “light touch” approach, restoring most of the building fabric, repairing and upgrading parts where needed, and replacing other parts to improve climatic and acoustic conditions.

The garage’s former showroom, a modernist curved glass building with 20-metre-tall interiors, was converted into a gallery space topped with a publicly accessible rooftop.

“Rather than a spectacular gesture, our proposal offers an attitude of ‘radical optimism’ – open and non-prescriptive, spontaneous and instinctive – much like the spirit of modern progress in which it was created,” said Atelier Kanal.

“The interior is a fine example of elegant industrial engineering, while the glass facades clearly express early modernism,” it continued.

“Our ambition has been to trust the building as we found it, embracing its industrial character and many layers of use.”

Three new buildings were added inside the existing structure, including a four-storey volume with a basement level that contains art galleries, and another volume housing a 378-seat auditorium and the Kanal offices.

The third volume is the new home for Brussels’ museum and archive of architecture, Kanal Architecture, which was formerly known as CIVA.

Rising nine stories on the north-east side of the campus, across from the art galleries, the structure includes exhibition spaces, a library, archives, research centre, bookshop and workshop spaces.

Architecture collective Assemble designed an indoor playground on the first floor of the museum, which features playscapes informed by volcanoes, planets, and piles of coal that were once transported on the canal.

Elsewhere in the building are a library, bookshop, rooftop bar, restaurants and an in-house bakery.

Kanal’s year-round programme of exhibitions was developed in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou art museum in Paris.

“Kanal invites citizens, organisations, collectives and communities to appropriate and inhabit large parts of the building, for production, performances, events, informal gatherings or simply to spend time,” said Atelier Kanal.

“The museum extends beyond curated art, becoming part of the city and its fabric,” it continued. “In this sense, Kanal departs from the traditional museum and instead offers a place for civic gathering, responding to the growing absence of shared public spaces in our cities today.”

Other museums that have recently opened in historic buildings include the London Museum, located in a transformed Victorian market building, and a bank in Santander that was transformed into the Faro Santander museum.
