item.title: Meet BC Architects & Studies & Materials, Marina Tabassum's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: in-depth look at an innovative architectural practice

Meet BC Architects & Studies & Materials, Marina Tabassum’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, two of BC Architects & Studies & Materials’ founders discuss how their ideas have gone from being perceived as the product of “young idealism” to being taken seriously by the construction sector.

The Brussels-based studio is at the forefront of bio-regional and circular design, with a whole arm of its practice dedicated to the development of new materials, often making use of construction waste.

Recently, the studio worked with UK studio Assemble and circular design lab Atelier Luma to create Le Magasin Électrique at Luma Arles in France, with a palette that included everything from rammed earth and construction waste to salt and algae.

Alongside these likeminded practitioners, BC Architects & Studies & Materials is at the forefront of a recent wave of interest in bio-based materials and vernacular methods – ideas that the studio has been championing for some 15 years, pushing for systemic change in the industry.

Founded between 2009 and 2012 by Ken De Cooman, Wes Degreef, Nicolas Coeckelberghs and Laurens Bekemans, the origins of BC Architects & Studies & Materials were – as its tripartite name suggests – not particularly conventional.

The studio is comprised of three different legal entities: BC Architects, an architecture cooperative; BC Studies, a non-profit “education laboratory”; and BC Materials, a material production co-operative.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s approach and outlook was borne out of a series of early projects in Burundi, Morocco and Ethiopia – where the studio briefly had a satellite office – which were grounded in working with local communities and materials.

“A lot of our first experiences in architecture were linked to different construction cultures,” said De Cooman. “I lived in Ethiopia for five years, others were in Morocco for a long time, and at the same time, we were finding our way in Belgium.”

“It was a different path to learning architecture as a practitioner,” he continued. We learnt to work with local materials and short supply chains, to make do with what you find around.”

The studio’s first built project was the Library of Muyinga in Burundi, developed using an open-source template from the OpenStructures network and constructed from compressed earth bricks alongside members of the local community.

It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture

BC Architects & Studies & Materials also designed several school buildings and a women’s shelter in Morocco, often using the construction process itself as an opportunity for the sharing of knowledge around vernacular construction techniques and materials.

According to De Cooman, however, this strand of the studio’s work was never intended to be long-term.

Challenging a tendency in the industry to view these methods and techniques as solely belonging to the realm of “humanitarian” architecture, BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s aim was to apply them to the business-as-usual processes of architecture and construction back home in Belgium.

“It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture,” said De Cooman.

“It was a huge learning process, and now we’re really focussing on the here and now because it’s here that we need to actually change the most.”

While a big part of this change is the studio’s use of alternative materials, it was also based on the idea of building being an opportunity for shared learning, driven by BC’s belief in the the need for architects to be more engaged with the construction process.

We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other field

Several of the studio’s early projects in Belgium the result of these learning workshops. Maison de Chasse, a rammed-earth hunting house, was constructed over the course of the first rammed earth workshop in Belgium, based on the techniques of Martin Rauch and Anna Heringer.

In 2017, the renovation of a series of warehouses in Ghent into an artist’s studio for Pascale Marthine Tayou was achieved via a five-week “Urban Construction Camp”, in which volunteers created a new hempcrete structure inside an existing metal shell.

“We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other fields, not on paper, but with the heart and the hands included,” explained De Cooman.

“It is crazy that we now have a system where, as an architect, you draw all the execution files and send them to a contractor to execute it exactly how you drew it.”

“The magic happens when everyone can get together – you can draw it together, find a passionate contractor to make it with.”

BC Architects & Studies & Materials was keen, however, to not be defined by this smaller-scale work, with the whole point being to demonstrate how these techniques and materials could be scaled up into larger contexts.

The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings

A key means to achieving this was the formal establishing of BC Materials in 2018, enabled by the interest generated by their earlier projects. Alongside consultancy, workshops and training, the BC Materials arm also offers its own range of earth and clay products, Léém.

“The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings,” says Wes Degreef.…

Why it is here: detailed description of an innovative office building design

RSHP centres cantilevered office building Sąvaržėlė around glass atrium

UK studio RSHP has revealed its first project in the Baltic region, a mixed-use office building in Lithuania designed as “a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking”.

Named after the Lithuanian word for paperclip, the seven-storey Sąvaržėlė is located in central Vilnius, between the UNESCO-listed Old Town and the city’s commercial district.

The stacked building has a cantilevered design and houses office space, a conference hall, a restaurant and a cafe across its 19,000-square-metre space.

“At Sąvaržėlė, we wanted to create a workplace that extends into the city – one that welcomes people, encourages collaboration and contributes new public spaces to Vilnius,” RSHP associate director Jack Evans-Newton said.

“Occupying a unique position between the historic centre and the city’s emerging business district, the building brings these two identities together through a calm and contemporary architectural expression,” he continued.

“Clarity of form, generous public spaces and carefully crafted detailing create a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking, reflecting the ambition of a growing business district while respecting the scale and character of its historic setting.”

Sąvaržėlė has large, adaptable floorplates, designed to create a flexible interior.

The building has a stacked, rectangular shape and was made from prefabricated steel components that were bolted together on site. On the east and west facades, RSHP placed external ribs that the studio said “echo the tones” of Vilnius’ historic architecture.

Sąvaržėlė is arranged around a central glass atrium with a striking yellow-lined elevator. It can be accessed via a number of different entrances that connect to the surrounding streets.

To enhance the building’s environmental performance, RSHP added a double-skin facade. This uses energy-efficient chilled beam cooling and automated natural ventilation to help reduce energy demand.

In addition, Sąvaržėlė has a 2,897-square-metre fully landscaped green roof.

RSHP has also recently designed a 45-storey skyscraper in Shenzhen and a curved-roof railway hub.

item.title: Carlo Ratti and AI assistant to curate Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism 2027
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: forward-thinking approach to an architecture biennale

Carlo Ratti and AI assistant to curate Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism 2027

Italian architect Carlo Ratti has been named the curator of next year’s Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism, for which he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach.

Taking place from 24 September 2027, the biennale will be used by Ratti as an opportunity to question the role of a curator today through the lens of architecture.

However, the event’s title, theme and full curatorial team will not be unveiled until 8 December.

“One assistant curator isn’t even human”

What Ratti has revealed so far is that he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach to the event.

Specifically, he will use an AI assistant, aiming to challenge traditional approaches to developing exhibitions by highlighting emerging tools that can help curators.

“I am delighted to take on the direction of the Seoul Biennale and to explore the future of cities together with the Seoul Metropolitan Government,” says Carlo Ratti.

“Seoul is perhaps the best place in the world to ask how artificial intelligence and the collective wisdom of its citizens might shape the city together,” he continued.

“At the upcoming pre-biennale event, we will begin to introduce the people who will join us, and I think there will be a few surprises – one assistant curator isn’t even human!”

Ratti is an Italian architect and engineer, and director of his eponymous studio Carlo Ratti Associati. He is also a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

Ratti succeeds Thomas Heatherwick

He was appointed by Seoul mayor Oh Se Hoon, succeeding British designer Thomas Heatherwick, who curated the 2025 event.

Heatherwick centred the event on a long, four-storey-high wall displaying images that reflected the ideals of his Humanise campaign.

The Seoul Biennale was established in 2017 by the Seoul Metropolitan Government as a festival of international architecture and urbanism.

“The Seoul Biennale is a place where architects and citizens from around the world think together about the future of cities and explore new possibilities,” said mayor Oh.

“Together with general director Carlo Ratti, who has connected architecture, cities, and technology, we will prepare so that the sixth Seoul Biennale offers a new perspective on cities and architecture and a meaningful experience for citizens.”

Ratti’s previous curatorial experience includes the Venice Architecture Biennale in 2025, for which the theme was Intelligens. Natural. Artificial. Collective. It explored how architecture can be adapted to increasingly unstable living environments through cross-disciplinary collaboration.

At the time, Ratti said, “Dezeen killed the traditional form of the biennale“.

The architect’s other recent projects include the French Pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka and a proposal for a children’s hospital housed in a one-kilometre “green ring”.

item.title: Base Design gives Visa a brand refresh "for the next generation"
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: analysis of a brand refresh with strategic implications

Design agency Base Design has created a more compact version of credit card company Visa’s logo and worked with Displaay Type Foundry on a new typeface, as part of a refresh of the brand’s visual identity.

While the 2021 Visa wordmark remains unchanged, the refresh included creating a shortened symbol for the brand, rolling out the new Visa Sans typeface, and creating a blocky hero graphic to market towards a younger generation.

“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition – it’s relevance,” said Base Design executive creative director Min Lew.

“Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the next generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”

As part of this strategy, the studio cut the V out of the existing wordmark to function as its own symbol. It will be used on credit cards and appear across digital platforms.

The studio also wrapped it in colourful bar, which will also be used on graphic elements such as posters, and to frame text.

“More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity,” said Lew.

“This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences.”

For Visa Sans, Base Design and Displaay Type Foundry also based the design on the existing logo.

The typeface features rounded edges akin to the rounded corner of the Visa V, and overall, extends “the logo’s character across the wider identity”.

Ultimately, the new identity was created to be used across different smaller, touchpoints according to the team, such as at tap-to-pay stations, at checkout, or online, as the brand appears “for only a moment” in day to day life.

“We have deep trust and recognition as a brand,” said Visa chief marketing officer Frank Cooper III. “This refresh gives us an opportunity to build on that.”

A more subtle approach to logo and branding updates has been popular in recent years, such as at Walmart and Google.

In contrast, the US restaurant chain Cracker Barrel recently took a hard swing at a logo update, which was immediately met with online backlash and promptly scrapped in favour of the original design.

Why it is here: detailed presentation of lighting designs with historical context

Five lighting designs listed by Marset on Dezeen Showroom

Spanish lighting brand Marset has showcased five of its products on Dezeen Showroom, including a mid-century reissue and a ceiling light that appears like a block of ice.

Marset‘s selection includes the Gambosa table lamp, created by designer Mathias Hahn to reinterpret the classic shade, stem and base as one smooth, glossy sculpture in steel and opal polycarbonate.

Gambosa is defined by its elegant composition, with a round-ended body that looks as if precariously balanced. It also features a considered cable design that sweeps down one side of the lamp like a signature.

It is distinguished by its select palette of colours, with combinations of orange, moss grey, black, pale pink and opal that evoke mid-century style combined with contemporary curation.

With the Lauro collection, Marset has revived a genuine 1970s design classic from its own catalogue, featuring chunky tubes of bent steel.

Created by designers P Aragay and J Pérez Mateo, the Lauro lighting comes in table, floor and wall variants. According to Marset, the range represents the technical achievements of a time when bending steel was a huge challenge.

Another of the highlights from Marset is the Ringo lighting, crafted by designer Joan Gaspar from transparent polycarbonate that is rotomoulded, giving it a dimpled texture reminiscent of a melting block of ice.

Available in flush-mounted or pendant styles, the design has a simple cylindrical shape, with scale and materiality bringing fresh life and visual impact.

Another of Gaspar’s designs is Domus, an angular bollard-style outdoor light that, through simple gesture, recalls a warmly lit house at night.

The design is available in three heights. Units can be optionally combined to create a sculptural look and the illusion of multiple windows.

Geometric glass volumes, metal detailing and glowing bar-shaped lighting elements meet in the Fragile collection, designed for the brand by Jaume Ramírez.

The lights come in pendant, wall and table formats, each made up of spherical and conical shades that lend them a playful aesthetic.

The roots of the Marset brand stretch back to the 1940s, when Francisco “Paco” Marset established a small metal foundry in Barcelona.

His grandchildren Javier and Carlos Marset helped reposition the company as the global design brand it is today when they took over in the 1990s, bringing on board designers such as Gaspar, who is a frequent collaborator.

item.title: Lucy McRae creates replicant birth bags for Blade Runner 2099 show where "violence and femininity coexist"
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: creative application of design in a sci-fi context

Lucy McRae creates replicant birth bags for Blade Runner 2099 show where “violence and femininity coexist”

Los Angeles-based artist Lucy McRae has created tactile, custom-made designs for sci-fi mini-series Blade Runner 2099 that veer away from the traditionally cold and metallic aesthetic of the films.

The show, which premiered on Wednesday on Amazon Prime, is the latest in the Blade Runner universe and follows Cora, a human fugitive played by actor Hunter Schafer.

She goes undercover as a replicant – a synthetic human – blade runner with veteran replicant Olwen, played by actor Michelle Yeoh, to track down a runaway carrying a secret that could destabilise the city.

McRae joined the production in 2022 as the official futurist of the show, after showrunner Silka Luisa saw her previous work exploring the relationship between emerging technology and human biology.

Her speculative work on body futurism later became direct visual references for the show and McRae was asked to speculate on human consciousness in 50 years’ time, with a specific focus on memory, bio-engineering, replicants’ sensuality, sex and family.

“I created a world-build of those questions, through scale models, building concepts through physical materials,” McRae told Dezeen. “These ideas begin to transpire within the show.”

McRae designed the film’s birth bags, which are incubator-like sacks used to birth or transform replicants.

She also made the crèche set, the facility and replicant birth system that support the birth bags, as well as a skin polymer traction machine that was used for healing the protagonist Cora.

McRae also designed the material and colour palette for replicants, which includes pipes, quilting and industrial materials that fit the interiors of Olwen’s spacecraft and the padding around the traction machine.

The birth bag is a new iteration of McRae’s Compression Cradle, a project presented at the 2019 Milan Triennale exhibition Broken Nature.

It was a machine that offered a simulated hug to a person craving intimacy using an inflatable device.

In Blade Runner 2099, the design scale expanded dramatically, with nine vertical Compression Cradles created inside the Tyrell building where they functioned as birth bags in the show.

McRae often describes herself as a “body architect”. At Future Sensitive, the art-research lab she leads, her work revolves around using the body as a means to speculate on the future.

A few of her recent projects have explored what McRae calls the touch crisis – the idea that, with the rise of technology, digital devices might start to vie for human affection, and physical contact with other humans might suffer as a result.

Her Heavy Duty Love, for example, created for the Venice Architecture Biennale 2021, imagines a machine replacement of a parent’s embrace in a world where humans are grown in artificial wombs.

With The Future Day Spa, meanwhile, she presented a machine that could replace human contact altogether.

McRae’s says her focus on material tactility – such as creases, wrinkles, and squishy textures – adds a femininity to the show.

The series is built on the sci-fi intellectual property that followed from the original 1982 film and its aesthetic was historically labelled as metallic, cold, slick and masculine.

“The physicalisation of the work I do, the texture, achieves the femininity the show was after,” said McRae. “It’s an absolute masterpiece where both violence and femininity coexist.”

She also believes that by domesticating science and rendering technology malleable and wet, it creates a positive future that feels within human grasp and participation.

“It feels positive because it feels within my grasp. I feel I can participate and I can contribute,” said McRae. “Whereas if it’s a future that doesn’t look or feel or belong to something that I understand, then it feels like it’s a closed door.”

The designer said her work for the series, and in general, aims to focus on plausible futures rather than pure fantasy, while raising open-ended questions and encouraging audiences to navigate uncertainty with hope.

“What’s important for Silka and for my work is that anything I’m dealing with is never fantasy,” said McRae.

“I think physicalising possibility allows us to wear it, touch it and be able to get close to something that is far away but then allows us to see if it’s a fit, see if it belongs.”

“What I’m trying to do is create opportunities for people to ask these questions themselves and for me to not answer them. It’s going to be open-ended and unanswered because we don’t live in a world where one answer or many answers fit.”

item.title: The Bombmaker Next Door
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth reporting, original content, and clear, well-structured English.

When John Nelson died in the summer of 2025, he left behind more than 400 explosive devices, a literal minefield that ran through his home in the suburbs between Manchester and Liverpool. The painstaking work of clearing Nelson’s home of explosives prompted “one of the largest domestic evacuations of its kind in recent British history,” writes Andrew Kersley, who spent months interviewing the experts who kept Nelson’s home from exploding, as well as the neighbors who seemingly loved him. “I guess it was just his pastime,” one tells Kersley. Indeed!

During a second search after Nelson’s death, police had discovered a small tobacco tin containing explosives, with wires protruding from it. RY set up his X-ray machine and stepped into the adjoining room while it scanned the tin. As he reached for the door, he almost triggered the first booby trap: a fishing line wrapped around the handle that was attached to a rigged shotgun cartridge. Suddenly the contents of the house looked rather different. If one door had been trapped, any of them might be. So might any of the shoulder-high piles surrounding him.

More stories about neighbors

How I Became the Villain of El Cerrito’s Nextdoor

“I had a panic attack. Then I wrote an apology letter.”

What I Found When I Tried to Walk Across Dallas in a Day

item.title: Vegetabilities: A Harvest of a Reading List on Vegetables
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Thoughtful exploration of a topic with a focus on learning and originality.

Thoughtful stories for thoughtless times.

And they’re all funded by readers like you. Become a member today.

Whenever I clean spinach or other greens, I get a curious feeling. I see a post-apocalyptic future, where a white-haired version of me is cleaning greens amid the ruins, salvaging every tiny, edible leaf. I then imagine my ancestors doing the same thing a hundred thousand years ago. Nothing heroic about this work, no high drama, no awesome mammoth-hunting. Just the fundamental stuff that keeps life going.

“In the temperate and tropical regions where it appears that hominids evolved into human beings, the principal food of the species was vegetable,” Ursula K. Le Guin reminds us in her classic The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction. “Sixty-five to eighty percent of what human beings ate in those regions in Paleolithic, Neolithic, and prehistoric times was gathered; only in the extreme Arctic was meat the staple food.”

Vegetables have quietly sustained us, season after season, year after year, for millennia. Down-to-earth and seemingly mundane, they claim deep love and reverence from those who care to look. Over time, we have even come to imbue vegetables with drama, heroes, stories. Are they (and we) made better by the act? Or do they only require simple, loving attention?

When Edward Espe Brown, Zen monk and chef, was a young student at the Tassajara Zen Mountain Center in California, he asked his teacher, Shunryū Suzuki Rōshi, for advice on working in the kitchen. “When you wash the rice,” Rōshi told him, “wash the rice. When you cut the carrots, cut the carrots. When you stir the soup, stir the soup.”

It takes a long time to understand vegetables, cooking, and giving and receiving nourishing food. But what if that is only one half of the truth, one way of looking at things? What if it also takes no time at all, and we can understand everything right this moment? “Appreciate this carrot, cabbage, cucumber, and cress, this time with the less than perfect,” Brown reminds us. “The remarkable flavor you have searched for is everywhere. Let it come home to your heart.” Bon appétit!

Can Babies Learn to Love Vegetables? (Burkhard Bilger, The New Yorker, November 2019)

Every Halloween, Linus sits in the “most sincere” pumpkin patch with a signboard, awaiting the arrival of The Great Pumpkin. Will he come this year? Watch the 1966 classic “It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown” on Apple TV.

I’ve always been a vegetarian. You might think that would make me biased toward vegetables, and you’d be right. But when I was little, I routinely fantasized about installing a zipper in my belly so I could just shove the little devils in without ever taking my eyes off my comics. I eventually grew to love them, but could something have been done to smooth the way earlier?

The title question must be asked, for that’s where the story begins—babies and their smushed-up veggies. Bilger seeks an answer.

The enemy in question is kale. The four cups are all filled with raw kale leaves whipped into a smooth purée, or slurry, as food researchers call it. One sample is plain, another sweet, another sweeter still, and the last one salted. Sugar and salt can mask the bitterness in kale, but this baby isn’t fooled. No matter which sample he’s offered, he grimaces and turns his head, purses his lips, and swats the spoon away. The more his mother tries, the grumpier he gets, till he kicks his foot so hard that he jostles the electrode, disrupting the signal.

Stalking the Vegetannual (Barbara Kingsolver, Orion, March/April 2007)

Way before the Potato of Immaculate Conception, in the Middle Ages, there was the Vegetable Lamb of Tartary—“a strange hybrid creature, half-animal, half-plant.” Thom Sliwowski investigates old vegetable fancies for The Public Domain Review in “Animal, Vegetable, Lamb: The Zoophyte from Tartary.”

“Wait a minute,” a friend asks Kingsolver, “When you say, ‘the potatoes are up,’ what do you mean?” An urban, gourmet chef, she tries to puzzle it out some more: “What part of a potato comes up?” I find it somewhat hard to believe that a chef might not know the potato has a plant part, but who knows with us modern humans? We buy the vegetables that look appealing (and feel affordable) at the shop, never mind the season or the provenance.

Kingsolver has a remedy. She gives us “a roadmap to eating with the seasons”—a beautiful visual mnemonic, if you will, one you’re unlikely to forget once you’ve successfully pictured it. What’s better, it’s actually useful.

To recover an intuitive sense of what will be in season throughout the year, picture an imaginary plant that bears over the course of one growing season all the different vegetable products we can harvest. We’ll call it a vegetannual. Picture its life passing before your eyes like a time-lapse film: first, in the cool early spring, shoots poke up out of the ground. Small leaves appear, then bigger leaves. As the plant grows up into the sunshine and the days grow longer, flower buds will appear, followed by small green fruits. Under midsummer’s warm sun, the fruits grow larger, riper, and more colorful. As days shorten into the autumn, these mature into hard-shelled fruits with appreciable seeds inside. Finally, as the days grow cool, the vegetannual may hoard the sugars its leaves have made, pulling them down into a storage unit of some kind: a tuber, bulb, or root.…

Source: Longreads | Published: 2026-11-26 11:00 UTC | Difficulty: 41/100

item.description:

Why it is here: Engaging and informative, with a focus on a specific event and its context.

Black and tan coonhound Rocker is top dog at the 2026 National Dog Show

An enthusiastic black and tan coonhound with a glossy coat and big floppy ears named Rocker is top dog at this year's National Dog Show — the most widely viewed dog competition in the country.

Rocker took the prestigious best in show prize after defeating six other dogs who each won top honors in their groups. Rocker earned first place among the hound group.

Best in show judge Lorraine Bisso commended Rocker's looks and physical agility.

"He's got a very masculine head. It's correct for the breed in terms of length and width," Bisso said. "He has beautiful feet. He has a lovely forechest — which is necessary, because he's going to run for 25 miles. I mean, this is a hunting hound."

Bisso extended her praise to Rocker's handler, Mandy Clevenger, who has handled the coonhound since he started his career as a show dog as a pup.

"The mark of a good handler is to fade into the background and let the dog speak for itself," Bisso said.

Judges assess the competitors based on the codified ideals of their respective breeds, judging them on physical structure and temperamental characteristics. Around 2,000 canines compete each year for honors like best of breed, first in group, and the top best in show title.

"I just didn't expect it," said Clevenger of the win, adding that Rocker appeared to enjoy himself throughout the competition. "He loves the crowd," Clevenger said.

Rocker, who is owned by Traci Mitchell of Bedford, Iowa, is used to earning top honors. Thursday's title was Rocker's 15th best in show. The coonhound is expected to compete at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show early next year in New York City.

Victors in the other six groups for 2026 include a lhasa apso named Kissy in the non-sporting group; Biggie Smalls, a Newfoundland in the working category; and, in the terrier contest, a Norfolk terrier named Rambo.

NBC broadcast the annual event on Thanksgiving, as the network has done since 2002. It was also streamed on Peacock. Former Seinfeld star John O'Hurley, sports commentator Mary Carillo, and canine expert David Frei hosted the show, which was held in person at the Greater Philadelphia Expo Center on Nov. 14 and 15.

Last year's best in show winner was Soleil, a Belgian sheepdog.

The Kennel Club of Philadelphia originally launched its dog show in 1879 – and has organized it annually since 1933 – long before the televised National Dog Show era began in 2002 with NBC's partnership with the club and sponsor Purina.

Owing to the rescheduled Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, NBC plans to rebroadcast the National Dog Show on Saturday from noon to 2 p.m., following the rescheduled parade.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Slapping someone in the face is now a sport. Yes, I’m surprised too. But in an era of ever-shrinking attention spans, getting to the point (or the slap) within seconds seems to be the surest way to hold viewers. According to its founder, Dana White, “Power Slap has secured more sponsorship revenue in its first two years than UFC did in its first decade.” Stuart McGurk deftly guides us through the rise of the slap, and talks with those who fear the consequences of hitting someone round the head as hard as you can.

The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. Victory can be earned on points – the three judges look for clean technique and the impact a strike makes – but about half are won via knockout. The podium is padded, as the competitors sometimes collide with it on the way down. Behind each competitor stand two catchers to grab them as they fall. When Power Slap introduced a super-heavyweight division, where contestants can weigh the same as an upright piano, they hired professional strongmen for the job.

I Went to the White House Brawl and Watched the Manosphere Go Limp

“It was supposed to be an exhibition of freedom without restraint: a bombastic birthday boy, fourteen uncontrollable athletes, and a South Lawn build-out that was piss-your-pants patriotic. But what united onlookers, in the end, was the sudden realization that American machismo had hit a hard limit.”

item.title: How propagandists weaponize archaeology to rewrite the past
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The historian Eric Hobsbawm once said, “Historians are to nationalism what poppy-growers … are to heroin-addicts. [They] supply the essential raw material.” The same holds true for archaeologists. The heritage archaeologists reveal helps groups of people forge collective identities and anchor our fleeting lives in something enduring. Spectacular discoveries — King Tut’s mask, the bronzes of Benin, Irish harps — also become national icons and rallying points.

Regrettably, people with political agendas know this and often treat the past as ready-made propaganda — a bin to root through for “evidence” that justifies their goals. And if they can’t find what they need, they have no compunctions about twisting archaeology to suit their purposes.

Consider the Peking Man fossils from China. Despite the singular name, these fossils consist of 40-odd men, women, and children unearthed 30 miles from Beijing starting in 1929. They belong to a hominin subspecies called Homo erectus pekinensis and lived 410,000 to 780,000 years ago.

It’s unlikely that Peking Man was a direct ancestor of modern humans. Homo sapiens originated in Africa 300,000 years ago, then spread globally. Along the way, we interbred in Asia with two other hominins (Neanderthals and Denisovans), so there’s a chance we interbred in China with later ancestors of Peking Man, but most scientists don’t think so. Regardless, archaeologists unanimously trace humankind’s ultimate ancestry to Africa.

Unanimous outside China, at least. Again, humankind does have a modest amount of non-African ancestry — a few percentage points — but ideologues within China push the notion of non-African ancestors way too far. They insist that Peking Man was the very wellspring of humanity.

Sometimes this manifests itself in harmless ways. Before the 2008 Olympics in Beijing, Chinese officials lit the ceremonial relay torch at the quarry where the fossils first turned up. But other beliefs about Peking Man have a sinister edge. In 2012, China’s top propaganda minister published a paper noting that certain traits separate humans from apes — hairless bodies, an upright gait, long legs relative to our arms. He then asserted, with zero evidence, that everyone “knows” Chinese people have the least body hair, the flattest butts when standing, and the shortest arms of any race. The Chinese must “therefore” have evolved into humans first and are farthest along the evolutionary road to perfection.

Sadly, Chinese archaeologists who challenge such claims have been smeared as traitors and “scum.” Worse, opposition to African origins often deteriorates into abuse of African people. As one critic commented, in China, “the most fundamental of scientific questions — where we come from — has been subordinated to the demands of nation, pride, and self-image.”

Grateful for curious minds

This Thanksgiving, get 15% off Big Think membership and join a community of idea explorers. Use code BIGTHANKS15 at checkout. Valid on annual plans for new members only.

Archaeology has been dragged into the dispute over Taiwan, as well. In 2024, the Keqiutou Archaeological Museum opened in Pingtan, an island off mainland China that practically stares Taiwan in the face. The museum proposes a radical reinterpretation of Taiwanese history.

Since the 1980s, archaeologists have known that Taiwan’s indigenous, non-Chinese peoples began making excursions to islands in the Pacific Ocean starting 5,000 years ago. Those pioneers eventually settled greater Polynesia. Linguistic, artifactual, and genetic evidence supports this, further demonstrating that Taiwan had a thriving, pre-Chinese culture.

In contrast, the Keqiutou museum argues that Taiwan lacked culture until mainland Chinese people moved to Taiwan 6,500 years ago. It also claims that it was those ethnic Chinese who colonized Polynesia. Curators base this claim on supposed similarities between ancient pottery at different sites and the carbon dating of rice and millet — connections that the vast majority of archaeologists find specious.

Nevertheless, such claims allow the Chinese government to insist that indigenous Taiwanese culture is “really” Chinese deep down, and that Taiwan should therefore belong to mainland China today. Chinese president Xi Jinping himself has alluded to these claims in speeches.

China’s neighbor India also uses archaeology to push nationalistic agendas.

To simplify somewhat, there’s a divide in Indian history between Dravidians and Aryans. (In this context, Aryans are not Caucasians, but an ancient cultural group.) Nowadays, the descendants of Aryans predominate in northern India, while Dravidians inhabit the south. But that tidy split masks a long, fraught relationship.

The standard view of Indian history holds that Dravidians once ranged across all India, north and south. Then, roughly 4,000 years ago, Aryan males began migrating into India from western Asia. The details are murky, but these men probably arrived in waves over several centuries and imported both their language (which became Sanskrit) and the religious practices that shaped modern Hinduism. During this migration, Dravidians were pushed south, and the proto-Hindu culture of the incoming Aryans eventually dominated the subcontinent.

Still, a key detail of the migration remained unknown. Did Aryans push south peacefully and accumulate power gradually, or storm in and conquer?

In the early 1900s, the conquest theory reigned supreme, to the delight of the Aryans’ descendants. They’d long scorned Dravidians as backward and claimed that their ancestors brought culture to a savage land.…

item.title: 10 facts you (probably) didn't know about the Middle Ages
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

10 facts you (probably) didn't know about the Middle Ages

How much do you really know about the Middle Ages? Here, John H Arnold, professor of medieval history, reveals 10 facts about the medieval period that might surprise you

They weren’t all knights or serfs or clergy

Although certain medieval writers described their society as divided into ‘three orders’ – those who prayed, those who fought, and those who laboured – that became an increasingly inaccurate picture after about 1100.

The population of Europe increased hugely across the 12th and 13th centuries, with cities and towns getting much larger. Paris grew about tenfold (and London nearly as much) in this period. In the cities, people had all kinds of jobs: merchants, salesmen, carpenters, butchers, weavers, food sellers, architects, painters, jugglers.

And in the countryside, it was not at all the case that everyone was an impoverished ‘serf’ (that is, ‘unfree’ and tied to the land). Many peasants were free men – and women – and owned their own land, while others who were to some degree ‘unfree’ in fact bought and sold land and goods, much like other free men. There certainly were poor, oppressed serfs, but it wasn't a universal condition.

People had the vote

Well, some people at least. Not a vote for national, representative government – because that really wasn't a medieval thing – but a vote in local politics. In France, in the 12th and 13th centuries and beyond, many towns and villages were run at a local level as a commune, and there were often annual elections for ‘consuls’ and ‘councillors’, where most of the male inhabitants could vote.

A more complex form of election and government was used in the city states of north Italy, with more tiers of elected officials. Women could not usually stand as officials, nor vote, but some of them were noted in the agreed charters of ‘liberties’ that French towns proudly possessed.

The church didn't conduct witch hunts

Large-scale witch hunts and the collective fear of the stereotypical ‘evil witch’ belong chiefly to the early modern period. There were some witch trials in the Middle Ages, and these became more widespread in German-speaking lands in the 15th century, but those doing the prosecuting were almost always civic authorities rather than ecclesiastical ones.

For much of the Middle Ages, the main message that churchmen gave in regard to magic was that it was foolish nonsense that didn't work. When Heinrich Kramer wrote the infamous Malleus Maleficarum in the late 15th century, his motive was to try to persuade people of the reality of witches. In fact, the book was initially condemned by the church, and even in the early 16th century, inquisitors were warned not to believe everything that it said.

They had a Renaissance, and invented experimental science

When people talk about ‘the Renaissance’, they usually mean the very self-conscious embrace of classical models in literature, art, architecture and learning found at the end of the Middle Ages. This is usually taken to be one of the ways in which we moved from ‘medieval’ to (early) ‘modern’ ways of thinking.

But in fact, medieval intellectuals also had a ‘renaissance’ of classical learning and rhetoric. This was in the 12th century, and depended particularly on the transmission of works by Aristotle and other classical authors via Arabic philosophers and translators.

One of the outcomes was to prompt an enquiring and reflective approach to the physical world, and it led Roger Bacon (c1214–94), among others, to think about how one might observe and experiment with the physical world to learn more about it.

They travelled – and traded – over very long distances

It may be the case that the majority of medieval people – particularly those who lived in the countryside – rarely travelled very far from where they lived. But that would be the case with quite a lot of people in much later ages also.

It is not the case, however, that medieval people never travelled. Many went on pilgrimage, sometimes journeying thousands of miles to do so. And those involved in trade certainly travelled, linking parts of the world together via merchandise across extraordinary distances.

Even in the early Middle Ages, all kinds of high-status goods were transported from very distant shores to various European lands: silk from China; spices from Asia, brought to Europe via the Middle East; amber and furs from the Baltic. A few intrepid travellers even wrote journals charting their journeys: William of Rubruck’s Journey to the Eastern Parts of the World describes his three-year journey, which began in 1253, through the lands we now know as Ukraine and Russia.

There was also immigration in the Middle Ages – although the residents of medieval England didn't always roll out the red carpet for Welsh, Scottish and Irish immigrants.

They had some great ‘folk’ customs

Much of the public culture of the Middle Ages was shaped by (or at least informed by) Christianity. But there were also some quite curious customs, usually tolerated by the church, but which may have had older roots.

One was the practice – found in many different parts of Europe – of rolling burning barrels down a hill on Midsummer’s Eve. Another was to throw wheat over the heads of a newly married couple. It was also common to raise money for charity by holding a ‘help ale’: brewing up a batch of ale, having a big party to drink it, and collecting donations.

There were undoubtedly a number of things that look to us like ‘superstitions’, often to do with invoking supernatural protection against disease or failure of harvest. But the Midsummer festivals, and the ales, also sound like they were a good laugh.

You didn't have to get married in church…

item.title: Lina Ghotmeh: archaeology of the future
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The Lebanese architect Lina Ghotmeh is known for works that preserve memories of the past but are built for the future. These notably include her design for the Estonian National Museum (completed in 2016), which transformed a former Soviet airfield, and Stone Garden (completed in 2020), an apartment building in her home city of Beirut, whose facade openings, filled with greenery, evoke bullet scars and shelling. This short documentary from the London-based director Stephen Pook deconstructs Ghotmeh’s approach to architecture, revealing how her designs and thoughtful use of materials are born of a process in which history matters as much as the physical environment. In particular, the film focuses on her aesthetics and philosophy in the context of another work that demands deep sensitivity to the past and a vision for the future: her redevelopment of the Western Range at the British Museum in London, which constitutes about a third of the iconic museum’s total gallery space.

item.title: The Cutthroat Business of Shipwrecks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars. Two Portuguese ships, so huge they were referred to as “floating cities,” had shipwrecked off the coast of Bordeaux, spilling luxury goods into the waves.

The disaster quickly threatened to become an international incident. The owners of the cargo (unsurprisingly) wanted their goods back—but the coast dwellers claimed that anything that washed up on shore was theirs by the ancient droit du naufrage, the “right of wreck.”

It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims. The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns: in his travels through Norfolk, Daniel Defoe wrote that the “country people had scarce a barn, or a shed, or a stable…but what was built of old planks, beams, wales and timbers, &c. the wrecks of ships, and ruins of mariners and merchants’ fortunes.”

That said, in legal terms, the right of wreck was a little more complicated than “finders keepers.” In many places, it wasn’t actually the person who stumbled on the shipwrecked goods who held the right to them; rather, they became the property of the local lord. In the earliest iterations of this idea, poor shipwreck survivors could find themselves roughly stripped of all their goods—as King Richard I of England found when his fleet was unlucky enough to wash up off the coast of Cyprus, circa 1191. His fiancée and his sister were taken as captives by the emperor of the island, who also helped himself to all the treasure they’d been traveling with. (This didn’t end well for the emperor, who lost his throne in the ensuing war.)

Neither wealthy merchants nor traveling kings were particularly enthusiastic about the idea that an accident at sea could mean forfeiting all their cargo. On the other hand, powerful landowners were eager to preserve their right to the occasional random windfall. As international trade increased, the right of wreck was slowly reshaped by centuries of legal wrangling. Courts battling over who could keep what ended up creating, for instance, highly specific legal definitions for terms like “flotsam” (goods that just happened to float to the surface after a wreck) and “jetsam” (goods intentionally tossed from a ship to make it lighter).

More to Explore

Lonely Diarist of the High Seas

The resulting patchwork of rules meant that every shipwreck was a complex negotiation between competing interests. Usually, the owners of the shipwrecked goods were entitled to their property back, in exchange for some kind of fee. Whether that was a ransom or a fair reward for helping salvage the goods is a matter of perspective.

In 1236, King Henry III of England issued an edict stating that if “man, dog, or cat” escaped the shipwreck alive, finders were obligated to hold on to the wrecked goods for three months, allowing the survivors to claim them in that time. There is a bit of an issue with that rule: it’s easy to see how it could create an incentive for shore dwellers to do away with shipwreck survivors in order to claim their goods (whether those survivors be man, dog, or cat)

Legends of these dark deeds swirled for centuries, but there’s little evidence they really happened. Still, people could be rough in their efforts to “salvage.” In Estonia, for instance, where the local lords were entitled to rewards if they helped to save ships in distress, people developed a habit of launching into enthusiastic “rescue” operations, whether or not there was any real danger.

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

A particularly good wreck could spark a feeding frenzy. An account of the wreck of the Golden Grape in 1641 gives a sense of the chaos:

The first arrivals on the beach contented themselves with staving in barrels and filling linen bags and pockets with raisins or, stripping off their waistcoats, used the sleeves as bags. But soon bands of men appeared from the various villages… Some gangs or men took away a score or two of barrels of raisins or the same number of jars of oil, but they were lucky if they did not have to share their booty with a stronger gang before they could gain a place of safety.

Not everything washes ashore, of course; many of the treasures lost in wrecks sank under the waves. There were fortunes to be made, but in a time before diving equipment, the trouble was how to reach it. In the early modern era, for the most part, even European sailors could hardly swim. But Africans living by the sea in Senegambia and the Gold Coast were highly skilled swimmers and divers—leading them to be targeted by enslavers, who knew their specialized skills could be turned to the recovery of underwater riches. As historian Kevin Dawson writes in “History Below the Waterline: Enslaved Salvage Divers Harvesting Seaports’ Hinter-Seas in the Early Modern Atlantic”:

The African-honed expertise that enslaved underwater divers carried throughout the Atlantic world allowed them to quickly recover several tons of gold, silver, and other items from shipwrecks, especially old Spanish treasure hulks. Possessing proficiencies held by few in the world, divers exchanged their unique ability to rapidly produce capital for semi-independent lives of privileged exploitation.

Their skills were so irreplaceable that they were able to negotiate for better treatment than most enslaved people, including a share of what they salvaged. Though, of course, a share isn’t much when you’re doing all the work.

Source: JSTOR Daily | Published: 2026-11-26 14:52 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: 6 Things Every '90s Kid Remembers About Black Friday
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Another Black Friday is upon us, and for kids and parents today, it will be a very different experience than you would have encountered back in the 1990s. In the days before the ubiquity of online shopping, physical stores were the only places to grab your bargains, and â90s kids will remember some distinctly different occurrences and âadventuresâ that colored every bargain-hunting trip.

Scouring the Catalogs

With no Google to turn to, finding discounts and sales was very much a manual job. It entailed searching through every newspaper, magazine, and catalog that came through the door, ideally with a big red marker pen in hand. Next, out came your notebook and calendar and it was into the phase of cross-planning. Which store or mall offered the best prices? When and where did each sale begin? Maps would need to be consulted, deals compared, diaries considered. Back then, hitting the Black Friday sales was akin to a military operation.

Queuing in the Cold

With little in the way of pre-ordering or home delivery available, bagging those bargains meant putting your feet on the ground. You want that fifty percent discount on a top-of-the-range LED television? You'd better make sure you're one of the first through the doors. That meant arriving early and queuing. A lot of queuing. We'd even go so far as to say an inordinate amount. With brick-and-mortar stores the only way to go, people would arrive hours before opening time for an especially attractive deal.

Parking Lot Mayhem

Shopping meant cars. Lots of cars, usually full of people. What better recipe could there be for stress and arguments than a harassed family crowded into one vehicle, competing against countless other families in the same predicament for a parking space at the mall. â90s kids may well remember endless loops of the lot, whilst charged by their parents with the vital task of looking out for any car that might just be about to pull out, or, miracle of miracles, an already empty space. Oh, the feeling of relief when you finally pulled in and switched off the engine. Then the real fun could begin.

In-Store Bust-Ups

We're not suggesting every Black Friday bargain hunter was an accidental push away from losing it, but in-store fistfights certainly did happen. Malls on Black Friday provided a perfect storm of stressed adults, swarming crowds, and exasperated kids, all on the hunt for the same limited stock. Perhaps these conditions awakened a long-dormant primal instinct of survival of the fittest. Spare a thought for those poor store workers, looking out through the windows at five minutes to nine, faced by a terrifying mob of soon-to-be invaders. Such scenes were regular sights back in the day.

Iconic Stores

Younger people won't remember some of the iconic 1990s stores that are sadly no longer with us. Remember Musicland? This fantastic chain provided a must-visit for record-loving adults and kids across the decades since the 1950s. It was around long enough to witness the transition from vinyl to cassette to CD and then, unfortunately for the company, to digital. As physical sales dwindled, the brand was passed on through several hands and today exists only in memory.

For the literary-minded, Waldenbooks was the book-lover's equivalent and had an even longer history. Founded in 1933, at its height the chain had over one thousand stores. As well as books, you could peruse a fantastic range of magazines. Waldenbooks was eventually merged with Borders before disappearing altogether. For kids, see also Kay Bee Toys, a major chain and serious rival to Toys "R" Us, and Warner Bros. Studio Store, both of which are now similarly defunct.

Scrambles for Must-Have Toys

Modern, Amazon-style infrastructure with advanced analytics and twenty-four delivery options didn't exist back in the 1990s, which led to several infamous manias for must-have toys that resulted in all-out chaos on the high streets. In pop culture, this was humorously reflected in the underrated 1996 movie, Jingle All the Way, which starred Arnold Schwarzenegger and Sinbad as rival fathers desperately trying to secure a Turbo Man action figure for their sons. In real life, Tickle Me Elmo figures, based on the popular Sesame Street characters, were the Cabbage Patch Kids of the '90s, with an absolute mania for them reportedly resulting in near riots across the country.

Other toys that reached similarly frenzied peaks of popularity during that decade include the Mighty Morphin Power Rangers range of action figures, the revolutionary Nintendo 64 gaming system, and Furby'sâthe interactive electronic plushies that enchanted thousands and gave just as many the absolute creeps.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-26 21:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: How a Thanksgiving Crisis Inspired the Invention of Swanson’s TV Dinner (1953)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne. “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a letter of objection from one Rosalie Levine of Lakewood, California.

“I live alone, I must control my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV dinner’s price “cannot possibly be bettered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready dinner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to prepare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up afterward.” While none of these advantages were accidental, the oft-told story of the concept’s emergence begins with a corporate crisis.

“In 1953, someone at Swanson colossally miscalculated the level of the American appetite for Thanksgiving turkey, leaving the company with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it. “Inspired by the trays of pre-prepared food served on airlines,” Swanson salesman Gerry Thomas set the machinery in motion to package the unwanted meat with gravy and sides like cornbread and sweet potatoes, ready for stocking in America’s frozen-food aisles.

The following year, Swanson sold ten million such “TV dinners,” a name attributed to both the shape of the boxes and the form of entertainment families tended to enjoy while eating the meals within. “In 1950, only 9 percent of U.S. households had television sets — but by 1955, the number had risen to more than 64 percent, and by 1960, to more than 87 percent,” writes Kovie Biakolo in a more recent Smithsonian piece. (Among the Smithsonian Institution’s holdings, incidentally, is an original Swanson TV dinner tray.) Another breakthrough came with the introduction of microwave-safe trays, bringing total preparation time under ten minutes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Americans rekindled their love affair with frozen meals, “spending nearly 50 percent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”

Where holiday and commercial lore intersect, the details tend to get complicated. Swanson’s TV dinner did have its precedents: the core technology for quick-freezing packaged foods was invented over a century ago by entrepreneur Clarence Birdseye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remembers as “little cryogenic miracles”), and in the late 1940s, different companies planned or attempted to bring frozen meals to market under brands like Strato-Plates, FridgiDinners, and One-Eyed Eskimo. None of those names tapped into the technology transforming not just American mass culture, but also the American way of life. In the fifties, associations with television (and, indeed, with air travel) carried a kind of sophistication they certainly don’t have today. Perhaps Craig Claiborne would be pleased that Americans never quite accepted microwaved TV dinners as a substitute for the Thanksgiving meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is another matter entirely.

item.title: 30 English Phrases for When You Don’t Know What to Say
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

Have you ever been in the middle of an English conversation and suddenly you don’t know what to say?

Maybe someone asks you a question and you need a few seconds to think. Maybe you don’t understand what the other person said. Or maybe the conversation reaches an awkward silence.

The good news is that you don’t need to have the perfect response ready at every moment. Native English speakers experience these situations, too – and we have lots of expressions that help us handle them naturally.

Today I’ll teach you 30 practical English conversation phrases for those moments when you don’t know what to say. These are great expressions to have ready in your mind so that you don’t freeze up when speaking English.

1. When you need a moment to think

Sometimes you understand the question perfectly, but you need a little extra time to formulate your answer in English. Instead of staying completely silent or saying “ummm” repeatedly, try these English conversation phrases.

Let me think for a second.

A simple, natural way to give yourself a few moments to think before responding.

- A: What was the most memorable part of your trip?

- B: Let me think for a second. Probably the day we went snorkeling.

That’s a good question.

You can use this expression to acknowledge someone’s question while giving yourself a little time to consider your answer.

- A: If you could change one thing about your job, what would it be?

- B: That’s a good question. I guess I’d like to have more flexibility.

How should I put this?

Use this when you know what you want to communicate, but you’re trying to find the right words to express it, especially if the topic is complicated or sensitive.

- A: Did you enjoy working with your previous manager?

- B: How should I put this? He was very talented, but he wasn’t particularly good at managing people.

Let me gather my thoughts.

This means you need a moment to organize your ideas before speaking.

- A: What did you think of the presentation?

- B: Let me gather my thoughts. There were some excellent ideas, but I have a few concerns as well.

Nothing comes to mind right now.

Use this when you can’t immediately think of an answer, example, or suggestion.

- A: Can you recommend any good restaurants around here?

- B: Nothing comes to mind right now, but I’ll let you know if I think of one.

I’m trying to find the right words.

This is especially useful for English learners because it lets the other person know that you’re still thinking about how to express yourself.

- A: How did you feel when you finally achieved your goal?

- B: I’m trying to find the right words. It was a mixture of excitement, relief, and disbelief.

2. When you don’t understand something

Don’t pretend to understand something when you don’t! Asking for clarification is a completely normal part of English conversation, even among native speakers.

Sorry, I didn’t catch that.

Use this when you didn’t hear or understand what someone just said, perhaps because they spoke quickly or there was background noise.

- A: We’ll meet at the entrance on the north side of the building.

- B: Sorry, I didn’t catch that. Where are we meeting?

Could you run that by me again?

This is a conversational way to ask someone to repeat or explain something again.

- A: You’ll need to transfer the files before you update the software.

- B: Could you run that by me again?

I’m not quite following you.

Use this when you can hear the words someone is saying, but you’re having trouble understanding their explanation or train of thought.

- A: So technically, we’d save money by spending more money upfront.

- B: I’m not quite following you. How would that work?

What exactly do you mean by that?

Use this when someone’s statement is unclear, vague, or open to different interpretations.

- A: I think we need to take a different approach.

- B: What exactly do you mean by that?

Be aware that your tone of voice is important here. A curious, friendly tone makes this sound like a genuine request for clarification.

Could you give me an example?

Sometimes the easiest way to understand an unfamiliar concept is to ask for a specific example.

- A: You need to make your writing more engaging.

- B: Could you give me an example?

So, are you saying that…?

This is a great way to check your understanding by expressing the other person’s idea in your own words.

- A: We won’t be able to start until everyone has submitted their documents.

- B: So, are you saying that one missing document could delay the entire process?

This technique is particularly useful because it gives the other person an opportunity to confirm or correct your understanding.

3. When you can’t think of a word in English

You might know exactly what you want to say, but there’s one specific English word you can’t remember. Here are some English conversation phrases to handle that situation without abandoning your sentence.

What’s the word I’m looking for?

You can say this out loud when you’re searching for a particular word.

- The instructions were really… what’s the word I’m looking for?… misleading! That’s it.

It’s on the tip of my tongue.

This idiom means you feel that you’re very close to remembering a word, name, or piece of information, but you can’t quite remember it.

- A: Who’s the actor who played the main character?

- B: Oh, I know his name! It’s on the tip of my tongue.

I can’t think of the word, but it’s…

Instead of stopping completely, try describing the thing you’re talking about.

- I can’t think of the word, but it’s a tool you use to remove the skin from vegetables.

The word in this case is “peeler.”

This is an excellent strategy for English learners. You can often communicate successfully even when you don’t know the exact vocabulary word.

For lack of a better word……

Source: Espresso English | Published: 2026-11-26 19:13 UTC | Difficulty: 41/100

item.title: 40 English Phrases For Love, Friendship & Relationships
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

Have you ever met someone and immediately felt comfortable with them? Have you ever lost touch with an old friend, had your heart broken, or fallen head over heels in love?

Relationships are a huge part of our lives, and English has some wonderful expressions for describing the connections we have with other people – from the excitement of falling in love to the challenges of maintaining a friendship.

Today you’ll learn 40 English phrases and expressions about love, friendship, and relationships. Some are simple, everyday phrases, and others are more colorful idiomatic expressions that will help you express yourself more naturally in English.

10 English Expressions About Dating & Falling in Love

1. Have a crush on someone

To have romantic feelings for someone, often without that person knowing about it.

- I had a huge crush on one of my classmates in high school, but I was too shy to talk to him.

2. Ask someone out

To invite someone on a date.

- They’ve been flirting with each other for weeks, and he finally asked her out.

If someone asks you out, there’s generally a romantic intention behind the invitation.

3. Go on a blind date

To go on a date with someone you’ve never met before.

- My sister set me up on a blind date with one of her coworkers.

Notice the expression set someone up with someone – this means to arrange for two people to meet because you think they might be romantically compatible.

4. Hit it off

To immediately like someone and enjoy interacting with them when you first meet.

- We hit it off on our first date and ended up talking for four hours.

You can also use this expression for friendships. It doesn’t necessarily imply romantic attraction.

5. Have chemistry

To have a natural, exciting connection with someone, especially a romantic one.

- They have amazing chemistry. You can tell just by watching them interact.

We sometimes talk about feeling a spark with someone – experiencing that initial feeling of romantic attraction.

6. Fall for someone

To develop romantic feelings for someone.

- I never expected to fall for him, but the more time we spent together, the more I liked him.

This is an informal alternative to saying “fall in love with someone,” although it doesn’t necessarily imply equally deep feelings.

7. Be head over heels in love

To be completely and intensely in love with someone.

- She’s head over heels in love with her new boyfriend. She can’t stop talking about him!

You can also say you’re head over heels for someone.

8. Make the first move

To be the first person to express romantic interest or take action to start a romantic relationship.

- They were both interested in each other, but neither of them wanted to make the first move.

9. The feeling isn’t mutual

This means that one person has romantic feelings for another person, but the other person doesn’t feel the same way.

- He’s really interested in her, but unfortunately, the feeling isn’t mutual. She just sees him as a friend.

The word mutual means shared or experienced by both people. If someone says they like you and you feel the same way, you can say, “The feeling is mutual!”

10. Sweep someone off their feet

To make someone fall in love with you, often in a sudden, exciting, or romantic way.

- He swept her off her feet with his charm, sense of humor, and thoughtful gestures.

Imagine being so impressed or excited by someone that you’re almost lifted off the ground!

10 English Expressions About Friendship

11. Get along well

To have a friendly, positive relationship with someone.

- I get along really well with my neighbors. We often have dinner together.

In British English, you’ll also hear get on well with someone.

12. Have a lot in common

To share many interests, experiences, opinions, or characteristics with someone.

- We have a lot in common – we both love hiking, cooking, and traveling.

Having things in common often helps people form friendships.

13. Go way back

To have known someone for a very long time.

- Sarah and I go way back – we’ve been friends since elementary school.

This informal expression emphasizes the long history you share with someone.

14. Be like two peas in a pod

To be extremely similar to each other in personality, appearance, or behavior.

- Those two are like two peas in a pod. They have the same sense of humor and enjoy all the same activities.

Imagine two little green peas growing next to each other inside the same pod.

15. Be inseparable

To spend so much time together that you’re rarely apart.

- My cousin and I were inseparable when we were kids.

This word can describe close friends, siblings, romantic partners, or even a person and their pet.

16. Keep in touch

To continue communicating with someone, especially when you no longer see each other regularly.

- Even though we live in different countries now, we still keep in touch.

At the end of a conversation with someone you might not see again for a while, you can say, “Let’s keep in touch!”

17. Catch up with someone

To talk to someone you haven’t seen or spoken to recently and exchange news about your lives.

- I’m meeting an old friend for coffee this weekend so we can catch up.

You can also say, “We have a lot of catching up to do!”

18. Be there for someone

To give someone emotional or practical support when they need it.

- When I was going through a difficult time, my friends were always there for me.

If someone is struggling, you can tell them, “I’m here for you.”

19. Have someone’s back

To support, protect, or defend someone, especially in a difficult situation.

- I wasn’t worried about facing the criticism alone because I knew my friends had my back.

This is an informal expression that communicates loyalty and trust.

20. Through thick and thin

Through both good times and difficult times.

- We’ve been friends for over 20 years, and we’ve stuck together through thick and thin.

This expression emphasizes the strength and loyalty of a relationship, even when circumstances become challenging.…

Source: Espresso English | Published: 2026-11-26 18:30 UTC | Difficulty: 41/100

item.title: The Illustrated Version of “Alice’s Restaurant”: Watch Arlo Guthrie’s Thanksgiving Counterculture Classic
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: cultural and historical context

Alice’s Restaurant. It’s now a Thanksgiving classic, and something of a tradition around here. Recorded in 1967, the 18+ minute counterculture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter with the law, starting on Thanksgiving Day 1965. As the long song unfolds, we hear all about how a hippie-bating police officer, by the name of William “Obie” Obanhein, arrested Arlo for littering. (Cultural footnote: Obie previously posed for several Norman Rockwell paintings, including the well-known painting, “The Runaway,” that graced a 1958 cover of The Saturday Evening Post.) In fairly short order, Arlo pleads guilty to a misdemeanor charge, pays a $25 fine, and cleans up the thrash. But the story isn’t over. Not by a long shot.

Later, when Arlo (son of Woody Guthrie) gets called up for the draft, the petty crime ironically becomes a basis for disqualifying him from military service in the Vietnam War. Guthrie recounts this with some bitterness as the song builds into a satirical protest against the war: “I’m sittin’ here on the Group W bench ’cause you want to know if I’m moral enough to join the Army, burn women, kids, houses and villages after bein’ a litterbug.” And then we’re back to the cheery chorus again: “You can get anything you want, at Alice’s Restaurant.”

We have featured Guthrie’s classic during past years. But, for this Thanksgiving, we give you the illustrated version.

item.title: Can Tadej Pogačar win all three Grand Tours in a season?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The question for five-time Tour de France winner Tadej Pogačar came from Tuttobiciweb during a friendly round of media interviews at an annual padel tournament put on by his agent, Alex Carera. Eddy Merckx, the greatest men's road racer of all time, had suggested in a separate interview back home in Belgium that perhaps Pogačar could win all three of cycling's Grand Tours – the Giro d'Italia, Tour de France and Vuelta a España – in a single season.

The feat has never been accomplished, not by Merckx or any other man. So what did Pogačar think of an attempt? "I don't rule it out; in fact, I'll try it sooner or later," he replied. There are certain caveats to raise here. It's possible he was just engaging in some friendly banter and has no serious intention of making an attempt. It's possible he's loosely entertaining the possibility and will change his mind.

But as responses go, it's a step further than his answer the last time he spoke about it, roughly a year ago in a Sky Sports interview. When the question arose then, "I don't know if I would do it," he hedged, saying he'd need to discuss it with team management, in particular because it would prevent other talented riders on his UAE Team Emirates-XRG squad from targeting their own objectives. "I don't think it's fair if I claim all the big Tours," he said.

Now, apparently, it's sooner or later. But likely not sooner, and it's certainly not a slam dunk. Even for the greatest racer in several generations, and perhaps ever, there are a ton of obstacles that stand in the way. Why hasn't anyone ever accomplished the feat, and what needs to happen for Pogačar to be the one to do it?

Wait, no one's ever won all three in a season?
