Boxing chiefs to assess Fury mental health before fight

The British Boxing Board of Control is looking into Tyson Fury's comments about his schizophrenia diagnosis but is "fairly confident" the British heavyweight will be cleared to fight Anthony Joshua next month.

Fury, 38, is due to face Joshua at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December, with the ringwalk expected in the early hours of 12 December.

In a Netflix documentary out on Friday, he says he heard voices threatening him and his family in the months after he beat Wladimir Klitschko to become world champion in 2015.

"We are in the process of dealing with the matter but if there are any medical issues we wouldn't let anyone box, doesn't matter if it's Tyson Fury or not, it could be anybody," Robert Smith, the board's general secretary, told BBC Sport.

"I'm fairly confident he will be absolutely fine. We're dealing with it now and we'll have an answer very shortly."

Under regulation 8.1(b) of the British Boxing Board of Control's 2026 rules and regulations, external, schizophrenia is among the conditions that "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence, while for an existing licence holder the board "may take such action as in its absolute discretion it sees fit".

Smith would not say what the process would involve over the next few days, saying "it's a medical matter".

He said that all boxers on the card will undergo medical checks, adding: "If our doctors are satisfied he's fit to box, he will box."

In the documentary, Fury and his wife Paris recall his admission to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack.

Doctors said he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia after he left hospital, according to the film.

The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech.

"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury says.

The heavyweight, who struggled with drug and alcohol addiction after beating Klitschko, says a Halloween night out in 2017 prompted him to return to training, calling that a "turning point" after being "embarrassed by how I looked".

He went on to beat Deontay Wilder in 2020 to become world heavyweight champion for a second time.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Aaron Rodgers: Quarterback 'losing respect' as NFL reacts to stunning Mike McCarthy claims

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers claims that head coach Mike McCarthy was 'snoring' in a quarterback meeting in an explosive interview; Steelers president Art Rooney II comes out in "100 per cent" support of McCarthy after team releases Rodgers in light of comments

Thursday 26 November 2026 20:12, UK

Has Aaron Rodgers played his final game in the NFL? Was he wrong to publicly criticise Mike McCarthy? The four-time MVP quarterback is 'losing respect' following his explosive claims about the Pittsburgh Steelers head coach, according to Sky Sports NFL's Jason Bell.

Rodgers sent shockwaves through the NFL on Thanksgiving Eve as he used an interview on The Pat McAfee Show to claim McCarthy had been "falling asleep in meetings" while suggesting his entire team believed a change was required on the sideline.

It came after Rodgers was benched for Friday's matchup with the Denver Broncos following two straight defeats, with Mason Rudolph due to start under center.

The Steelers later released Rodgers 11 weeks into what is set to be the final season of the 42-year-old's career.

- How to watch NFL Thanksgiving week live on Sky Sports

- Jay-Z picks himself to headline Super Bowl half-time show

- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW

"First of all, I don't want to be on Aaron Rodgers' bad side. Let's start there. We all make mistakes, right? We all do things that aren't necessarily right in the moment," said Sky Sports NFL's Bell.

"But when I look at him as a player, he wasn't playing well. He wasn't helping his team.

"And you could could see him and his head coach arguing on the sideline with with each other. They weren't getting along.

"Whatever happens behind closed doors, that goes down, but the response to it is where I'm losing a little respect.

"In that locker room is a sanctuary. Some things we just don't let out. We don't have those conversations in public - it's a respect thing.

"If Rodgers was playing MVP football like he did before, he could say all these things and get away with it, but you have to know where you are in your career."

Rodgers suggested in his appearance on The Pat McAfee Show that the prospect of being benched had never been mentioned during recent conversations with McCarthy.

He accused McCarthy of snoring during meetings and rebuffing Rodgers' suggestions that he needed to make more of an effort of connecting with the Steelers' defensive players.

Rodgers added that the "final straw" came during half-time of a game when McCarthy closed a team talk by shouting 'one, two, three, Packers!'.

Rodgers and McCarthy spent 13 seasons together with the Packers from 2006-2018, reaching the playoffs nine times and winning one Super Bowl. They were reunited this past offseason when the Steelers hired McCarthy following the departure of Mike Tomlin.

"I'm not sure what's next for Aaron Rodgers. I think he will figure out that for himself over the next handful of months, or whatever his particular process is," said Super Bowl champion and Sky Sports NFL expert Ndamukong Suh.

"But I want to go back to what Jason [Bell] said in the way that you handle your business, especially from the perspective of a star. There's a way you go about handling things.

"Those things should be handled behind closed doors before trying to get ahead of the story - on either side. Have a conversation, have an understanding, and then go from there and address it.

"Going out to the media and doing all of these different things, The Pat McAfee Show, it's great for them and great for ESPN, but it's not the proper way I would want to handle that particular scenario."

Responding to Rodgers' comments, McCarthy admitted to his "embarrassing" moment when mentioning the Packers during half-time of their defeat to the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 11.

Steelers president gives McCarthy his "100 per cent" backing

Steelers president Art Rooney II defended McCarthy on Thursday in an interview with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, insisting he supports him "100 per cent".

"I just want to say that I have 100 per cent confidence in Mike McCarthy and I expect he'll be our coach this season, next season and beyond," Mr Rooney II told the Post-Gazette.

"The big thing, what happened this week, is insubordination can't be tolerated in any organization. When you start getting ultimatums, you can't live with that. There's maybe a time and place after the season if he wanted to kind of unload.

"He talks about wanting to be a good teammate, but you don't do that to your teammates a couple days before the game, that's for sure."

Rooney II underlined his belief that events in the locker room should be kept within the locker room, and downplayed Rodgers' comments regarding concerns for McCarthy's health.

The Steelers are 6-4 as they prepare to face the Denver Broncos (8-2) on Black Friday.

Omani sports journalist Issa Said, who covers Asian competitions, claimed on social media that what happened to Hattab was "due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus".

"He underwent a medical examination after the match and was not intoxicated, contrary to what has been circulating."

In their statement on the match, which was played in Asia's second tier continental competition, the Syrian Football Association backed Hattab.

"Following an assessment of his health, it has been confirmed - contrary to various claims circulating on social media - that the reports regarding his situation are entirely unfounded," they wrote.

Icelander Alexandersson, 44, has only been in charge of Rosenborg since June but has already emerged as the front-runner for the Swansea job.

The Norwegian top-flight club were in danger of relegation when he was appointed, but are fourth with just three games remaining in the season, which concludes in mid-December.

"I can confirm that there is strong interest from Swansea," Alexandersson told Norsk rikskringkasting AS ahead of Saturday's crucial match against Molde, who are just one place behind Rosenborg in the Eliteserien table.

"I have heard from them (Swansea). I've never been in this situation before. Even just that is a bit overwhelming. I have strong emotions towards Rosenborg and particularly the players and the staff that I am working with, so that part is a bit difficult.

"But the interest itself from a club in England [sic] which I have said before, it is my dream to be a coach in English football.

"That in itself is something I find a bit interesting.

"I have no other plans than that I will be standing here tomorrow and hold training, have meetings and preparations ahead of Saturday's match, and be standing at the match on Saturday.

"That is what I can say now, because what has happened has happened very fast. And the last 24 hours I have only had focus on Rosenborg. I have had talks with (Rosenborg sporting director Alfred) Finnbogason, so I am only focusing on Saturday's match."

Alexandersson previously worked for another Norwegian side, Brann, but was sacked earlier this year after 15 months in charge.

While Alexandersson admits he is unsure whether Swansea have made an official approach to Rosenborg for him, he did confirm he had spoken to the Welsh club.

When asked if he had been offered the Swansea job, Alexandersson replied: "Well, I cannot comment on that because Rosenborg and Swansea... I don't think there are negotiations even, I don't know what Alfred is saying about it, so I cannot comment.

It is them who have come to me and that is of course a great honour to be the one they are hunting for. It is both ways.

item.title: 5 tips to maximize rewards and avoid debt this holiday shopping season
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Listicle with limited depth on a financial topic

Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.

But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.

Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.

Make a plan and a budget

First, map out your holiday shopping plans and set a realistic budget for spending. Who are you shopping for? How much are you planning to spend on gifts? What other expenses should you factor into your holiday budget?

These are all good questions to help you set expectations and prevent impulse buys that can lead to overspending.

A spreadsheet is a great way to keep track of spending and budgeting. You can simply insert your budget into a premade template or write it down on paper. If you already know what you plan to buy, insert links to the sales pages so you know how much it will cost.

While adjusting and finalizing your budget, remember to factor in additional costs due to extra gatherings, like larger grocery and dining expenses.

Utilize credit card perks and statement credits

One of the best things about rewards cards is that they often come with perks to help you save money.

Before making your holiday purchases, check whether your credit cards offer statement credits or other benefits that could help you save money.

For example, comes with an up to $75 quarterly statement credit (up to $300 annually) Lululemon credit that can be used at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) or online after enrollment. This is a great way to maximize purchases on clothing, yoga gear or other accessories.

Or, if you have a frequent jet-setter in your life, you can use a credit card’s Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit to cover their application fee of up to $120.

Statement credits aren't the only card benefits worth checking before you shop. For an expensive electronic device or other high-value gift, purchase protection or extended warranty coverage are other useful perks.

Don’t ignore shopping portals

We talk a lot about shopping portals during this time of year. That's because skipping them is essentially leaving money on the table.

By doing your online holiday shopping through a portal, you can earn bonus points or cash back at a massive number of online retailers. Most of the major U.S. airlines have shopping portals to help you earn additional miles on every eligible purchase, or you can use third-party portals such as Rakuten to earn cash back or Amex Membership Rewards or Bilt Points.

We suggest using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for each online purchase. That way, you don’t have to sift through each portal’s offers individually.

No matter where you shop, review any Amex Offers, Chase Offers or Citi Merchant Offers available on your cards. They vary by cardmember, and often stack with your card's standard rewards plus a shopping portal. Some require activation or enrollment before making a purchase.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

Use cash-back credit cards

We’re big fans of points and miles at The Points Guy — and for good reason. Points and miles can reduce the cost of future travel, but cash-back cards may be more useful if you want rewards to offset your holiday expenses directly.

A flat-rate cash-back card such as the (see rates and fees) is an easy way to earn rewards no matter where you shop since it offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase and another 1% cash back when you pay your bill. Redeeming those rewards as a statement credit helps reduce the size of January's bill.

The (see rates and fees) is another great option that earns at least 1.5% back on every purchase.

Related: Best cash-back credit cards

Take advantage of financing options

Paying your statement balance in full is generally best, but some rewards credit cards offer a 0% introductory annual percentage rate period on new purchases. That can give you time to pay for a planned expense without interest as long as you have a plan to pay it off completely before the introductory period ends.

Another option is to use one of the financing options some credit card issuers offer. Amex Plan It® and Chase Pay Over Time after purchase may allow eligible cardmembers to divide qualifying purchases of $100 or more into fixed monthly payments, generally with a fixed monthly fee instead of interest.

You’ll almost always save money using these programs compared to paying interest over time.

Related: Chase Pay Over Time and My Chase Loan: Should you opt in?

Bottom line

Holiday shopping doesn't have to derail your budget. By planning ahead, using the right rewards cards and taking advantage of statement credits and shopping portals, you can make your spending more rewarding without buying more than you can afford.

The key is to prioritize your budget over earning points, miles or cash back. After all, the value of those rewards can quickly disappear if you're carrying a balance and paying interest.

item.title: A Proven Way to Keep Teachers in Needy Schools is Losing Ground
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: clear reporting, useful vocabulary, and learning value

A Proven Way to Keep Teachers in Needy Schools is Losing Ground

Educators are more likely to leave disadvantaged schools because they’re more challenging to teach in. Extra pay for teachers in those schools can help address this problem.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

States and school districts all across the country face the same problem: Teachers are far more likely to leave high-poverty schools, creating constant churn that hurts students from low-income families.

This pattern shows up literally everywhere I can find data: Alaska, Florida, Missouri, New York City, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Virginia, Wisconsin, and Washington state.

Many challenges in education are hard to understand and difficult to solve. This is not one of them. Educators are more likely to leave disadvantaged schools because they’re more challenging to teach in. Extra pay for teachers in those schools can help address this problem and create a more stable workforce.

But only 12 states have such pay incentives, according to a recent analysis by the National Council on Teacher Quality. The number has actually declined in recent years. “States [are] ignoring this as a possible policy lever to improve teacher effectiveness and to attract and retain more great teachers where we really need them,” says Heather Peske, president of NCTQ.

This problem is long-standing. In Missouri, for instance, in every single year since at least 2009, far more teachers left the state’s highest-poverty schools, often at twice the rate of more affluent ones. Or consider New York City, the country’s largest school system, which is highly stratified by economic need. The city’s most disadvantaged schools lost nearly 1 in 6 teachers in 2024; better-off schools lost just 1 in 12.

In high-poverty schools, constant and cumulative churn means more inexperienced teachers who struggle to manage a classroom. For administrators, all the turnover means it’s difficult to sustain new initiatives or a strong school culture. In recent years, more teachers have left the classroom overall, exacerbating existing challenges in high-needs schools.

Fortunately, there is a solution: extra pay. A Dallas program, for instance, paid teachers between $8,000 and $14,000 (adjusted for inflation) to work in struggling schools. This helped bring in more experienced and effective teachers, researchers found. Alongside a series of other reforms, student achievement rose substantially. Once the extra pay ended, though, teacher turnover rose and test scores fell.

Studies in North Carolina, Florida, San Francisco, Tennessee, Texas, and Washington have also found that pay bumps or bonuses make the school more appealing for outside applicants or help keep existing teachers. “We do see pretty clearly that they work,” says Christopher Redding, a University of Florida education professor who has studied teacher turnover in the state.

As the NCTQ report shows, however, such salary incentives remain rare at the state level. Even when they do exist, the extra pay is typically too small to fully close turnover gaps between needy and advantaged schools.

So why is this research-supported idea so uncommon?

Well, extra pay for educators in high-needs schools costs money and is competing against a bevy of other priorities. And there is no strong political constituency for this. Parents in those schools do not have lobbyists, and school district leaders may prefer to get extra money directly, which often does not translate into higher teacher pay. When salary incentives are put in place, they may be cut in tight budget times.

Politically influential teachers unions have been skeptical of pay incentives. “Bonuses for teaching certain subjects or working in hard-to-staff schools may help attract educators, but they are not a substitute for addressing the underlying challenges facing public education: inadequate resources, support, and working conditions,” National Education Association President Princess Moss said in a statement. “Our goal should be to make every school a place where educators want to work.”

A spokesperson for the American Federation of Teachers, the country’s other large educator union, said AFT is open to salary incentives, pointing to the union contract in Philadelphia. It allows the district to pay bonuses of up to $5,000 for teachers in certain hard-to-staff schools.

Arthur Steinberg, the head of the Philadelphia union, told me this idea came from management as a way to stabilize schools that were constantly losing teachers. It’s not the approach the union would have preferred. “All of our teachers are underpaid, so our initial reaction was: Pay everybody,” he said. The union accepted the incentives as part of the give and take in negotiation. “We were able to secure some other wins in exchange for this,” Steinberg said. He declined to say whether the union would back this measure in future contract negotiations.

States with weaker teachers unions are more likely to have pay incentives for high-poverty schools, though plenty of states with weak unions don’t.

It is more common for large school districts to offer such incentives but they tend to be small in size and have limited reach. Much of the turnover gap is about differences across districts — Philadelphia versus its more advantaged suburbs, for instance — rather than within a single district.

To step back, the reason why these large teacher turnover gaps exist is because low- and high-income students often don’t go to school together.Policymakers could address this through economic integration, effectively limiting the number of highly disadvantaged schools where teachers are reluctant to work. Or they could make sure any disadvantaged schools are staffed by relatively stable teacher workforces using the proven lever of teacher pay bumps.

If policymakers don’t pursue either option, no one should be surprised by the consequences.…

item.title: Texas Sports Academy, Tied to AI-Driven Alpha School, is Texas’ Biggest Voucher Recipient So Far
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail, and learning value

Texas Sports Academy, Tied to AI-Driven Alpha School, is Texas’ Biggest Voucher Recipient So Far

Students at Texas Sports Academy, which schedules two hours of academics a day, have received $6.5 million in voucher payouts.

The biggest recipient of Texas’ new school voucher program so far is a sports academy connected to Alpha School, the artificial intelligence-driven private school chain that the state’s education board rejected for a charter school last year.

Texas Sports Academy, which calls itself an “elite sports academy built for serious student-athletes,” had received $6.5 million in voucher dollars as of Oct. 30, according to the Texas Comptroller’s online dashboard. That’s more than twice the amount received by the second-largest recipient, San Antonio-based Cornerstone Christian Schools, which had gotten roughly $2.8 million.

The disclosure comes a little more than a year after the State Board of Education voted 10-3 to reject Alpha leaders’ bid to open a publicly funded charter school. Board members raised concerns about the company’s use of AI to teach, about students’ screen time and about the large test-score gains Alpha leaders presented. Texas Sports Academy, which has several schools across the state in addition to a virtual campus, is one of numerous institutions across the country connected to Alpha.

But Alpha’s rejection by the SBOE did not prevent it from participating in the voucher program, which allows families to receive state funding for use at private schools and for home schooling. As of September, the chain had roughly quadrupled its Texas private schools in the state to more than 30 virtual and in-person campuses, and most were accepted into the voucher program, an investigation by The Texas Tribune and ProPublica found.

Alpha’s model has students complete core academics online in two hours a day using AI software, a tool the state’s education commissioner, Mike Morath, and his agency have helped get into at least three public school districts this year. At Texas Sports Academy, an AI tutor “guides students through each lesson,” according to the school’s website, a setup that it says “leaves the rest of the day free for sports training, developing life skills, pursuing passions, and just being a kid.”

After a couple hours of academics, the rest of the day is filled with various sports classes, such as soccer training, speed and agility training, and strength training, according to a sample student schedule. On Fridays at 3:30 p.m., an hour can be set aside for NBA watch parties.

The figures are public on a dashboard that outgoing Texas Comptroller Don Huffines said Friday his office is in the process of expanding. In a news release, Huffines said the expansion is intended to increase “insight into how TEFA funds are being used while maintaining protections for student and family privacy.” TEFA stands for Texas Education Freedom Accounts, the program’s formal name.

Other top recipients included First Baptist Academy, which received almost $2 million; Yeshiva Torat Emet, a Jewish school in Houston which received nearly $1.6 million; and The Christian School at Castle Hills which received a little more than $1.5 million.

Texas lawmakers, led by Gov. Greg Abbott, approved the voucher program in 2025. It gives families public funds to help pay for their children’s private school tuition, roughly $10,500, and up to $2,000 for home-schooling expenses.

The program also covers a wide range of approved educational expenses, like private tutoring and school supplies. The comptroller’s dashboard shows that Amazon was by far the largest private vendor, receiving $12.3 million. The next largest, Rainbow Resource Center, Inc., received $2.3 million.

Lexi Churchill contributed to this report.

item.title: Burnham says UK net migration now under 'sufficient' control
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on UK net migration, with concrete details and useful vocabulary.

Burnham says UK net migration now under 'sufficient' control

Andy Burnham said he believes there is now a "sufficient degree of control" of net migration in the UK after it fell to 77,000 in the year to the end of June.

The prime minister said the country is "getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see" but added that there was more work to do.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said it is the lowest recorded net migration estimate since 1997, excluding the coronavirus pandemic.

The Conservatives said the fall was "mainly a result of changes" they made in government, while Reform UK said the figures were "no cause for celebration".

- UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated, according to the ONS.

In the previous 12 months, UK net migration was recorded as 204,000. It peaked at 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The 77,000 net migration figure released on Thursday comes more than 16 years after former Conservative leader David Cameron pledged to cut it to below 100,000 before he came to power in 2010.

Speaking to broadcasters, Burnham said: "These figures begin to answer what the public has been saying, we want to see much greater control over the system.

"I'm not going to say all of the work is done and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally, as a country, getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

It was put to Burnham that some people may argue this was a "benefit of Brexit", in light of his desire to explore closer ties with the European Union.

Asked if freedom of movement should be up for discussion as part of the UK's future relationship with the EU, Burnham said in his reply: "I don't think you can say that Brexit did anything other than weaken control of immigration in this country."

The ONS said net migration had "fallen to levels not typically seen since the 1990s".

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

A fall had been expected because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp argued the Conservatives should receive credit for the decrease in net migration.

He added: "We now need to go even further with an annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels.

"British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour's high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesman Paul Kohler said Britain faces "serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage welcomed the drop in numbers, but said he was concerned about "a lot of high skilled big tax paying people" leaving the UK and being replaced by people "who are paying far less in tax".

Meanwhile, his party's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said the fall "came about solely because I went to see Rishi Sunak" in 2023 whilst an immigration minister in the Conservative former prime minister's government.

Jenrick, who defected to Reform earlier this year, told the BBC: "I threatened to resign unless he made a series of changes. He did".

"And as a result of those changes to the immigration system, we've got where we are today".

But he added that the changes "didn't go as far as I wanted to," adding this had been behind his resignation from the Tory government a few days later.

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and asylum seekers is not a measure of success."

Additional reporting by Thomas Mason

item.title: Mandelson kept shares as ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth look at a conflict of interest involving a former ambassador, with substantial detail and context.

Mandelson kept shares as ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show

Lord Mandelson still held shares in his lobbying company eight months after becoming US ambassador, despite government concens about conflicts of interest, newly released documents show.

The peer was sacked as ambassador last year by Sir Keir Starmer following revelations about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This 85-page release is the third since MPs voted to publish documents aiming to reveal behind-the scenes-discussions about how he was appointed to the role.

The documents were previously withheld due to the Metropolitan Police investigation into allegations Lord Mandelson had passed market-sensitive government information to Epstein.

Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as head of the Foreign Office by Sir Keir Starmer during the scandal when it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The newly released documents highlight that Lord Mandelson was able to keep his shares in Global Counsel, the lobbying company he co-founded, while serving as ambassador to Washington.

They reveal civil servants' concerns about the risk of perceived conflict of interest.

But selling the shares was clearly not a condition of him taking up the role.

Part of that is because of the desire in Sir Keir's government at the time to have Lord Mandelson in Washington as quickly as possible.

That is exemplified in an email from Sir Olly, saying a process to police Mandelson's conflicts of interest could be "up and running in a light touch way".

Another factor is selling shares in a private company like Global Counsel, which advised high-profile clients including Chinese-owned TikTok, US tech firm Palantir and pharmaceutical firm GSK. requires finding a new buyer or selling them back to the company.

But the documents also reveal Lord Mandelson had not sold his shares back to Global Counsel because their offer was not the "fair value". Another attempt to sell to a different buyer fell through.

The result was Mandelson kept his shares, and while in office tried to set up a meeting between Global Counsel and a key Donald Trump advisor, as well as taking the firm's advice on a speech on Britain's role in the world.

Lord Mandelson remained a shareholder until February 2026, the same month the company went into administration.

Emails about his dealings with his Washington counterparts show a close relationship, with one message from an unnamed White House official in April 2025 telling Lord Mandelson his label as the "Prince of Darkness" could not be "farther from the truth".

Ahead of a speech he was due to give on Britain's role "in the age of Trump", documents show him seeking advice from a Global Counsel employee in August 2025, during his time as ambassador.

The exchange contains feedback from an unnamed Global Counsel director, who suggested he should use "warmer language" about China and tone down "parts of your apologia of the Trump administration".

The director warned: "Scepticism of [the Trump administration] is now so deep â at least in the public policy-interested world outside government â that it would be counterproductive/unpersuasive if you came across as having drunk the Kool Aid."

Lord Mandelson responds to say he would water down his language, and in another email tries to arrange an "under the radar" lunch meeting to discuss China and trade between a GC employee and someone from the US President's Council of Economic Advisers.

On the domestic front, Lord Mandelson also sent texts to Sir Keir's then chief of staff Morgan McSweeney in September 2025 offering advice on a cabinet reshuffle.

He suggested moving Darren Jones to lead the science and technology department as a way to "solve your Darren issue", although McSweeney did not respond until after the reshuffle decisions had been made, with Jones given a newly-created role as chief secretary to the prime minister.

Lord Mandelson has yet to comment on the most recent release of papers relating to his appointment.

He has repeatedly let it be known he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

No charges have been made. A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC: "Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing."

Speaking to journalists in the Downing Street garden following the release of the documents, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would address culture change for Westminster as part of his 10 year plan, which he said will be published next month.

He said: "I've come back in as something of an outsider into the system and I see a lot of things that I think need to change to improve the political culture of this country and to strengthen the public interests when it comes to all of these issues."

Security minister Dan Jarvis told MPs: "The government recognises that action needs to be taken in response to the issues raised by Mandelson's appointment."

He said action had already been taken to strengthen the vetting and appointments process, including strengthening the management of conflicts of interest.

Future appointments will not be made before security clearance has been granted, he said, adding that review by Sir Adrian Fulford of vetting procedures was nearing completion.

A separate review by Sir Anthony Finkelstein into use of personal messaging services including WhatsApp and Signal for business purposes is expected to be published in January next year.

item.title: Trump administration proposes new tariffs on goods from major U.S. trading partners
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Detailed analysis of proposed tariffs by the Trump administration, with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Trump administration proposes new tariffs on goods from major U.S. trading partners

President Trump's new proposed tariffs are already meeting pushback from Democrats and some free trade advocates.

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:

The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on goods from 14 of the U.S.'s biggest trading partners, including Japan, the EU and China. It's arguing that these new tariffs fight other countries' unfair trade practices, but it's not clear that they will actually do that.

For more, we have NPR White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben. Danielle, what did the White House outline yesterday?

DANIELLE KURTZLEBEN, BYLINE: Well, it's new proposed tariffs on goods from major trading partners - the ones you mentioned, and also South Korea and Cambodia, for example. And the rates could go as high as 40% on Chinese goods, also 35% on goods from Vietnam and 20 or 25% on goods from other countries. They're also proposing additional tariffs on sugar and aircrafts from Brazil, and that would add to previous tariffs the U.S. imposed there.

MARTÍNEZ: When could these plans actually become real?

KURTZLEBEN: Well, they could go into effect within a couple of months. That's what U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said yesterday. Now, as for what the rates will be, well, that's still unclear, and that's because for each country, excepting those additional tariffs on Brazil, the White House has two rates they've listed - a proposed rate and a deal rate. To give an example, the tariff on China could be 20%. That's the deal rate. But depending in part on how ongoing discussions go, the rates on Chinese goods could go as high as 40%.

MARTÍNEZ: Forty percent. Now, yeah, the Supreme Court struck down some of Trump's earlier tariffs. So how is the White House legally justifying these new ones?

KURTZLEBEN: Well, these are being implemented under a law known for short as Section 301, which is meant to counter other countries' unfair trade practices. And so here the White House is alleging that these other countries have what's called structural excess capacity in various manufactured goods. And the administration has described this as when another country has policies that cause a good to be overproduced, which then distorts a global market for that good. And so those practices, according to the administration, can include all sorts of things, like labor practices, subsidies and tax breaks.

Now, the administration imposed other sweeping 301 tariffs earlier this year, and there's a lawsuit in process challenging those, with the key argument being that those tariffs were just way broader than the 301 law calls for.

MARTÍNEZ: Now, you mentioned a lawsuit. Could these new tariffs face similar legal challenges?

KURTZLEBEN: You know, they could. We'll see what happens. But I talked to Sara Albrecht. She's chairman and CEO of the nonpartisan Liberty and Justice Center (ph), which filed that lawsuit against those earlier tariffs. And she said these new tariffs are not being used the way 301 tariffs are supposed to.

SARA ALBRECHT: It is a negotiating tactic. That is not what tariffs, in a broad sense, are supposed to be. Like, you can do that on a country-by-country basis if they're addressing a specific problem, not just general, hey, we want better trade deals.

KURTZLEBEN: In addition, both she and other trade experts say they think the White House is just proposing these new tariffs as a way to replace the sweeping tariffs the Supreme Court struck down earlier this year.

MARTÍNEZ: Now, we all just found out how unpopular these tariffs were in the midterm elections. So how are these new tariffs landing politically?

KURTZLEBEN: Well, we've heard some real pushback from congressional Democrats. Richard Neal, top House Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, said in a statement, quote, "Trump is putting everything from family budgets to our national security at risk to keep his tariff scheme in place."

Now, congressional Republicans have been quieter, and this does come a few weeks after they lost dozens of seats in the election, which is widely attributed, in large part, to high prices, and tariffs do cause higher prices.

MARTÍNEZ: All right, that's NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben. Danielle, thanks a lot.

KURTZLEBEN: Of course.

item.title: Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., shares why he opposes Trump's proposed tariffs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Opinion piece on the impact of tariffs, offering a clear stance and useful economic vocabulary.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., shares why he opposes Trump's proposed tariffs

NPR's A Martinez speaks with Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine about the Democrat's opposition to President Trump's new tariffs.

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:

All right. Let's go now to one of the lawmakers who's been trying to fight the president's tariffs in Congress. Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia backed multiple bills meant to curb or refund the administration's tariffs, including legislation that would constrain the president's ability to impose new tariffs at all.

Senator, happy Thanksgiving. Thanks for joining us on Turkey Day.

TIM KAINE: A, very glad to be with you. And our Turkey Day is going to cost about 6% more than it cost last year...

MARTÍNEZ: (Laughter).

KAINE: ...Partly because of tariffs. So this is a good topic.

MARTÍNEZ: Well, let's get into that. So the president says the objective is to counter unfair foreign trade practices. What's your view of that rationale?

KAINE: Well, in the big picture, what the president has said is this tariff strategy applied everywhere is going to increase manufacturing jobs in the United States. To the contrary, manufacturing jobs in the United States have declined during President Trump's second term. He also said it would reduce our trade deficit. The trade deficit has increased during President Trump's second term. So neither of the goals that he has have been achieved by his tariff strategy. And one of the things he promised to do - bring prices down - has been dramatically affected in the negative way you saw the inflation numbers yesterday. We're seeing dramatic inflation driven by tariffs in the Iran war. So this is an economic strategy that is a big failure.

MARTÍNEZ: You mentioned manufacturing jobs are not happening in the way that we were told they would happen. But how do you square that with the Steelworkers Union who says that the new tariffs are long overdue?

KAINE: There are particular sectors that like them. I mean, the steel industry likes more steel production in the U.S. But overall, if you look at manufacturing, generally, manufacturing jobs are down. They were up during the Biden administration. They're down during the Trump administration with President Trump saying that the tariffs were going to cause this big manufacturing renaissance.

MARTÍNEZ: So I mentioned your efforts in the Senate to fight the president's tariffs. What is your strongest argument for passing legislation to stop the president from imposing these particular tariffs?

KAINE: So there's a broad argument, and then there's kind of a narrow focused one. So here's the broad one. The Constitution gives tariff power to Congress, not the president. And Congresses of both parties, in my view, have made mistakes over decades in handing off this power, delegating it to the president and allowing the president to impose tariffs on his own. Just to allow one person to impose taxes is not a good idea. And so there are a variety of strategies. I - we - I did work with Senator Paul of Kentucky, and we led the effort against the president's use of the IEEPA statute to impose tariffs. The Supreme Court ultimately struck down...

MARTÍNEZ: International Emergency Economic Powers Act, yeah.

KAINE: That's right, yeah. And the Supreme Court ultimately struck down any imposition of tariffs under that statute. But we're looking at the remaining statutes that Congress has sort of handed the power to the president in one of two ways. You can either repeal those statutes and eliminate any presidential ability to impose tariffs. Or recognizing that presidents sometimes need to move quick - quicker than Congress can - you could allow the president to impose tariffs for a limited period of time, say 60 or 90 days, but those tariffs would expire unless Congress affirmatively validates them and continues them.

So those are some of the legal solutions that are on the table. And with Democratic majorities, I think we have a very good chance of getting some of these bills to President Trump's desk.

MARTÍNEZ: You have 56 U.S. senators in - next year. What's the likelihood that you're going to get enough Republicans that share your view? You mentioned Rand Paul, but you're going to need more if you want to pass legislation that the president can't veto.

KAINE: We will. We - my prediction is we're going to get enough Republican votes in the aftermath of the election, which was really a repudiation of tariffs and the war. We'll get enough Republican votes to put tariff bills on President Trump's desk. Now, here comes the next challenge. If he vetoes those bills, would we have enough to have a two-thirds vote in both Houses to override his veto? That's a - more of an uphill climb. But we're going to test that. We're going to put bills on his desk, dramatically limiting his tariff powers to try to help Americans' pocketbooks. And then we'll say to him, if you veto this bill, you're just going to hurt people. So why don't you just sign it?

MARTÍNEZ: What message do you think these new tariffs are sending to U.S. trading partners? I mean, it's been a few years of, you know, going back and forth on tariffs.…

item.title: Morocco’s Royal Industrial Vision: A Global Strategic Opportunity
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Exploration of Morocco's industrial vision, with useful economic and political vocabulary.

Morocco is among the last remaining democratic monarchies in the world; this feature is also one of Morocco’s most innovative aspects. King Mohammed VI came to the throne in 1999 and, ever since, has proven to be a leader in social, legal, and infrastructural reforms alongside his constitutional reforms of 2011. Under his leadership, Morocco has been transforming into a modernized, sophisticated economy, one now increasingly taking its place as a leader in African investment, manufacturing, technology, and energy, while strengthening its place as a bridge between the EU, Africa and Asia.

The economic and industrial development now taking shape across Morocco comes on the heels of socioeconomic transition from a primarily agricultural society to a middle-class industrialized one. Morocco has, for example, become a leading auto supplier and global producer of phosphates, primarily for fertilizer, witnessing a boom in GDP growth from $46.3 billion in 1999 to over $125 billion by 2025. As part of the changes, foreign investors have moved direct investments into the nation as well, preparing the way for hosting the 2030 World Cup, for critical minerals diversification, and for North Africa’s security needs.

This month, King Mohammed VI announced a new iteration of his development plan for the Kingdom, the Defense Industry Facilitation and Acceleration Agency. The agency will be dedicated to mobilizing private investment for defense and for developing advanced technologies like drones, autonomous systems, cyberdefense, and artificial intelligence. Morocco also announced that 40 percent of the equipment needs of its military would come from domestic production by 2035.

The amplification of Morocco’s industrial sector matters significantly to its neighbor, Europe, and the many African countries that rely on Morocco as a supplier and trade facilitator. Ali Seddiki, the head of Morocco’s investment and export promotion agency, already announced that 65% of its revenue is expected to come from exports. The royal strategy, named the ‘Morocco Offer’ is an ambitious roadmap to build a national defense and security industrial base for Morocco, but it also comes as American, Asian, and European businesses have become more involved in the domestic Moroccan economy. In fact, from 2024 to 2025, Morocco saw a 91 percent increase in foreign direct investment in its economy.

King Mohammed VI’s plan, and his consistency in delivering economic growth, forecasts another step in Morocco’s standing as a leading African country. By 2035, the country may look much different than it does now, and with the addition of heightened levels of defense spending, an additional security sector could expand across Northern Africa. Through the Morocco Offer, the nation plans to create around 50,000 direct and indirect jobs and create new industrial defense zones in Benguerir and Benslimane using a 4-billion-dirham contribution from the Hassan II Fund for Economic and Social Development.

Since King Mohammed VI took the throne, his leadership and reformation have carried the nation into a position of leadership for Africa and for the region. In the midst of social reforms, the King has maintained a steady vision of economic reinvigoration through trade, onshoring manufacturing, and attracting international investment. In so doing, Morocco has become a clear competitor to East Asian made goods, offering an attractive choice for businesses seeking to diversify their supply chains.

For a country like the United States, which has made diversification a core concern under the Trump administration, Morocco’s position in Africa, near Europe, and its economic independence from China make it a prime candidate for American investment. King Mohammed VI’s strategy subtly acknowledges this international need for diversification, and the new focus placed on building a defense industry shows that Morocco could offer both quality weapons systems and the ability to replenish them at scale.

Morocco already offers a long slew of strengths for international market competitiveness, with impacts that extend all the way to East Asia. From political continuity, established relationships with Western economies, proximity to European markets, access to African markets, and a growing record of attracting international manufacturing investment, Morocco presents a compelling case. Its existing automotive and aerospace industries further provide a foundation for advancing specialized production. The strategy is poised to incentivize American defense companies to look to nearshore their supply chains across the Atlantic, particularly when looking at the impending threat from China.

King Mohammed VI’s strategy is not new; it follows a top-down centrally planned industrial policy, paired with careful reforms. These are tied to a clear national vision, and the King has positioned Morocco as a politically stable manufacturing hub, growing regional actor, and independent player in the growth of global supply chains. Morocco has made itself known as open to investment capital without depending on any single partner, and is among the few African countries operating without the constraints of Chinese influence. And this strategic step into the defense sector will move Morocco from simply supplying foreign markets to building a sovereign industrial base. The strategy is one that can supply its own military, serve as a regional security anchor, and export to partners across the Atlantic.…

item.title: Is the Philippines Isolated Within ASEAN?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of the Philippines' position within ASEAN, with geopolitical vocabulary and context.

The Philippines has been forceful in asserting its territorial claims in the South China Sea, at times resorting to legal means. In response to its escalating confrontation with China over these claims, Manila has deepened defense cooperation with its treaty ally, the United States. In adopting a foreign and security policy anchored in the U.S. alliance within the framework of U.S.-China rivalry, the Philippines stands apart from other ASEAN member states.

This July also marked the tenth anniversary of the South China Sea Arbitral Tribunal Award issued by the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in 2016, a case originally brought by the Philippines. Fourteen countries, including the Philippines, issued a joint statement reaffirming the award’s legal binding force. The other ASEAN states, however, did not join that statement.

Skirmishes between the Philippines and China have also been frequent: disputes over the drawing of baselines around Scarborough Shoal, and harassment by coast guard vessels and naval ships near Second Thomas Shoal, among other incidents. In June, China imposed sanctions on Philippine Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro and members of his immediate family, and during a telephone conversation this November, Beijing also criticized the conduct of a number of Philippine politicians. The gap between the Philippines and other ASEAN members in terms of their distance from China over the South China Sea issue appears to be widening.

That said, it should be noted that other ASEAN claimant states have also experienced their own friction with China. In March of this year, Vietnam protested China’s land reclamation and facility construction in the Paracel Islands, demanding an immediate halt. Malaysia, too, announced that it was monitoring Chinese Coast Guard (CCG) vessels transiting within its exclusive economic zone (EEZ) off Sarawak, and stated that it would continue to maintain its own presence in those waters. While there are differences in how these countries respond to the PCA arbitration award, all of them have experienced various forms of friction with China as positions remain at an impasse.

The deepening of ties between the Philippines and Vietnam is also worth noting. In June, Vietnamese President To Lam visited Manila and elevated the relationship to an “Enhanced Strategic Partnership,” signing a memorandum on defense cooperation. Vietnam did not join the joint statement marking the tenth anniversary of the PCA arbitration award, but on the same day the statement was issued, it released its own separate statement calling for a peaceful resolution in conformity with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). This has been interpreted as an implicit endorsement of the PCA arbitration award.

In other words, while the U.S.-Philippines alliance does set the Philippines apart within ASEAN, the Philippines and the other South China Sea claimant states are hardly at opposite extremes on the issue. Moreover, the Philippines has avoided aggressively pressing its own positions on the South China Sea within ASEAN forums, prioritizing its role as a consensus-builder when it holds the chair. The South China Sea section of the Joint Communiqué of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in July 2026 showed almost no change in wording from the previous year.

Even as tensions have deepened, China and the Philippines also appear to be avoiding a decisive deterioration in the relationship. As 2026 has progressed, skirmishes have continued, but so has the search for de-escalation, through resumed dialogue, foreign ministers’ meetings, and telephone diplomacy. It is also worth noting that China’s sanctions on the defense minister were directed at an individual rather than at the Philippines as a whole. This can be read as a strategy to exploit divisions within the Philippines over China policy, but it can equally be interpreted as aimed at avoiding further escalation between the two countries.

The Philippines, in short, is not entirely aligned with the West. It is raising tensions with China while avoiding a decisive rupture. And while at a slower pace than other ASEAN states, the Philippines is itself becoming integrated into Chinese-centered supply chain networks. The historical precedents of the Arroyo and Duterte administrations make clear that a government more oriented toward economic ties with China could well produce shifts in China policy.

Defense cooperation between the Philippines and Japan has been strengthening since the first 2+2 meeting in April 2022, through the entry into force of the Japan-Philippines Reciprocal Access Agreement (RAA), bilateral and multilateral joint exercises, capacity-building assistance, and the transfer of defense equipment and technology. For the Philippines, this is part of an effort to secure its own defense by reinforcing partnerships beyond the United States. Nonetheless, the Philippines maintains its channels to China and retains room for flexible policy adjustments in the future. This is a subtly different position from Japan’s, which is struggling even to resume a substantive dialogue with China. If the Philippines-Japan win-win relationship is to be made sustainable, both sides will need the composure to discern clearly where their positions converge and where they differ.

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-26 06:12 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: South Korean Chief Justice’s Impending Impeachment
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Discussion of South Korea's Chief Justice's impending impeachment, with political vocabulary and context.

Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae has been in the limelight since before President Lee Jae-myung became president in June 2025. These days, his name drapes over most news as the ruling Democratic Party (DP) resolved to impeach him during its general meeting on November 20.

“Despite Cho’s violation of the Constitution, we have been restraining ourselves while awaiting the public’s understanding. But now, we cannot further condone his attempt at justifying collaboration with insurrection and distorting history,” Kim Min-seok, the DP leader, said.

Accordingly, the party set up an impeachment task force, planning to submit Cho’s impeachment motion to the National Assembly (NA) in early December. There are a few grounds for the impeachment cited by the DP, but let’s consider three major ones here.

First, on the night of former President Yoon Suk-yeol’s failed self-coup on December 3, 2024, Cho idled by – legally and symbolically. As a bastion of constitutional rule of law and democracy, the Supreme Court failed to counteract Yoon’s unconstitutional declaration of martial law. Rather, the meeting presided over by Cho at the Supreme Court in the early morning hours of December 4, 2024, concluded that “the command and supervision of the judiciary transfers to the martial law commander.” The court decided to “prepare its future steps according to the martial law commander’s instructions and the martial law manual.”

The DP holds that, at a time when even those lacking legal knowledge immediately knew that Yoon’s martial law was unconstitutional in every sense, the Supreme Court reneged on its duty to uphold the constitutional rule of law and protect people’s right to life and property. Cho’s acquiescence to Yoon’s martial law feels all the more chilling in hindsight given how, as per the constitution, the Supreme Court is the final arbiter over court martial cases. It means that, had Yoon’s self-coup succeeded, the Supreme Court under Cho could have – not that it would have, because we would never know – provided legitimacy to Yoon’s martial law.

Second, Cho has been refusing to recommend a new candidate for a Supreme Court justice. Under the constitution, the chief justice recommends a candidate and the president appoints them. And the convention is for the former to coordinate with the latter in advance to agree on the candidate.

There has been an empty justice seat since March 2026, yet Cho delayed recommending a replacement until August. Even then, he did so without consulting President Lee Jae-myung. Former President Yoon packed the Supreme Court with right-leaning justices – eight out of 12 Supreme Court justices were appointed by him, in addition to Cho as chief justice. Lee rejected the recommendation for a more balanced composition, asking for another recommendation. Cho hasn’t budged.

The DP maintains that Cho’s unilateral decision infringes upon the president’s right to appoint personnel and that Cho abandoned his constitutional duty to make the Supreme Court whole for the people to receive fair trials.

On the other hand, Cho argued that “there’s no constitutional ground for the National Assembly and the president to interfere with the procedure for the chief justice’s recommendation.” He went so far as to describe the president’s behavior as “unconstitutional.” Of course, he’s entitled to his opinion, but it’s inappropriate for him to publicly express his personal constitutional interpretation. That’s entirely up to the Constitutional Court, whose sole job is to clear up any ambiguities in the constitution.

Plus, Cho’s public denouncement of the democratically elected president as “unconstitutional” seemed nothing more than the judiciary’s foray into the executive. (Remember that Cho had been thoroughly silent on Yoon’s declaration of martial law – which was palpably unconstitutional from the outset and hence ruled as unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court.) Despite the constitution’s lack of elaboration on the Supreme Court justice nomination, the convention of presidential-judicial consultation has come to reflect the original intention of constitutional legislators. The DP is calling Cho’s decision to snub this convention an example of “judicial elitism,” the judges’ sense of entitlement that they trump the other two branches of the government and the people’s sovereignty represented by elected officials.

The third rationale for impeachment is Cho’s track record of procedural impropriety in criminal justice. In May 2024, ahead of the June presidential snap election, Cho disregarded all procedural regularity and the Supreme Court’s regulations on judicial deliberation to expedite the case against Lee Jae-myung, then the DP’s presidential candidate and odds-on favorite to win the election. The Supreme Court rushed to overturn an appellate court verdict that found Lee innocent; a guilty verdict would have barred him from running for the June election. At the time, all the 10 justices who ruled against Lee were appointed by Yoon, and they did so within nine days, during which they purportedly read all the 70,000 pages of documentation.

For another instance, Cho ignored the special counsel legislation. The Supreme Court should rule on cases indicted by the special counsel within three months of the appellate judgment. Former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo received a 15-year sentence for having aided Yoon’s attempted insurrection at the Seoul High Court. The Supreme Court, however, missed the deadline of August 7 to review the conviction. Instead, it dragged the case until November 19, overturning it in the end to partially acquit him. Eight out of nine justices who supported his partial acquittal were appointed by Yoon or Han himself when the latter was acting president following Yoon’s impeachment.…

item.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Reporting on UK net migration, with useful statistical vocabulary and context.

UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall

- Published

Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.

Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.

- Three charts that show how migration surged and then fell

- Published3 hours ago

- German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds

- Published16 hours ago

- What are the planned changes to immigration rules?

- Published3 November

The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.

The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.

Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".

"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."

This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.

That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.

In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".

Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.

"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."

In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.

As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.

The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.

As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.

Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration".

"This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."

A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

item.title: I Don’t Like Your Tone
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: essential for emotional intelligence and mindfulness

Does this sound familiar? You’ve decided to host a gathering and spent far more time and money on it than you expected. But that’s OK. Because you really wanted to extend yourself, but now you are just a little more frazzled than you wanted to be. But you ignore your difficult feelings and press on.

Or maybe everything has lined up perfectly for your event and then one of your guests arrives and tells you that they forgot to mention that they don’t eat gluten, dairy, meat, beans, fiber, or sugar and now you feel totally unprepared. Or maybe a well-meaning family member says something they think is funny, and you find it hurtful and it makes you want to close down.

Suddenly your perfect event is going sideways and you find yourself looking for a crawlspace to hide in or someone to snap at. These are the moments when mindfulness can help us pause, take a breath, and acknowledge that things aren’t going as planned. Rather than getting swept up in frustration, we can reconnect with our original intention: bringing people together in a welcoming, loving atmosphere.

Social gatherings can give us a rich and wonderful opportunity to strengthen bonds of love and connection. But even the best-laid plans can quickly turn into emotional meltdowns unless we make a point of pausing to recognize when we get caught up in the impossible task of trying to get everything right.

Instead, you can plan a new kind of to-do list. One that puts self-care and the creation of a loving atmosphere as the top priority.

I am usually the person in my family who hosts the celebrations. Yet every year, I seem to get amnesia about how tired, overwhelmed, and irritated I feel by the time the first person gets there.

I go the extra mile to make an overflowing amount of hand crafted food. I take time to create a charming atmosphere. But by the time my guests arrive, I have barely slept in a week and have long forgotten why I wanted to bring everyone together in the first place. Somewhere along the way, my self-imposed expectations had taken over. Instead of being the warm, welcoming host I’d hoped to be, I became the anxious, overburdened kitchen help, desperately trying to keep the food train going.

During a particularly big event when I really tried to outdo myself, a close friend and two family members told me I seemed uptight and terse. And, as if that weren’t enough, they didn’t like my tone!

“You don’t like my TONE? What? How dare you! Ungrateful clods.”

After skulking away in a state of icy fury, my years of mindfulness practice eventually kicked in and a few hundred breaths later I managed to notice how I had lost sight of my heartfelt intention of creating a welcoming haven for love and connection.

Instead, I’d become so focused on getting everything done that I’d turned the gathering into a military operation.

I regularly remind myself how valuable it is when I take a moment to be curious, rather than certain. When I could finally get there, my investigations helped me notice that my shoulders were up and I was holding my breath.

I could feel the tightness in my face every time someone interrupted me with their warm hellos. I could recognize that somewhere along the way, I had lost sight of my true desire to help nourish joy for myself and everyone else.

Expecting ourselves to regulate our emotions perfectly in the middle of a difficult moment is asking a lot.

I needed some space and time to process what had happened before I could do anything other than snap at someone or run away.

Although I was too reactive in the moment to appreciate the honest feedback about my tone, once I had time to step back and reflect, I could recognize and accept, without having to like it, that my tone was sharp, and not in keeping with my intention for the event.

At the same time, looking more closely at my reactions helped me see how worn out I was feeling and that I really needed to offer myself wisdom and self-care.

So what can mindfulness offer us in moments like these?

Mindfulness is an umbrella that contains practices to help calm our nervous system, stabilize the mind and emotions, be more in touch with our bodies and give us ways to practice anchoring our attention in the present.

This may sound boringly obvious, but if you pay attention, you might notice how often your mind swings between thoughts of the past and fears about the future, spending surprisingly little time in the present.

Mindfulness is the encouragement to recognize that the attitude you bring to your moment-by-moment experiences has a great effect on your body’s stress response. You can notice whether being patient leads to greater feelings of peace more than being impatient. Mindfulness attitudes include acceptance, gratitude, and generosity. What do you notice about how it makes you feel to practice these attitudes?

Mindfulness can help you see the importance of non-judgement to help you have a wider view, and to cultivate the possibility of seeing and experiencing the world with fewer biases. Just like any learned skill, it is a practice and is strengthened through repetition.

In my case, it took me a while to see that I was doing things the same way every year, hoping for a different result. Only after several people irritated me with their honesty did I let myself notice whether I might be more uptight than I realized. By recognizing my reactions without judging myself, I could see how I might want to do things differently in the future so I could enjoy the gathering alongside my guests.

But first I had to notice what I was doing in the present, and check in regularly to confirm that I was following through on my intention to put connection above trying to turn my place into a pop-up restaurant.…
