item.title: Kitchen of the Week: An Artful Conversion of a Garage in Bath, England
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique and artistic home transformation

“The customer is always right—and we like to consider the building our client, too. A specialist in lyrical and meticulous period restorations, Patrick, when we first met him in 2015, was living in a mid-19th-century East London apartment that he had entirely freed of its recessed halogen lights, laminate flooring, and other “developer rubbish”: see Reinventing the Past with a Salvage Hunter-Upcycler-Philosopher.

Much has happened since then. Patrick, his wife and business partner, Neri Kamcili, and their two daughters relocated to Bath, England, and have a portfolio that has landed Berdoulat on the House & Garden Top 100 Interior Designers since 2020. They specialize in working with antiques and salvaged materials, a while back they opened a shop below their own living quarters in the heart of Bath (it’s now an online shop). And they recently published a book, The House Rules, too.

They recently moved just outside of Bath and today we’re revisiting part of their former home, a cluster of three conjoined structures that included, in the back, a 19th-century wine and provisions shop that was being used as a garage. “It was looking rather sorry for itself,” says Patrick. “Behind a galvanized roller shutter was just a concrete slab and asbestos-lined ceiling. But matchboarded walls gave a clue to it former use, and on further investigation, we found a photograph taken the morning after the Blitz showing the building with six-over-six sashes and a shopfront.” Join us for a look at the muse house they created—and scroll to the end for a floor plan and glimpse of the building’s past history.

Photography by Berdoulat Studio, unless noted.

The paneling was created from parts of the garage ceiling and a wall that was removed elsewhere in the building: “none was where it is now,” says Patrick. The insulated floor is reclaimed six-inch pine boards bought on eBay and painted Fired Earth’s Burnt Juniper (“discontinued,” notes Patrick, “but similar to Farrow & Ball’s Mahogany and Edward Bulmer’s London Brown”).

The rise-and-fall period lights are from Un Coin Du Passé, a brocante in southeastern France run by friends of Patrick and Neri’s. The walls are painted a Fired Earth blue called Tempest. Photograph by Paul Whitbread.

As for the show stopping double ceramic sink, it was sourced from one of Patrick’s haunts, Norfolk Reclamation and likely came out of a laundry room. It’s raised on a cement plinth to make it a comfortable height. Patrick’s sister gave them the rug.

Floor Plan

The Building, After the Blitz

Before

After

Go to Berdoulat & Breakfast to see the 1748 house in Bath where the family recently lived (with two rooms to rent).

- ‘Mama Mia’ Produce Nick Gilpin’s Stylishly Revived Georgian Manse

item.title: This Low-Profile Roborock Vacuum and Mop Is $500 Off During Black Friday
item.description:

Why it is here: detailed review of a robot vacuum and mop

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

For those who can make room in their budget, the next thing to plan around is space, since the Arc Ultra measures a little over 46 inches across and weighs about 13 pounds, making it a natural match for a larger TV. The biggest drawback is connectivity, since the Arc Ultra has a single HDMI eARC port with no passthrough, which can leave you short on inputs for a console or streaming box, and no optical port.
